Spaced Repetition

Forget, then retrieve — that’s where the learning happens.

What the Research Says

The brain remembers things better when you review them just as you’re about to forget them. Cram everything the night before and it’s gone within a week. Revisit the same material on day one, day three, day seven, day fourteen and it sticks for months. This is the single biggest difference between students who peak in mocks and students who peak in the real exam.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Ebbinghaus (1885)Without revisiting, 50% of what you learn is lost within an hour and 80% within a day.The forgetting curve is real — and steeper than most students realise.
Cepeda et al. (2006)Meta-analysis of 254 studies: spaced practice beat massed practice in 259 out of 271 comparisons.Spacing works across ages, subjects, and skills.
Kang (2016)Optimal gap ≈ 10–20% of the time until the test. For a May exam, that means revisiting material every 3–6 weeks from Year 10.You can plan exactly when to revisit a topic.
Sisti et al. (2007)Neurons form stronger connections during the “almost forgotten” moment of retrieval.Struggling to recall IS the learning, not a sign you’ve failed.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Learn a topic today — read the lesson, watch the video, write notes. Mark it in a diary or app with today’s date.
  2. 2
    Review in 24 hours — do a retrieval practice brain dump, or redo the knowledge check. 5–10 minutes.
  3. 3
    Review again in 3 days — if you got it right yesterday, push the gap. Repeat the retrieval.
  4. 4
    Review again in 7 days — by now the material is consolidating into long-term memory.
  5. 5
    Review again in 2–3 weeks — gap the next review to 14 days, then 30, then 60.
  6. 6
    If you fail a review — reset the schedule. Back to day 1. Don’t skip the reset — it’s the point of the system.
Example 1

Day 1: study the four factors of production (land, labour, capital, enterprise) along with their respective rewards (rent, wages, interest, profit). Day 2: brain-dump all four factors with definitions and rewards from memory, and write one real-world example for each. Day 7: test yourself again, this time adding a sentence explaining how each factor applies to a specific business (for example, a factory’s machinery as capital earning interest for its lender). Day 14: attempt a question asking you to analyse how a firm might respond to a rise in the wage rate — using your factor knowledge cold.

Example 2

After first studying income elasticity of demand (YED), schedule five reviews. By day 7, you should be able to recall not just the formula (% change in QD ÷ % change in income) but also the difference between normal goods (positive YED) and inferior goods (negative YED), and examples of each. By day 30, you should be applying YED to explain why demand for budget own-brand food rises during a recession — a high-mark analysis question on Paper 1.

Common Pitfalls

  • Reviewing too often. If it’s easy, the gap is too short. Make it harder by stretching the interval.
  • Reviewing too late. If you’ve completely forgotten, you’re essentially re-learning from scratch — you lose the benefit of spacing.
  • No written schedule. Spaced repetition works only if you actually do the reviews. Use a calendar, the StudyVault flashcard system, or a simple Leitner box.
  • Skipping resets when you fail. If you couldn’t recall the material, you haven’t learnt it — regardless of how far through the schedule you were.

When to Use This

This is the organising principle of your whole revision year — not a technique you pull out near the exam. From the first lesson of Year 10, log every topic you cover and schedule reviews at 1 day, 3 days, 7 days, 14 days, and 30 days. The StudyVault flashcard system does this automatically via the Leitner method — questions move between five boxes with intervals of 1, 2, 4, 7, and 14 days. When a card comes up, do it. When it doesn’t, don’t.

Deep thinking

Elaborative Interrogation

Ask “why?” and “how?” until the facts become explanations.

What the Research Says

Facts in isolation are fragile. Facts connected by explanations survive. Elaborative interrogation is the habit of asking “why is that true?” and “how does that work?” about every fact you learn — and forcing yourself to answer. The answer doesn’t need to be perfect. The act of trying to answer is what builds the mental connections that turn memorised lists into understood explanations. This is exactly what examiners reward in the ‘explain’, ‘discuss’ and ‘evaluate’ questions.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Pressley et al. (1988)Asking “why?” during reading boosted recall by 40–70% compared to silent reading.Works even when the answer is imperfect.
Dunlosky et al. (2013)Rated “moderate utility” — robust across subjects and ages, especially when applied to new material that builds on existing knowledge.Best for consolidating material you half-know.
Smith & Holliday (2006)Students who self-explained while studying scored significantly higher on transfer questions requiring application.Builds the ability to USE the knowledge, not just recall it.
Chi et al. (1994)Self-explanation was a stronger predictor of understanding than prior knowledge.Even weaker students catch up by explaining to themselves.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Study a chunk of content — a lesson, a paragraph, a key fact. Anything where facts are being introduced.
  2. 2
    After each fact, ask “why?” — why is this true? Why does it matter for sport? Why did the examiner include it?
  3. 3
    Then ask “how?” — how does this connect to the topic? How does it lead to what comes next? How would you explain it to someone else?
  4. 4
    Try to answer out loud or in writing — even if your answer is wrong, the attempt activates deeper processing. Write your answer in the margin.
  5. 5
    Check your answer against the source — does the lesson support your explanation? If not, update it. The correction matters more than the first guess.
  6. 6
    Build chains — once you’ve asked “why?” once, ask it again of your answer. Push until you hit a genuinely fundamental fact. This is where deep understanding forms.
Example 1 — Sportsmanship vs gamesmanship

Fact: sportsmanship means playing within the letter and spirit of the sport. Ask “why does the ‘spirit’ part matter?” — because the rules cannot capture every situation; spirit covers the unwritten norms that make the game fair. Ask “how does gamesmanship differ?” — it follows the letter of the rules (so is technically legal) but deliberately seeks advantage by exploiting the gaps — for example, a Crescent FC player taking an unnecessarily long throw-in to waste time at 1–0. Ask “why is gamesmanship still controversial?” — because it erodes the spirit of the game without breaking the law. That three-step chain is the reasoning structure a 4-mark applied question expects.

Example 2 — Why hosting a major event increases national pride

Fact: hosting a major event can boost national morale. Ask “why?” — because shared media coverage creates a collective experience that citizens identify with, even if they do not attend. Ask “how does that translate into measurable outcomes?” — London 2012 reported a 10% increase in voluntary sport participation in the months following the Games, suggesting the spectacle changed behaviour. Ask “why might that effect fade?” — because without maintained facility investment (as happened in Athens 2004, where venues fell into disrepair), the participation boost disappears. You have just built the evaluation structure the 8-mark extended-response question rewards: positive, evidence, counter-argument, condition.

Common Pitfalls

  • Accepting “I don’t know”. Take a guess. Even a wrong guess activates the processing. Then check and correct.
  • One “why?” and moving on. The real gains come from the third or fourth “why?”, when you hit the fundamentals.
  • Only asking the obvious questions. Push toward the explanations your teacher never gave you — those are where genuine learning happens.
  • Skipping the check. Unchecked wrong answers reinforce misunderstanding. Always verify against the source.

When to Use This

Any time you are covering conceptual material — not just listing named items. Particularly powerful with cause-and-effect topics in Sport Studies: why does low self-esteem create a barrier to participation? How does the Whereabouts Rule deter doping? Why can a hosting legacy be negative even after a ‘successful’ event? Build it into every lesson revisit, not as a separate session. It adds around 50% to your reading time but makes everything else — retrieval, exam answers — significantly easier.

Quick Reference
Adds ~50% to reading time, transforms recall

The chain

  1. Read the fact
  2. Ask “why is this true?”
  3. Ask “how does it work?”
  4. Write your answer
  5. Check against the source
  6. Ask “why?” again of your answer

Exam conditions

Timed Practice

Simulate the real thing — including the time pressure.

What the Research Says

Knowing the content is only half of an exam. The other half is managing time, reading questions accurately under pressure, writing neatly when your hand hurts, and staying calm when you don’t know one of the questions. These are all skills — and like any skill, they need practice. Timed practice is how you build them.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Soderstrom & Bjork (2015)Transfer-appropriate processing: performance is best when the practice conditions closely match the test conditions.Practise in the conditions you’ll be tested in.
Agarwal et al. (2017)Students who did timed practice tests scored higher even on unseen questions.Builds generalisable exam skill, not just familiarity.
Yerkes & Dodson (1908)Performance is best at MODERATE arousal — some pressure helps, too much hurts.Simulated pressure builds tolerance for real pressure.
Hinze & Rapp (2014)Students who experienced test-like practice reported 30% less exam anxiety.Familiarity reduces fear. Fear reduces performance.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Start small — begin with one timed question or one section. Don’t jump straight to full papers. Build the muscle gradually.
  2. 2
    Match the exam mark-to-time ratio — Economics papers allocate approximately 1 minute per mark. A 9-mark evaluation question should take no more than 9 minutes; a 12-mark question no more than 12. Time yourself accordingly.
  3. 3
    Remove distractions — phone in another room, no music, no notes. The real exam hall has none of these.
  4. 4
    Handwrite — the exam is handwritten. Typing is faster and feels more productive, but it doesn’t train the same skill. Your hand will hurt on the day and that’s normal.
  5. 5
    Mark with the mark scheme honestly — use StudyVault’s per-question mark schemes or a teacher-provided one. Be harsh on yourself — underscoring now prevents overconfidence later.
  6. 6
    Do a full paper under conditions a month before the exam — uninterrupted, correct time, no music. One per subject, one per week in the final stretch.
Example 1

Set a 9-minute timer and attempt this question cold: “Evaluate the likely effects of a rise in the national minimum wage on workers, businesses, and the wider economy.” Write by hand, no notes. When the timer goes, stop. Mark it against the mark scheme: check that your answer includes a developed chain of analysis (higher wages → higher labour costs → possible redundancies OR higher consumer spending → higher demand), at least one evaluation point (it depends on how much wages rise; businesses with inelastic demand for labour may absorb the cost; the effect differs for large and small firms), and a reasoned conclusion. The gap between what you wrote and what the scheme awards is exactly what to practise next.

Example 2

Work through a 12-mark evaluation question on fiscal policy under timed conditions: “Evaluate whether an increase in government spending is the best way to reduce unemployment.” Allocate roughly 2 minutes to plan your evaluation scaffold: size of the multiplier effect; time lags before spending reaches the economy; whether unemployment is demand-deficient or structural; the risk of crowding out private investment; alternative policies such as supply-side measures. Write your answer in the remaining 10 minutes, then stop regardless of whether you have finished. Record which parts of the scaffold you reached — if you ran out before covering evaluation, practise planning speed in the next session.

Common Pitfalls

  • Stopping when the timer runs out and ignoring the unfinished bit. Note what you’d have written — that’s the data about your pace.
  • Using notes during “timed” practice. It’s not timed practice — it’s open-book practice. Useful, but different.
  • Only doing it in the last fortnight. Too late — you’ve not left time to fix the weaknesses the practice reveals.
  • Not marking honestly. Marking your own work gently protects feelings now and destroys results later.

When to Use This

From 10 weeks out, do at least one timed practice per subject per week — usually a single section at first, building to full papers. In the final month, do at least one full timed paper per subject. Always mark it against the actual scheme and note your pace. For the 9- and 12-mark evaluation questions specifically, practise the evaluation scaffold (size of change, time period, elasticity, state of the economy, who is affected) until it becomes automatic before the exam.

Structured notes

Knowledge Organisers

One page per topic — everything you need to know, nothing you don’t.

What the Research Says

A knowledge organiser is a single page that captures all the essential facts, definitions, named lists and examples for one topic. The page itself is not the product — redrawing it from memory is. When you can reconstruct a complete knowledge organiser without looking, you have achieved the kind of well-organised memory that makes exam questions feel familiar rather than surprising.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Kirschner, Sweller & Clark (2006)Structured, explicit knowledge organisation significantly outperforms unguided discovery for complex material.Organised knowledge is recalled faster and more accurately.
Sweller (1988) — Cognitive Load TheoryBreaking complex content into manageable chunks prevents working memory from becoming overloaded.One-page structure prevents the “where do I start?” freeze.
Rosenshine (2012)Reviewing key information in small doses and checking for understanding produces the highest retention rates.Brief, structured review beats long unstructured sessions.
Willingham (2009)Prior knowledge is the single biggest predictor of how much new knowledge sticks. Well-organised schemas grow themselves.Building strong knowledge organisers early accelerates all later learning.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Choose one topic — one lesson or one spec topic area. Not a whole unit at once — the page must fit on one side of A4.
  2. 2
    Plan the sections — key terms and definitions, named lists (exact spec wording), advantages/disadvantages where applicable, a mini applied example. These sections cover the structure of every topic in this subject.
  3. 3
    Build the page using the lesson as source — write in your own words. If you cannot paraphrase it, you do not understand it yet.
  4. 4
    Turn the page face-down and reconstruct it — blank paper, no notes. Fill in as much as you can. This converts the note-making activity into retrieval practice.
  5. 5
    Compare and mark in red — every item you missed gets circled. Those circles are tomorrow’s revision targets.
  6. 6
    Repeat at spaced intervals — reconstruct the same organiser on day 3, day 7, day 14. Each attempt should take less time and produce fewer red circles.
Example 1 — Values in sport knowledge organiser

Build a one-page organiser for the values and ethics topic. Sections: (1) The seven sporting values — team spirit, fair play, citizenship, tolerance and respect, national pride, excellence, etiquette — each with one applied example. (2) Olympic values (three): Excellence, Friendship, Respect. (3) Paralympic values (four): Courage, Determination, Inspiration, Equality. (4) Key distinction — sportsmanship: within letter AND spirit; gamesmanship: within letter, against spirit. (5) Mini applied scenario — Kingsmere AC captain kicks ball out for an injured opponent (sportsmanship); Ferndale Rovers player delays a restart to protect a lead (gamesmanship). Reconstruct on day 3 — the Olympic/Paralympic distinction is consistently the first section students drop, revealing exactly where the exam mark risk sits.

Example 2 — NGB functions knowledge organiser

Build a one-page organiser for National Governing Bodies. Sections: (1) Definition of an NGB — a body that governs and develops a specific sport in a country. (2) Seven NGB functions — promote participation, develop coaching and officiating, organise competitions, amend rules, ensure safety, lobby for funding, provide insurance and technical guidance. (3) Named NGBs — The FA (football), RFU (rugby union), ECB (cricket), LTA (tennis). (4) Applied example — The FA introduced VAR across the Premier League to improve officiating accuracy. Turn face-down and reconstruct. The NGB functions list and named examples are the two areas most students fail to reproduce in full — the reconstruction pass makes those gaps visible before the exam.

Common Pitfalls

  • Making it too long. If it doesn’t fit on one A4 side, split it into two topics. Length signals you haven’t condensed the content yet.
  • Copying instead of paraphrasing. If you paste sentences from the lesson word-for-word, you are not processing — you are transcribing. Rephrase everything.
  • Never reconstructing from memory. A knowledge organiser you don’t rebuild from scratch is just a note. The reconstruction is the revision.
  • Building all pages at once. Spreading organiser-building across the year — one page per lesson — works far better than building ten pages the week before the exam.

When to Use This

Build each organiser within a day of studying the lesson — while the material is fresh enough to paraphrase. Then use spaced reconstruction to keep the knowledge active. For Sport Studies, the highest-value organisers to build are: the twelve user groups with named characteristics, the nine barriers and matched solutions, the seven sporting values, the Olympic and Paralympic values comparison, the three event types with spec examples, and the NGB functions list with named governing bodies. These are the named-list topics that carry the most marks in the short-answer and context-based sections of the exam.

Retrieval Practice

Test yourself — don’t just re-read.

What the Research Says

Retrieval practice is the act of pulling information out of your memory, rather than pushing it in. It sounds simple but it is the most powerful revision technique we have — stronger than highlighting, stronger than re-reading, stronger than watching videos. The harder the retrieval feels, the more your long-term memory is strengthening.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Roediger & Karpicke (2006)Students who self-tested once remembered 50% more a week later than those who re-read four times.Self-testing > re-reading, even when it feels harder.
Karpicke & Blunt (2011)Retrieval practice beat concept-mapping and elaborative study on a delayed test by ~50%.Works better than other “active” strategies that feel productive.
Agarwal et al. (2017)Low-stakes retrieval quizzes raised GCSE-equivalent test scores by an average of one grade.Short regular quizzing moves your real exam score.
Smith et al. (2016)Students who practised retrieval scored higher even on questions testing information they didn’t specifically retrieve.Builds the skill of remembering itself, not just the facts.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Study a chunk of content — read through a StudyVault lesson, watch a video, or cover a topic in class. Don’t try to memorise. Just understand.
  2. 2
    Close everything — book shut, tab closed, notes flipped over. The whole point is that you cannot see the material.
  3. 3
    Write down everything you can remember — no looking back. This is called a “brain dump.” Write until you run out. It should feel uncomfortable.
  4. 4
    Check against the source — open the lesson. Mark what you missed in a different colour. Don’t just glance — properly compare.
  5. 5
    Target the gaps — re-study only the parts you missed. Not the whole lesson again. Just the holes.
  6. 6
    Retest tomorrow — hit the same topic again within 24 hours. The second attempt is where the learning locks in.
Example 1

After studying Myth & Religion, close the book and brain-dump all twelve Olympians from memory — name, domain, and at least one symbol for each (for example: Apollo — sun, prophecy, music — bow and lyre; Athena — wisdom, war, crafts — owl and aegis; Poseidon — sea and earthquakes — trident). Then extend the challenge: for each god, add one myth or cult site that links to their domain. When you check back, pay particular attention to the gods whose symbols you confused or omitted — these are exactly the details that earn or lose marks on 4-mark source questions.

Example 2

After covering the Odyssey, brain-dump the prescribed books you have studied and write down one key episode from each — the encounter with Polyphemus (nobody / the stake / the escape under the sheep), the year with Circe (the drug, the pigs, Hermes’ moly, the prophecy), and the homecoming (the bow contest, the slaughter of the suitors, Penelope’s test of the marriage bed). For each episode note: which value of Homeric society it illustrates (xenia, kleos, cunning), one specific quotation or detail from the text, and one piece of material evidence from the Mycenaean world that connects. Check back and mark what you missed. The cross-referencing between text and material culture is exactly what higher-mark questions demand.

Common Pitfalls

  • Peeking. If you look back during the brain dump, you’re not doing retrieval — you’re doing copying. Harder is better.
  • Only doing it once. One pass strengthens memory a little. Spaced repeats strengthen it permanently. Come back to the same topic 2–3 times over a week.
  • Doing it too soon after studying. If you retrieve while the material is still in short-term memory, it’s too easy to count. Leave at least 30 minutes between studying and testing.
  • Stopping when it feels difficult. Desirable difficulty is the whole point. If it feels easy, your memory isn’t being challenged and you’re not learning.

When to Use This

Build it in every week, from the start of the course through to your exams. Aim for 15–20 minutes per subject, two or three times a week. The last two weeks before an exam is when retrieval practice becomes your main tool — swap passive reading for brain dumps and flashcards. On StudyVault, the Knowledge Check and Flashcard buttons in every lesson sidebar are retrieval practice in disguise — use them.

Quick Reference

Exam conditions

Timed Practice

Simulate the real exam — build the judgement no amount of revision can replace.

What the Research Says

Knowing the content is necessary but not sufficient. The exam tests whether you can recall it, apply it to an unfamiliar scenario, and communicate it clearly under time pressure — all at once. The only way to build that combined skill is to practise it under the same conditions. Timed practice is the final layer of preparation that converts revision knowledge into exam performance.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Lyle & Crawford (2011)Students who practised retrieval under timed conditions scored significantly higher than those who studied without time constraints.The time pressure itself trains the memory and decision-making you need.
Kornell & Bjork (2007)Interleaved, timed retrieval practice was the condition most predictive of delayed exam performance.Timed + interleaved is the most effective combination for exam prep.
Roediger et al. (2011)Regular low-stakes testing significantly reduced exam anxiety alongside improving performance.Timed practice reduces nerves as well as raising scores.
Butler (2010)Students who practised applying knowledge in test conditions showed better transfer to novel questions than those who studied without testing.Timed practice prepares you for questions you have never seen before.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Start with one question — choose a question type you find hard. Allocate time: roughly 1 minute per mark. Set a timer.
  2. 2
    Attempt under strict conditions — no notes, no phone. Write the answer as you would in the real exam, not as bullet points.
  3. 3
    Mark against a model answer — be honest. A point you wrote in a way the mark scheme would not credit does not count.
  4. 4
    Annotate why you missed marks — was it recall (didn’t know the fact)? Application (knew it but didn’t link it to the scenario)? Communication (wrote the right idea too vaguely)? Different causes need different fixes.
  5. 5
    Build up to a full paper — one question → one topic-area section → half a paper → full paper under exam conditions.
  6. 6
    Debrief every paper — three minutes reviewing where marks were lost is worth more than an hour of extra revision on topics you already know.
Example 1 — The 4-mark ‘describe with example’ question

The written exam regularly asks 4-mark questions in the format: “Describe how [barrier] affects [user group] and suggest one solution. Use a sporting example in your answer.” Practise these under strict time: allow 4 minutes. Use a scenario you haven’t seen before: “Aoife O’Donnell works full time. Describe one barrier she faces in participating in sport and suggest one solution, using a sporting example.” Aim for: name the barrier precisely (time / inflexible session times), explain the impact, name the solution (flexible evening or weekend sessions at Kingsmere AC), apply to sport. If you overrun 4 minutes, note it — that is the gap to fix.

Example 2 — The 8-mark evaluation (Section C)

The 8-mark extended-response question requires balanced evaluation with a substantiated judgement. Practise with questions like: “Evaluate whether the long-term legacy of hosting a major sporting event is always positive. Use examples in your answer.” Aim for: two positives with evidence (London 2012 transport legacy, increased national participation), two negatives with evidence (Paris 2024 cost overrun, Athens 2004 unused facilities), a counter-point, and a final judgement with a condition (“the legacy is positive when facility investment is sustained, but negative when it is not”). Mark your answer using the banded mark scheme: Band 3 requires balanced points, at least one named example, and a clear judgement — those are the three boxes to tick.

Common Pitfalls

  • Doing timed practice too early. If you don’t know the content yet, timed practice just practises failure. Retrieval, spaced repetition and knowledge organisers come first.
  • Not applying to the scenario. The exam gives you a context for a reason. Answers that ignore the scenario and write generic theory will stall in the middle performance band regardless of how correct the theory is.
  • Marking too generously. A vague or half-formed answer is not a mark. Apply the mark scheme strictly — the exam will.
  • Practising only the questions you find easy. Timed practice on familiar material is comfortable but not useful. Target the question types where you consistently lose marks.

When to Use This

Begin single-question timed practice once you have covered each topic area. In the final six weeks before the exam, attempt at least one timed section per week. In the final two weeks, do at least one full timed paper. The written exam is 1 hour 15 minutes and 70 marks — that is roughly one minute per mark, with a little time for planning the Section C extended response. Use the StudyVault practice questions for structured low-stakes timed retrieval — then work up to past papers and mark-scheme marking for the higher-mark questions.

Terminology

Active Recall with Flashcards

Master definitions, equations, and key facts

What the Research Says

Flashcards force active recall — you see a prompt and must generate the answer from memory before flipping the card. This is far more effective than passively reading definitions. Science is terminology-heavy: you need precise definitions (osmosis, electrolysis, electromagnetic induction), equations (for Physics calculations), and factual knowledge (functions of organelles, properties of groups in the periodic table). Flashcards are the most efficient way to drill this material.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Kornell (2009) Students who used flashcards with spacing scored significantly higher than those who studied notes Flashcards + spacing is a powerful combination
Dunlosky et al. (2013) Practice testing (including flashcards) rated HIGH utility for long-term retention Works across all subjects and age groups

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Create cards by topic — Group your flashcards by topic (e.g. “B1 Cell Biology”, “C5 Chemical Changes”, “P7 Electromagnetism”). Put a question or term on the front and the answer on the back. Keep answers concise — no more than 2–3 bullet points.
  2. 2
    Include different card types — Mix definitions (“What is osmosis?”), equations (“Write the equation for GPE”), processes (“Describe the stages of mitosis”), and application cards (“Why does ice float?”). Variety prevents rote memorisation without understanding.
  3. 3
    Say the answer out loud before flipping — This is crucial. Looking at the back too quickly turns flashcards into passive re-reading. Force yourself to produce an answer, even if it’s wrong.
  4. 4
    Sort into three piles — After each session, sort cards into Got It, Nearly, and Not Yet. Next session, start with Not Yet, then Nearly, then a quick run through Got It to maintain confidence.
  5. 5
    Use Anki or Quizlet for digital spacing — Apps like Anki automatically schedule cards using spaced repetition algorithms. Cards you get wrong appear more frequently; cards you know well appear less often.

When and How Often

Create cards
15 min Drill session
15 min Sort & review
5 min

Spend 15 minutes creating cards, then 15–20 minutes drilling. Do short flashcard sessions daily — 10 minutes on the bus, 15 minutes before bed. Little and often beats long marathon sessions.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Making cards too detailed — A card with a paragraph-long answer becomes passive reading. Keep answers to 1–3 key points.
  • ❌
    Only making definition cards — Definitions are useful, but you also need cards for equations, processes, practical methods, and application questions.
  • ❌
    Flipping too quickly — You must attempt an answer before flipping. The effort of retrieval is what builds the memory.

Active recall

Retrieval Practice

Test yourself, don’t just re-read

What the Research Says

Retrieval practice means pulling information out of your memory rather than putting it back in. Every time you successfully recall a fact, the memory trace gets stronger. Re-reading your notes feels productive, but it creates a false sense of confidence — the information looks familiar without actually being learned. For Science, where you need to recall equations, definitions, processes, and experimental methods under exam pressure, retrieval practice is essential.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Roediger & Karpicke (2006) Students who practised retrieval remembered 80% after one week; those who re-read remembered 36% More than double the retention
Dunlosky et al. (2013) Major review of 10 revision strategies rated practice testing as HIGH utility One of only two top-rated techniques
Karpicke & Blunt (2011) Retrieval practice outperformed concept mapping for learning science texts Works even for complex scientific material
EEF Cognitive Science Report (2021) Recommended retrieval practice as one of six key principles for effective learning Endorsed for UK classroom use

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Read one topic — Spend 5 minutes reading through a single topic, such as cell structure, bonding, or energy transfers. Don’t highlight or make notes yet — just read to understand.
  2. 2
    Close your notes — Put everything away. No peeking. This is the crucial moment where learning actually happens.
  3. 3
    Brain dump on a blank page — Write down everything you can remember about the topic. Include key terms, equations, diagrams, processes, and examples. Use bullet points, sketches, or tables — whatever comes to mind. Aim for 5–8 minutes.
  4. 4
    Check and highlight gaps — Open your notes and compare. Use a different colour pen to fill in anything you missed or got wrong. These gaps are your priority for next time.
  5. 5
    Repeat on the gaps — Next session, focus your retrieval attempt on the parts you couldn’t remember. Keep cycling until the gaps are filled.

When and How Often

Read
5 min Brain dump
8 min Check gaps
5 min

One full cycle takes about 18 minutes. Do 2–3 cycles per revision session, covering different topics. Use retrieval practice every time you revise — it should be your default method, not an occasional extra.

First attempt — from memory only

Cells have a nucleus, cell membrane, and cytoplasm. Plant cells also have a cell wall and chloroplasts. Mitosis is cell division. DNA is in the nucleus. Cells need energy from respiration…

After checking — gaps filled in green

Cells have a nucleus (contains genetic material as chromosomes), cell membrane (selectively permeable, controls what enters and leaves), and cytoplasm (where most chemical reactions take place). Plant cells also have a cell wall (made of cellulose, provides structural support), chloroplasts (contain chlorophyll for photosynthesis), and a permanent vacuole (filled with cell sap, maintains turgor pressure). Mitosis is cell division (produces two genetically identical diploid daughter cells; stages: prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase). DNA is in the nucleus (as a double helix; DNA is a polymer of nucleotides). Cells need energy from respiration (aerobic: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water; C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O).

What this reveals: The first attempt had the right structures but missed specific functions, the stages of mitosis, the equation for aerobic respiration, and the permanent vacuole. These gaps become the focus of the next retrieval attempt.

Use these to test yourself without notes. Cover the answers, then check:

  • Name the three states of matter and describe the particle arrangement in each.
  • Write the word equation and balanced symbol equation for photosynthesis.
  • What are the differences between ionic, covalent, and metallic bonding?
  • State Newton’s three laws of motion and give an example of each.
  • Name three types of specialised cell and explain how each is adapted to its function.
  • What is the reactivity series? List the first five metals in order.
  • Describe the structure of the atom, including the charges and masses of subatomic particles.
  • Write the equation for calculating speed, and rearrange it to find distance.
  • Explain the difference between aerobic and anaerobic respiration.
  • What happens during electrolysis of an ionic compound?

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Re-reading instead of recalling — Reading your notes five times feels like revision but barely strengthens memory. Close the book and test yourself.
  • ❌
    Peeking at notes too soon — The struggle to remember is the point. If you look at your notes the moment you get stuck, you skip the part that builds memory.
  • ❌
    Only testing what you already know — It feels good to recall photosynthesis perfectly, but the real gains come from practising the topics you find hardest — like balancing equations or remembering the reactivity series.
  • ❌
    Not returning to the same topic — One brain dump is a start, not the finish. You need to revisit each topic multiple times at increasing intervals (see Spaced Repetition).

Exam readiness

Practice Questions Under Timed Conditions

Write like it’s the real thing

What the Research Says

Practising under exam conditions trains your brain to retrieve and apply knowledge under pressure. It also builds time management skills — in AQA Science papers, you have roughly one minute per mark, so a 6-mark question should take about 6 minutes. Without timed practice, students routinely spend too long on low-mark questions and run out of time on the high-value extended responses.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Roediger & Karpicke (2006) Testing under exam-like conditions improved long-term retention by 50% compared to re-reading Exam simulation produces real learning
AQA Chief Examiner Reports Time management is consistently cited as a reason students underperform — especially on 6-mark questions Timed practice directly addresses the most common exam weakness

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Choose your question set — Start with individual questions on one topic, then build up to full papers. Use AQA past papers, the StudyVault practice questions, or your teacher’s question bank.
  2. 2
    Set a timer — Allow roughly 1 minute per mark. A 1-mark question gets 1 minute; a 6-mark question gets 6 minutes. For a full paper (70 marks in 75 minutes for Higher), that’s just over a minute per mark.
  3. 3
    Write in exam conditions — No notes, no phone, no distractions. Use pen on paper (not a screen). This simulates the real exam environment and trains your handwriting speed.
  4. 4
    Self-mark against the mark scheme — This is the most important step. Don’t just check if your answer is “about right” — compare it word by word against the mark scheme. Note which marking points you hit and which you missed.
  5. 5
    Rewrite missed questions — For any question where you dropped marks, rewrite the answer immediately using the mark scheme as a guide. This corrective feedback cements the correct response.

When and How Often

Timed questions
20 min Self-mark
10 min Rewrite gaps
10 min

Start with single-topic question sets (20 minutes), then progress to half-papers and full papers in the final weeks. Aim for at least 2 timed sessions per week across all three sciences.

Question: Describe the process of natural selection. [6 marks]

Student’s timed answer (5 minutes)

Animals that are better adapted survive. They pass on their genes. Over time, the species changes. The ones that are not adapted die. This is survival of the fittest.

Mark scheme check:

  • ✔ Organisms with advantageous characteristics are more likely to survive (1 mark)
  • ✔ They reproduce and pass on genes/alleles (1 mark)
  • ❌ Missing: Variation exists within a population (1 mark)
  • ❌ Missing: There is competition for resources (1 mark)
  • ❌ Missing: Over many generations, the advantageous allele becomes more common (1 mark)
  • ❌ Missing: This may lead to speciation if populations become isolated (1 mark)

Score: 2/6. The answer has the right idea but misses four specific marking points. Rewrite including: variation, competition, “over many generations”, and allele frequency change.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Spending too long on low-mark questions — A 1-mark question needs a single word or short phrase. Don’t write a paragraph.
  • ❌
    Skipping the self-marking step — Without checking against the mark scheme, you don’t know what you’re missing. Self-marking is where the learning happens.
  • ❌
    Only practising topics you like — It feels comfortable answering questions on your favourite topics, but you need to target your weakest areas for the biggest improvement.

Maths skills

Equation Practice and Calculations

At least 20% of your marks depend on maths

Why This Matters

AQA Science papers allocate at least 20% of marks to mathematical skills. In Physics, this can rise to 40%. You need to recall equations (some are given on the equation sheet, others must be memorised), rearrange them, substitute values with correct units, and present answers to an appropriate number of significant figures. In Chemistry, you’ll calculate relative formula masses, moles, concentrations, and atom economy. In Biology, maths questions involve magnification, percentages, and data analysis. Students who don’t practise calculations lose easy marks.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Learn which equations must be memorised — AQA provides an equation sheet in the exam, but not all equations are on it. For Higher tier Physics, you must memorise equations like F = ma, E = mcΔθ, and V = IR. Make flashcards for the “recall” equations and drill them until automatic.
  2. 2
    Practise rearranging — Use the formula triangle method or algebraic rearranging. For every equation, practise making each variable the subject. For example: speed = distance ÷ time can become distance = speed × time, or time = distance ÷ speed.
  3. 3
    Convert units before substituting — Always convert to SI units: km to m, g to kg, mA to A, kJ to J, cm² to m². Write the conversion next to the value before substituting into the equation.
  4. 4
    Show every step of working — Write the equation, substitute values with units, calculate, and state the unit of the answer. Even if the final number is wrong, you can earn marks for correct method.
  5. 5
    Check significant figures and standard form — Give answers to an appropriate number of significant figures (usually 2 or 3 s.f.) and use standard form for very large or very small numbers (e.g. 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s).

When and How Often

Equation recall
5 min Calculation practice
15 min Check & correct
5 min

Spend 20–25 minutes per session. Start with equation recall (flashcards or brain dump), then work through 5–8 calculation questions. Practise at least 3 times per week — maths skills fade quickly without regular use.

QuantityEquation

Newton’s Second LawF = m × a

GPEGPE = m × g × h

Chemistry — Key Calculations

  • Relative formula mass (Mr) = sum of relative atomic masses
  • Moles = mass ÷ Mr
  • Concentration (g/dm³) = mass ÷ volume
  • Atom economy = (Mr of desired product ÷ Mr of all products) × 100
  • Percentage yield = (actual yield ÷ theoretical yield) × 100

Biology — Key Calculations

  • Magnification = image size ÷ actual size
  • Percentage change = (change ÷ original) × 100
  • Mean, median, mode, and range from data tables

Question: A 0.5 kg ball is dropped from a height of 12 m. Calculate its speed just before hitting the ground. Assume g = 10 m/s² and no air resistance. [3 marks]

Model answer

Step 1: GPE lost = m × g × h = 0.5 × 10 × 12 = 60 J
Step 2: KE gained = GPE lost = 60 J (conservation of energy)
Step 3: KE = ½ × m × v² → v² = 2 × KE ÷ m = 2 × 60 ÷ 0.5 = 240 → v = √240 = 15.5 m/s (3 s.f.)

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Forgetting unit conversions — Using km instead of m, or g instead of kg, gives answers out by factors of 1000. Always convert first.
  • ❌
    Not showing working — An answer without working earns 0 marks if the number is wrong. Show every step to pick up method marks.
  • ❌
    Missing the unit of the answer — Always state the unit (J, N, m/s, mol). Marks are often lost for missing units.

Exam Paper Walkthroughs

Work through complete papers to master exam technique

Why This Matters

Doing individual questions builds knowledge, but only complete paper walkthroughs build exam strategy. A walkthrough means working through an entire past paper, question by question, understanding why each answer earns marks. You learn how AQA structures papers, how topics are tested in different ways, and how to pace yourself across the full 75 minutes. Examiner reports reveal what thousands of students got wrong — learning from their mistakes prevents you from making the same ones.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Gather materials — Download a full past paper, the corresponding mark scheme, and the examiner’s report from the exam board's website. You need all three for a proper walkthrough.
  2. 2
    Attempt the paper under timed conditions — Set a timer for 75 minutes (Higher tier), close your notes, and write your answers on paper. This gives you a baseline score and highlights which topics you need to revise.
  3. 3
    Mark with the mark scheme — Go through every question. For each one, circle the marking points you hit and highlight the ones you missed. Calculate your total score and grade boundary.
  4. 4
    Read the examiner’s report for each question — The report tells you what most students got wrong and what examiners were looking for. Note the common misconceptions and the specific phrases that earned marks.
  5. 5
    Rewrite your weakest answers — Pick the 3–5 questions where you lost the most marks. Rewrite each answer using the mark scheme as a model. Then close the mark scheme and try again from memory.

When and How Often

Attempt paper
75 min Mark & review
30 min Rewrite weak answers
20 min

Do one full paper walkthrough per subject per week in the final 4–6 weeks before exams. That’s about 2 hours per walkthrough including marking and rewriting. Earlier in your revision, use individual topic questions instead.

Practical skills

Required Practicals Revision

Know the method, variables, hazards, and evaluation for every practical

Why This Matters

the exam board has 21 required practicals across Biology, Chemistry, and Physics (8 Biology, 8 Chemistry, 10 Physics for Separate Sciences; fewer for Combined). Questions about required practicals appear on every paper and can account for 15% of the total marks. You don’t repeat the experiments in the exam — but you must know the method, the variables, the equipment, the hazards, how to improve accuracy, and how to evaluate the results. These are some of the most predictable marks on the paper if you revise them properly.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    List all required practicals — Use the specification to create a checklist of every required practical for your course. Tick each one off as you revise it. Don’t rely on memory — use the spec.
  2. 2
    For each practical, write a summary covering — (a) Aim: what the practical tests; (b) Method: step-by-step procedure; (c) Variables: independent, dependent, and control variables; (d) Equipment: key apparatus including resolution; (e) Hazards and precautions; (f) Expected results and how to process data; (g) How to improve accuracy and reliability.
  3. 3
    Draw the set-up from memory — Many practicals require a labelled diagram in the exam. Practise drawing the apparatus set-up with labels until you can do it quickly and accurately.
  4. 4
    Answer past paper practical questions — AQA reuses practical contexts. Practise questions from past papers that are based on required practicals — you’ll see the same practical tested in different ways.
  5. 5
    Learn the key vocabulary — Examiners expect precise terminology: “reproducible” (different people get the same results), “repeatable” (same person gets same results), “resolution” (smallest interval on a measuring instrument), “anomalous” (a result that doesn’t fit the pattern).

When and How Often

Summary notes
10 min Draw set-up
5 min Past paper Qs
15 min

  6. Photosynthesis — effect of light intensity on rate of photosynthesis

  8. Plant responses — effect of light or gravity on seedling growth

  1. Making salts — preparation of a pure, dry sample of a soluble salt
  2. Electrolysis — electrolysis of aqueous solutions
  3. Temperature changes — investigating exothermic and endothermic reactions
  4. Rates of reaction — effect of concentration on rate (e.g. sodium thiosulfate)

  2. Thermal insulation — investigating the effectiveness of different materials

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Confusing independent and dependent variables — The independent variable is what you change; the dependent variable is what you measure. Get these the wrong way round and you lose marks on the very first line.

    Forgetting control variables — Every practical has variables that must be kept the same for a fair test. “To make it a fair test” is not enough — you must name the specific variables you controlled.
  • ❌
    Not mentioning repeats — “Repeat 3 times and calculate the mean” is expected in almost every practical method. It improves reliability and helps identify anomalies.

Scheduling

Spaced Repetition

Spread it out over days and weeks

What the Research Says

Spaced repetition is the practice of reviewing material at gradually increasing intervals. Instead of cramming everything the night before, you revisit topics after 1 day, then 3 days, then 7 days, then 14 days. Each time you revisit, the memory gets stronger and lasts longer. For Science, where you need to retain hundreds of definitions, equations, and processes across Biology, Chemistry, and Physics, spacing is the difference between short-term cramming and genuine understanding.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Ebbinghaus (1885) Without review, 70% of information is forgotten within 24 hours Forgetting is rapid without spacing
Cepeda et al. (2006) Spacing study sessions produced 10–30% better recall than massed practice Consistent across all subjects
Dunlosky et al. (2013) Distributed practice rated as HIGH utility — one of only two top-rated strategies Strong evidence across hundreds of studies

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Create a topic list — Write out every topic you need to revise for each paper (Biology Paper 1, Chemistry Paper 2, etc.). Use the specification checklist to make sure nothing is missed.
  2. 2
    Assign topics to days — Spread topics across your revision calendar. Don’t do all of Biology in one week — interleave Biology, Chemistry, and Physics topics each day.
  3. 3
    Use the 1-3-7-14 rule — After first learning a topic, review it after 1 day, then 3 days, then 7 days, then 14 days. Each review can be shorter than the last — a 5-minute retrieval quiz is enough for the later reviews.
  4. 4
    Mark confidence levels — After each review, rate the topic as Red (can’t remember), Amber (partial recall), or Green (solid). Red topics get reviewed sooner; green topics can be spaced further apart.
  5. 5
    Track with a revision timetable — Use a calendar, spreadsheet, or app (Anki is excellent for flashcards with built-in spacing). Colour-code by subject so you can see the balance at a glance.

When and How Often

Day 1: Learn
20 min Day 2: Review
10 min Day 4: Review
5 min Day 8+: Quick test

Start spacing at least 8 weeks before the exam. The earlier you begin, the more review cycles you can fit in. Even 10 minutes a day on previously covered topics makes a huge difference.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Cramming the night before — Massed practice feels productive but fades fast. Spaced practice feels harder in the moment but lasts much longer.
  • ❌

  • ❌
    Skipping the hard topics — The topics you find hardest need more frequent review, not less. Use your RAG ratings to prioritise.

Deep thinking

Elaborative Interrogation

Ask “why?” and “how?” until the facts become explanations.

What the Research Says

Facts in isolation are fragile. Facts connected by explanations survive. Elaborative interrogation is the habit of asking “why is that true?” and “how does that work?” about every fact you learn — and forcing yourself to answer. The answer doesn’t need to be perfect. The act of trying to answer is what builds the mental connections that turn memorised facts into understood explanations.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Pressley et al. (1988)Asking “why?” during reading boosted recall by 40–70% compared to silent reading.Works even when the answer is imperfect.
Dunlosky et al. (2013)Rated “moderate utility” in the APS review — robust across subjects and ages, especially when applied to new material that builds on existing knowledge.Best for consolidating material you half-know.
Smith & Holliday (2006)Students who self-explained while studying scored significantly higher on transfer questions requiring application.Builds the ability to USE the knowledge, not just recall it.
Chi et al. (1994)Self-explanation was a stronger predictor of understanding than prior knowledge.Even weaker students catch up by explaining to themselves.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Study a chunk of content — a lesson, a paragraph, a key fact. Anything where facts are being introduced.
  2. 2
    After each fact, ask “why?” — why is this true? Why does it matter? Why did the Greeks respond this way?
  3. 3
    Then ask “how?” — how does this idea work? How does it connect to the next topic? How would you explain it to someone who has never studied the ancient world?
  4. 4
    Try to answer out loud — even if your answer is wrong, the attempt activates deeper processing. Write your answer in the margin.
  5. 5
    Check your answer against the source — does the text support your explanation? If not, update it. The correction matters more than the first guess.
  6. 6
    Build chains — once you’ve asked “why?” once, ask it again of your answer. Push until you hit a genuinely fundamental fact. This is where deep understanding forms.
Example 1

Fact: “Xenia — the code of guest-friendship — is central to the Odyssey.” Ask why: because in a world without hotels or embassies, travellers depended entirely on the hospitality of strangers for food, shelter, and safe passage. Ask why again: because a guest who was treated well would honour the host’s name and reciprocate the courtesy if the roles were ever reversed — it was a social contract enforced by Zeus himself (Zeus Xenios). Ask how: this explains why Odysseus judges every community he encounters by how they treat guests: the Cyclops is monstrous because he violates xenia (eating guests instead of feeding them); the Phaeacians are civilised because they follow it perfectly (gifts, feasting, safe transport home). Ask why that matters for an exam answer: it connects a specific Homeric value to both literary evidence (Polyphemus episode) and the wider question of what the poem teaches us about Greek society.

Example 2

Fact: “Greek cities used myth as a symbol of political power.” Ask why: because claiming descent from a god or hero legitimised a ruling dynasty and gave a city divine protection — Athens claimed Athena had chosen the city as hers over Poseidon, which is why the Parthenon sits at the heart of the city. Ask how: the myth was displayed in stone — the pediments of the Parthenon showed the birth of Athena and her contest with Poseidon, making political theology visible to every visitor. Ask why that matters: it shows that myth was not just story but active propaganda, and it explains why source questions about temples ask you to link architectural decoration to religious and civic meaning. Ask why the connection between art and myth matters for the exam: higher-mark questions reward students who can explain why a piece of material evidence was made, not just describe what it shows.

Common Pitfalls

  • Accepting “I don’t know”. Take a guess. Even a wrong guess activates the processing. Then check and correct.
  • One “why?” and moving on. The real gains come from the third or fourth “why?”, when you hit the fundamentals.
  • Only asking the obvious questions. Push toward the explanations your teacher never gave you — those are where genuine learning happens.
  • Skipping the check. Unchecked wrong answers reinforce misunderstanding. Always verify against the source.

When to Use This

Any time you’re covering conceptual material — not just listing facts. Particularly powerful with Classical Civilisation’s recurring themes: why xenia matters in the Odyssey, why Heracles’ labours were culturally significant, why Mycenaean citadels were built the way they were, and why myths were depicted on temple friezes. Build it into every lesson revisit. The exam rewards students who can explain the significance of evidence, not just identify it.

  2. How does it work?

Distributed practice

Spaced Repetition

Forget, then retrieve — that’s where the learning happens.

What the Research Says

The brain remembers things better when you review them just as you’re about to forget them. Cram everything the night before and it’s gone within a week. Revisit the same material on day one, day three, day seven, day fourteen and it sticks for months. This is the single biggest difference between students who peak in mocks and students who peak in the real exam.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Ebbinghaus (1885)Without revisiting, 50% of what you learn is lost within an hour and 80% within a day.The forgetting curve is real — and steeper than most students realise.
Cepeda et al. (2006)Meta-analysis of 254 studies: spaced practice beat massed practice in 259 out of 271 comparisons.Spacing works across ages, subjects, and skills.
Kang (2016)Optimal gap ≈ 10–20% of the time until the test. For a May exam, that means revisiting material every 3–6 weeks from the start of Year 10.You can plan exactly when to revisit a topic.
Sisti et al. (2007)Neurons form stronger connections during the “almost forgotten” moment of retrieval.Struggling to recall IS the learning, not a sign you’ve failed.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Learn a topic today — read the lesson, watch the video, write notes. Mark it in a diary or app with today’s date.
  2. 2
    Review in 24 hours — do a retrieval practice brain dump, or redo the knowledge check. 5–10 minutes.
  3. 3
    Review again in 3 days — if you got it right yesterday, push the gap. Repeat the retrieval.
  4. 4
    Review again in 7 days — by now the material is consolidating into long-term memory.
  5. 5
    Review again in 2–3 weeks — gap the next review to 14 days, then 30, then 60.
  6. 6
    If you fail a review — reset the schedule. Back to day 1. Don’t skip the reset — it’s the point of the system.
Example 1

Day 1: study the twelve Olympians — their names, domains, and principal symbols. Day 2: brain-dump all twelve with their attributes from memory, and write one myth, festival, or cult site linked to each (for example, the Panathenaic festival for Athena; the Oracle at Delphi for Apollo; the Olympic Games for Zeus). Day 7: test yourself again, this time also writing the Roman equivalent of each Olympian (Zeus / Jupiter; Poseidon / Neptune; Athena / Minerva and so on). Day 14: attempt a 4-mark source question cold, citing two named deities with correct attributes as supporting evidence.

Example 2

After first studying the material culture of Mycenae, schedule five reviews. By day 7, you should be able to recall not just the major features of the citadel — the Lion Gate, Grave Circle A, the Treasury of Atreus, the megaron — but also the specific details that earn marks: the dimensions of the Lion Gate lintel, the heraldic lions, what the shaft graves revealed about Mycenaean wealth and burial practice, and why the Mask of Agamemnon is significant as evidence. By day 30, you should be able to use these details as named material evidence in an extended response about the Homeric World, cross-referencing them with Odyssey descriptions of palace life.

Common Pitfalls

  • Reviewing too often. If it’s easy, the gap is too short. Make it harder by stretching the interval.
  • Reviewing too late. If you’ve completely forgotten, you’re essentially re-learning from scratch — you lose the benefit of spacing.
  • No written schedule. Spaced repetition works only if you actually do the reviews. Use a calendar, the StudyVault flashcard system, or a simple Leitner box.
  • Skipping resets when you fail. If you couldn’t recall the material, you haven’t learnt it — regardless of how far through the schedule you were.

When to Use This

This is the organising principle of your whole revision year — not a technique you pull out near the exam. From the first lesson of the course, log every topic you cover and schedule reviews at 1 day, 3 days, 7 days, 14 days, and 30 days. The StudyVault flashcard system does this automatically via the Leitner method — questions move between five boxes with intervals of 1, 2, 4, 7, and 14 days. When a card comes up, do it. When it doesn’t, don’t.

Active recall

Retrieval Practice

Test yourself — don’t just re-read.

What the Research Says

Retrieval practice is the act of pulling information out of your memory, rather than pushing it in. It sounds simple but it is the most powerful revision technique we have — stronger than highlighting, stronger than re-reading, stronger than watching videos. The harder the retrieval feels, the more your long-term memory is strengthening.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Roediger & Karpicke (2006)Students who self-tested once remembered 50% more a week later than those who re-read four times.Self-testing > re-reading, even when it feels harder.
Karpicke & Blunt (2011)Retrieval practice beat concept-mapping and elaborative study on a delayed test by ~50%.Works better than other “active” strategies that feel productive.
Agarwal et al. (2017)Low-stakes retrieval quizzes raised test scores by an average of one grade.Short regular quizzing moves your real exam score.
Smith et al. (2016)Students who practised retrieval scored higher even on questions testing information they didn’t specifically retrieve.Builds the skill of remembering itself, not just the facts.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Study a chunk of content — read through a lesson, watch a video, or cover a topic in class. Don’t try to memorise. Just understand.
  2. 2
    Close everything — book shut, tab closed, notes flipped over. The whole point is that you cannot see the material.
  3. 3
    Write down everything you can remember — no looking back. This is called a “brain dump.” Write until you run out. It should feel uncomfortable.
  4. 4
    Check against the source — open the lesson. Mark what you missed in a different colour. Don’t just glance — properly compare.
  5. 5
    Target the gaps — re-study only the parts you missed. Not the whole lesson again. Just the holes.
  6. 6
    Retest tomorrow — hit the same topic again within 24 hours. The second attempt is where the learning locks in.
Example 1 — The five life stages and their age bands

After studying the five life stages, close the lesson and write all five from memory with their exact age bands: infancy (0–2), childhood (3–10), adolescence (11–19), adulthood (20–64), later adulthood (65+). For each stage, add two PIES milestones — for example, “Infancy: sits unaided by 6 months (physical); first words by 12 months (intellectual).” Check back and highlight any stage you mis-labelled or whose age band you got wrong. Examiners award marks only for the specification wording, so precision on age bands is the whole game.

Example 2 — Piaget’s four cognitive stages

Brain-dump Piaget’s four stages completely from memory: sensorimotor (0–2), pre-operational (2–7), concrete operational (7–11), formal operational (12+). Many students mis-map these onto the wrong life stage or confuse the two middle stages. After the dump, write one care-setting example next to each stage: “Concrete operational — Bryn Roberts, aged 4, at nursery can sort blocks by colour but cannot yet think abstractly about rules.” Wait three days and retest cold. The stage-names-with-age-bands format matches exactly what the exam asks for.

Common Pitfalls

  • Peeking. If you look back during the brain dump, you’re not doing retrieval — you’re doing copying. Harder is better.
  • Only doing it once. One pass strengthens memory a little. Spaced repeats strengthen it permanently. Come back to the same topic 2–3 times over a week.
  • Doing it too soon after studying. If you retrieve while the material is still in short-term memory, it’s too easy to count. Leave at least 30 minutes between studying and testing.
  • Stopping when it feels difficult. Desirable difficulty is the whole point. If it feels easy, your memory isn’t being challenged and you’re not learning.

When to Use This

Build it in every week, from the start of your course through to your exams. Aim for 15–20 minutes per session, two or three times a week. The last two weeks before an exam is when retrieval practice becomes your main tool — swap passive reading for brain dumps and flashcards. On StudyVault, the Knowledge Check and Flashcard buttons in every lesson sidebar are retrieval practice in disguise — use them.

Timed Practice

Simulate the real thing — including the time pressure.

What the Research Says

Knowing the content is only half of an exam. The other half is managing time, reading questions accurately under pressure, writing neatly when your hand hurts, and staying calm when you don’t know one of the questions. These are all skills — and like any skill, they need practice. Timed practice is how you build them.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Soderstrom & Bjork (2015)Transfer-appropriate processing: performance is best when the practice conditions closely match the test conditions.Practise in the conditions you’ll be tested in.
Agarwal et al. (2017)Students who did timed practice tests scored higher even on unseen questions.Builds generalisable exam skill, not just familiarity.
Yerkes & Dodson (1908)Performance is best at MODERATE arousal — some pressure helps, too much hurts.Simulated pressure builds tolerance for real pressure.
Hinze & Rapp (2014)Students who experienced test-like practice reported 30% less exam anxiety.Familiarity reduces fear. Fear reduces performance.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Start small — begin with one timed question or one section. Don’t jump straight to full papers. Build the muscle gradually.
  2. 2
    Match the exam mark-to-time ratio — Classical Civilisation papers allocate approximately 1 minute per mark. An 8-mark essay should take no more than 8 minutes; a 10-mark question no more than 10. Time yourself accordingly.
  3. 3
    Remove distractions — phone in another room, no music, no notes. The real exam hall has none of these.
  4. 4
    Handwrite — the exam is handwritten. Typing is faster and feels more productive, but it doesn’t train the same skill. Your hand will hurt on the day and that’s normal.
  5. 5
    Mark with the mark scheme honestly — use StudyVault’s per-question mark schemes or a teacher-provided one. Be harsh on yourself — underscoring now prevents overconfidence later.
  6. 6
    Do a full paper under conditions a month before the exam — uninterrupted, correct time, no music. One per subject, one per week in the final stretch.
Example 1

Set an 8-minute timer and attempt this question cold: “How does Homer use the Cyclops episode to explore ideas about civilised and uncivilised behaviour?” Write by hand, no notes. Use the source-based argument scaffold: make a claim (the Cyclops represents the opposite of civilised Greek values), cite a specific literary detail (he eats his guests rather than hosting them — a direct inversion of xenia), add a material evidence parallel where you can (the contrast with the well-ordered Mycenaean megaron as a space for feasting and gift exchange), present an alternative view (the Cyclops is also portrayed with a degree of pathos — he prays to Poseidon, his own father — which complicates a simple monster reading), then reach a judgement. When the timer goes, stop. Mark it: did you make a claim, name a source, engage with an alternative, and conclude?

Example 2

Work through a 10-mark extended response under timed conditions: “How important was the concept of kleos in shaping the behaviour of Homeric heroes?” Allocate roughly 2 minutes to plan your argument scaffold before you write: define kleos (glory through great deeds, preserved in song); cite Odysseus’s behaviour (revealing his name to the Cyclops at the cost of Poseidon’s wrath — kleos overrides caution); the homecoming (the bow contest as public proof of identity and heroic status); the alternative view (Odysseus frequently uses disguise and deception, suggesting kleos is balanced against practical survival); your conclusion (kleos is the primary driver but Odysseus is unique among Homeric heroes in subordinating it when necessary). Write your answer in the remaining 8 minutes, then stop regardless of whether you have finished. Record which parts of the scaffold you reached — if you ran out before covering the counterargument, practise planning speed in the next session.

Common Pitfalls

  • Stopping when the timer runs out and ignoring the unfinished bit. Note what you’d have written — that’s the data about your pace.
  • Using notes during “timed” practice. It’s not timed practice — it’s open-book practice. Useful, but different.
  • Only doing it in the last fortnight. Too late — you’ve not left time to fix the weaknesses the practice reveals.
  • Not marking honestly. Marking your own work gently protects feelings now and destroys results later.

When to Use This

From 10 weeks out, do at least one timed practice per topic per week — usually a single question at first, building to full sections and then full papers. In the final month, do at least one full timed paper. Always mark it against the actual scheme and note your pace. For the 8- and 10-mark extended responses specifically, practise the argument scaffold (claim → named literary evidence → named material evidence → alternative view → judgement) until it becomes automatic before the exam.

  4. Full paper, timed
  5. Full paper, exam conditions

Interleaving

Mix topics in one session — don’t block them.

What the Research Says

Most students revise by blocking — an hour on the Olympians, an hour on Mycenae, an hour on the Odyssey episodes. It feels productive and the topic seems clear by the end. Interleaving is the opposite: you jump between topics inside a single session. It feels worse at the time, and you’ll make more mistakes. But when the real exam arrives, you will be dramatically better at knowing which concept to apply — and that is usually the hardest part of any Classical Civilisation question.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Rohrer & Taylor (2007)Students who interleaved topics scored 43% higher on delayed tests than blocked-practice students.Same time spent — huge difference in exam performance.
Birnbaum et al. (2013)Interleaved learners felt LESS confident during practice but performed BETTER in the test.If revision feels too easy, interleave.
Bjork & Bjork (2011)Desirable difficulties — including interleaving — create durable long-term learning at the cost of short-term performance.Short-term struggle is the price of long-term gain.
Taylor & Rohrer (2010)Benefit was largest when topics looked superficially similar — students learnt to DISTINGUISH them.Most useful where students confuse similar concepts.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Pick 3–5 related topics — topics that share a paper, a theme, or a question type. Similar enough that students confuse them.
  2. 2
    Make a mixed question set — 10–15 questions drawn randomly from all the topics. Don’t tell yourself which topic each question belongs to.
  3. 3
    Attempt each question cold — first step is identifying what’s being asked. That identification is the skill you’re training.
  4. 4
    Mark after every question — note which topic each one was. Pay attention to mis-identifications — those are the highest-value gaps.
  5. 5
    Rebuild a new mixed set tomorrow — same topics, different questions. Different order. Over time, misclassifications drop.
  6. 6
    Expect to feel worse than blocked practice — that’s the right feeling. Your exam self will thank you.
Example 1

Create a 15-question mixed set spanning Myth & Religion topics: the twelve Olympians and their attributes, the labours of Heracles, Greek temple architecture and the three orders (Doric, Ionic, Corinthian), religious festivals, foundation myths, and the geography of the underworld. Because all of these relate to Greek religion and myth, exam questions can sound deceptively similar. Working through them in random order forces you to identify whether a question asks about a specific deity, an architectural feature, a festival practice, or a mythological narrative — a distinction that separates short-answer identification marks from developed analytical responses.

Example 2

In the final weeks before the exam, interleave Myth & Religion source questions (for example, “What does this image of Heracles tell us about how the Greeks viewed heroism?”) with Homeric World source questions (for example, “What does the Cyclops episode reveal about the importance of xenia in Homeric society?”). Switching between literary analysis and material-culture analysis in one sitting closely mirrors the actual exam experience, where students must identify which type of source they are analysing — literary, visual, or archaeological — before they can deploy the right analytical approach.

Common Pitfalls

  • Random, not related. Interleaving Classical Civilisation with Geography is just subject-switching. Interleave WITHIN Classical Civilisation — related concepts that students confuse, such as Greek and Roman names for the same gods, or architectural orders.
  • Giving up when it feels hard. The discomfort is the signal that it’s working. Don’t revert to blocked practice because interleaving feels slow.
  • Labelling the topic at the top of each question. Defeats the point — the identification IS the training.
  • Using it too early in learning. You need baseline familiarity with each topic first. Interleaving is for consolidation, not first exposure.

When to Use This

Once you’ve covered a handful of related topics — usually partway through a term — start weaving them into mixed practice sessions. Very useful in the final 8–10 weeks before exams when you’re moving from learning to applying. Full past papers are the ultimate interleaving exercise, because they force you to identify question types cold and decide whether to draw on literary, visual, or material evidence.

Quick Reference
~30–45 minutes per session

Steps

  1. Pick 3–5 related topics
  2. Build a mixed set
  3. Attempt cold
  4. Mark & note topic
  5. Fix misclassifications
  6. Expect discomfort

Timed Practice

Simulate the real thing — including the time pressure.

What the Research Says

Knowing the content is only half of an exam. The other half is managing time, reading questions accurately under pressure, writing neatly when your hand hurts, and staying calm when you don’t know one of the questions. These are all skills — and like any skill, they need practice. Timed practice is how you build them.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Soderstrom & Bjork (2015)Transfer-appropriate processing: performance is best when the practice conditions closely match the test conditions.Practise in the conditions you’ll be tested in.
Agarwal et al. (2017)Students who did timed practice tests scored higher even on unseen questions.Builds generalisable exam skill, not just familiarity.
Yerkes & Dodson (1908)Performance is best at MODERATE arousal — some pressure helps, too much hurts.Simulated pressure builds tolerance for real pressure.
Hinze & Rapp (2014)Students who experienced test-like practice reported 30% less exam anxiety.Familiarity reduces fear. Fear reduces performance.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Start small — begin with one timed question or one section. Don’t jump straight to full papers. Build the muscle gradually.
  2. 2
    Match the exam mark-to-time ratio — OCR PE allocates approximately 1 minute per mark. A 9-mark extended response should take no more than 9 minutes. Time yourself accordingly.
  3. 3
    Remove distractions — phone in another room, no music, no notes. The real exam hall has none of these.
  4. 4
    Handwrite — the exam is handwritten. Typing is faster and feels more productive, but it doesn’t train the same skill. Your hand will hurt on the day and that’s normal.
  5. 5
    Mark with the mark scheme honestly — use StudyVault’s per-question mark schemes or a teacher-provided one. Be harsh on yourself — underscoring now prevents overconfidence later.
  6. 6
    Do a full paper under conditions a month before the exam — uninterrupted, correct time, no music. One per subject, one per week in the final stretch.
Example 1

Set a 9-minute timer and attempt this past-paper question cold: “Evaluate the use of interval training for a 400m runner. Refer to the principles of training in your answer.” Write by hand, no notes. When the timer goes, stop. Mark it against the OCR mark scheme: check that your answer names specific principles (progressive overload, specificity, reversibility), applies them to the athlete, and includes a reasoned evaluation — not just a list. The gap between what you wrote and what the scheme awards is exactly what to practise next.

Example 2

Work through a full Paper 2 section on sports psychology under timed conditions: allocate 1 minute per mark, answer all questions including the 9-mark extended response, and stop when the time is up regardless of whether you have finished. Mark your work and record which question types overran — typically the extended response and the 4-mark “explain using an example” questions. Practise those types specifically in the following session.

Common Pitfalls

  • Stopping when the timer runs out and ignoring the unfinished bit. Note what you’d have written — that’s the data about your pace.
  • Using notes during “timed” practice. It’s not timed practice — it’s open-book practice. Useful, but different.
  • Only doing it in the last fortnight. Too late — you’ve not left time to fix the weaknesses the practice reveals.
  • Not marking honestly. Marking your own work gently protects feelings now and destroys results later.

When to Use This

From 10 weeks out, do at least one timed practice per subject per week — usually a single section at first, building to full papers. In the final month, do at least one full timed paper per subject. Always mark it against the actual scheme and note your pace.

Quick Reference
Paper time + ~30 min marking

Build-up schedule

  1. One question, timed
  2. One section, timed
  3. Half a paper, timed
  4. Full paper, timed
  5. Full paper, exam conditions
  6. Mock week, all papers
