Interleaving

Mix topics in one session — don’t block them.

What the Research Says

Most students revise by blocking — an hour on development, an hour on life factors, an hour on health promotion. It feels productive and the topic seems clear by the end. Interleaving is the opposite: you jump between topics inside a single session. It feels worse at the time, and you’ll make more mistakes. But when the real exam arrives, you will be dramatically better at knowing which idea a question is testing — and that is usually the hardest part of the stimulus-based questions.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Rohrer & Taylor (2007)Students who interleaved topics scored 43% higher on delayed tests than blocked-practice students.Same time spent — huge difference in exam performance.
Birnbaum et al. (2013)Interleaved learners felt LESS confident during practice but performed BETTER in the test.If revision feels too easy, interleave.
Bjork & Bjork (2011)Desirable difficulties — including interleaving — create durable long-term learning at the cost of short-term performance.Short-term struggle is the price of long-term gain.
Taylor & Rohrer (2010)Benefit was largest when topics looked superficially similar — students learnt to DISTINGUISH them.Most useful where students confuse related ideas.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Pick 3–5 related topics — topics that share a paper, a theme, or a question type. Similar enough that students confuse them.
  2. 2
    Make a mixed problem set — 10–15 questions drawn from all the topics. Don’t label which topic each question belongs to.
  3. 3
    Attempt each question cold — the first step is identifying what’s being asked. That identification is the skill you’re training.
  4. 4
    Mark after every question — note which topic area each one was. Pay attention to mis-identifications — those are the highest-value gaps.
  5. 5
    Rebuild a new mixed set tomorrow — same topics, different questions, different order. Over time, misclassifications drop.
  6. 6
    Expect to feel worse than blocked practice — that’s the right feeling. Your exam self will thank you.
Example 1 — Development theory topic mix

Mix questions from Piaget’s cognitive stages, Kohlberg’s moral stages, and Bowlby’s attachment theory in one 40-minute session. Write 12 questions on separate slips: four from each area, shuffled. Before each question, ask yourself: “Is this about cognitive development, moral development, or social-emotional attachment?” Students frequently confuse Bowlby (the existence of the attachment bond) with Ainsworth (the categorisation into secure vs insecure) — the identification exercise in revision prevents losing marks on what should be easy questions about named theorists.

Example 2 — Life factors, lifestyle choices and life events topic mix

Mix questions from the thirteen life factors, lifestyle choices (diet, activity, smoking, drug use) and expected/unexpected life events in one session. A stimulus question such as “Iona Stewart (16, care leaver) has started smoking and recently experienced redundancy from her part-time job. Discuss the PIES impact on Iona” draws on life factor (care-leaver background), lifestyle choice (smoking) AND life event (redundancy) simultaneously — exactly what a 6-mark ‘discuss’ question demands. Blocked revision never practises this combination. Interleaving does.

Common Pitfalls

  • Interleaving before you know the basics. You need to know each topic individually first. Use interleaving once you’ve studied both units — not as a first-pass strategy.
  • Giving up because it feels hard. Difficulty during interleaved practice is the signal it’s working. Persist.
  • Mixing unrelated topics. Interleaving works best when the topics are related enough to be confused. Mix topics within the same unit — life stages, PIES, development theories — not with unrelated subjects.
  • Not checking mis-identifications. The mistake is the data. If you mislabelled a question as being about ‘life factors’ when it was about ‘lifestyle choices’, that confusion is exactly what needs fixing.

When to Use This

Start interleaving once you have studied all five topic areas at least once. In the final six weeks before the exam, replace most blocked revision with interleaved mixed sets. Particularly powerful the week before the exam when you want to simulate the scrambled order questions appear in on the actual paper.

Quick Reference
~40 minutes per interleaved session

Steps

  1. Pick 3–5 related topics
  2. Build mixed question set
  3. Identify the topic first
  4. Attempt the question
  5. Mark every question
  6. Rebuild tomorrow

Structured notes

Knowledge Organisers

One page per topic — the whole picture at a glance.

What the Research Says

A knowledge organiser is a single side of A4 that captures everything a student needs to know about a topic — key vocabulary, essential facts, core concepts, and connections between them. Used properly, it becomes the base layer of your revision: the thing you keep coming back to, the thing you redraw from memory, the thing you carry on the bus. Used badly, it becomes a wall of dense text that nobody reads.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Willingham (2017)Students need to store facts in long-term memory before they can think critically about them. Knowledge organisers are the storage scaffold.Not old-fashioned — cognitive prerequisite for analysis.
Counsell (2018)Used in UK schools to reduce cognitive load by pre-structuring the material students encounter.Reduces working memory demand during lessons.
Sweller (1988)Cognitive Load Theory: well-organised schemas free up working memory for higher-order tasks.A well-designed organiser makes hard questions easier.
Oakes & Griffin (2017)Students who made their OWN organisers outperformed those given finished ones.Making is learning. Receiving is not.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    One topic per organiser — a unit, a theme, a mythological cycle. Not the whole of Myth & Religion. Too broad and it becomes a dense textbook page.
  2. 2
    Divide the page into 4–6 sections — typically: Key Vocabulary, Key Sources (literary and material), Core Concepts, Sketch Visuals, Connections to Other Topics, Common Exam Questions. The structure forces you to categorise.
  3. 3
    Keep it to one side of A4 — the constraint is the point. If it doesn’t fit, the material isn’t yet compressed into the essentials.
  4. 4
    Use tiny structural visuals — a mini temple plan showing the naos and pronaos, a compact sketch of the Lion Gate, a small table of the three orders. Dual coding applies: words + visuals beat words alone.
  5. 5
    Redraw it from memory weekly — this is where the learning is. A finished organiser you never revisit is wasted. The redrawn one is retrieval practice in disguise.
  6. 6
    Annotate over time — when you learn something new that fits, add it. When a connection becomes clearer, draw the link. The organiser evolves.
Example 1

Create a knowledge organiser for the Olympian gods. Sections: Key Vocabulary (deity, attribute, epithet, cult, festival); a table of all twelve Olympians with their domain, principal symbol, and Roman equivalent (Zeus / Jupiter, Hera / Juno, Poseidon / Neptune, Demeter / Ceres, Athena / Minerva, Apollo / Apollo, Artemis / Diana, Ares / Mars, Aphrodite / Venus, Hephaestus / Vulcan, Hermes / Mercury, Dionysus / Bacchus); a mini sketch of one deity’s attributes; Key Myths (one per deity, maximum five words); Connections (links to temple architecture — which deities had the most important cult temples and why). Fit it on one side of A4, redraw from memory after three days. The Roman equivalents column is the most commonly dropped under exam pressure.

Example 2

Create a knowledge organiser for the material culture of Mycenae. Sections: Key Vocabulary (citadel, megaron, cyclopean, shaft grave, tholos tomb, fresco); Key Sites and Artefacts (Lion Gate — function + heraldic lions; Grave Circle A — shaft graves, gold masks, evidence of elite burial; Treasury of Atreus — tholos form, corbelled entrance, Bronze Age engineering; the megaron — central hearth, throne, four columns, fresco programme); a tiny annotated sketch of the citadel layout; Connections to the Odyssey (feasting in the great hall, the palace of Alcinous, descriptions of bronze and gold wealth). Redraw the sketch from memory a week later — the relative positions of the Lion Gate, Grave Circle A, and the megaron are the most frequently mixed up, and source questions reward students who can place artefacts in their architectural context.

Common Pitfalls

  • Copying the textbook. A dense page of 8pt text isn’t a knowledge organiser — it’s a photocopy. Compress ruthlessly.
  • One page per subject. Too much, too diffuse. One page per topic — one for the Olympians, one for temple architecture, one for Mycenae, one for the Odyssey episodes.
  • Making one and never revisiting. The value is in the redrawing — not the original creation.
  • Using a downloaded one instead of making your own. Research is clear: making beats receiving. Teacher-provided organisers are useful for structure only.

When to Use This

Start one at the beginning of each topic, as you’re learning it. Refine as your understanding grows. Redraw the whole set from memory in the final month before exams — one topic per day. Carry a folder of your organisers to every revision session. Use them as the spine of retrieval practice: cover the organiser, brain-dump, then check.

Quick Reference
~45 minutes to create, 15 to redraw

Sections

  1. Key Vocabulary
  2. Key Sources (literary + material)
  3. Sketch Visuals
  4. Core Concepts
  5. Connections to Other Topics
  6. Common Misconceptions

Elaborative Interrogation

Ask “why?” and “how?” until the facts become explanations.

What the Research Says

Facts in isolation are fragile. Facts connected by explanations survive. Elaborative interrogation is the habit of asking “why is that true?” and “how does that work?” about every fact you learn — and forcing yourself to answer. The answer doesn’t need to be perfect. The act of trying to answer is what builds the mental connections that turn memorised facts into understood explanations.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Pressley et al. (1988)Asking “why?” during reading boosted recall by 40–70% compared to silent reading.Works even when the answer is imperfect.
Dunlosky et al. (2013)Rated “moderate utility” in the APS review — robust across subjects and ages, especially when applied to new material that builds on existing knowledge.Best for consolidating material you half-know.
Smith & Holliday (2006)Science students who self-explained while studying scored significantly higher on transfer questions requiring application.Builds the ability to USE the knowledge, not just recall it.
Chi et al. (1994)Self-explanation was a stronger predictor of understanding than prior knowledge.Even weaker students catch up by explaining to themselves.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Study a chunk of content — a lesson, a paragraph, a key fact. Anything where facts are being introduced.
  2. 2
    After each fact, ask “why?” — why is this true? Why does it matter? Why does the body respond this way?
  3. 3
    Then ask “how?” — how does this process work? How does it connect to the next topic? How would you explain it to someone with no PE background?
  4. 4
    Try to answer out loud — even if your answer is wrong, the attempt activates deeper processing. Write your answer in the margin.
  5. 5
    Check your answer against the source — does the text support your explanation? If not, update it. The correction matters more than the first guess.
  6. 6
    Build chains — once you’ve asked “why?” once, ask it again of your answer. Push until you hit a genuinely fundamental fact. This is where deep understanding forms.
Example 1

Fact: “Stroke volume increases during exercise.” Ask why: because venous return increases, stretching the ventricle walls. Ask why again: because skeletal muscle contractions compress veins, and breathing patterns create pressure gradients (the Starling mechanism). Ask how: the stretched walls contract more forcefully, ejecting a greater volume per beat. Ask why that matters: it explains why cardiac output rises without heart rate increasing proportionally — a classic 4-mark chain of explanation on Paper 1.

Example 2

Fact: “Intrinsic motivation is more durable than extrinsic motivation.” Ask why: because intrinsic drives come from personal satisfaction and self-determination rather than external rewards, which can be withdrawn. Ask how: this connects to self-determination theory — autonomy, competence, and relatedness. Ask why that matters for a coach: setting outcome goals (extrinsic) alongside personal best goals (intrinsic) better sustains an athlete’s commitment when external rewards are absent — an OCR Paper 2 application question.

Common Pitfalls

  • Accepting “I don’t know”. Take a guess. Even a wrong guess activates the processing. Then check and correct.
  • One “why?” and moving on. The real gains come from the third or fourth “why?”, when you hit the fundamentals.
  • Only asking the obvious questions. Push toward the explanations your teacher never gave you — those are where genuine learning happens.
  • Skipping the check. Unchecked wrong answers reinforce misunderstanding. Always verify against the source.

When to Use This

Any time you’re covering conceptual material — not just listing facts. Particularly powerful with physiological cause-and-effect chains (cardiovascular, respiratory, musculoskeletal) and with analytical topics (psychology, ethics in sport, socio-cultural influences) where the exam rewards explanation and application over recall. Build it into every lesson revisit, not as a separate session.

Quick Reference
Adds ~50% to reading time, transforms recall

Questions to ask

  1. Why is this true?
  2. How does it work?
  3. Why does it matter?
  4. How does it connect?
  5. Why now and not before?
  6. How would I explain this to a friend?

Retrieval Practice for Spanish

Test yourself on vocab and grammar — don’t just re-read

What It Is

Retrieval practice means pulling Spanish vocabulary, grammar rules, and phrases out of your memory without looking at your notes. Every time you successfully recall a word like el medio ambiente (the environment) or a verb form like tengo (I have), the memory trace gets stronger. Re-reading your vocab list feels productive, but it creates a false sense of confidence — the words look familiar without actually being learned.

For GCSE Spanish, retrieval practice is essential because the exam tests you across four skills — listening, speaking, reading, and writing — and all of them depend on vocabulary you can access quickly and accurately under pressure.

Why It Works

Research by Roediger & Karpicke (2006) showed that students who tested themselves remembered 80% of material after one week, compared to just 36% for those who re-read. For languages specifically, retrieval practice forces your brain to strengthen the link between the English meaning and the Spanish word — exactly the connection you need in the exam.

The struggle to remember is the point. When you can’t quite recall the Spanish for “unemployment” (el desempleo), the effort of searching your memory — even if you fail — makes the word stick better when you check the answer.

How to Do It: Step-by-Step

  1. 1
    Pick a topic — Choose one theme from the spec, such as Theme 1: People and Lifestyle (family, relationships, technology) or Theme 3: Current and Future Study and Employment.
  2. 2
    Study for 5 minutes — Read through the vocabulary, key phrases, and grammar points for that topic. Don’t write anything yet.
  3. 3
    Close everything — Put your notes away completely. No peeking. This is where the learning actually happens.
  4. 4
    Brain dump in Spanish — Write down every Spanish word, phrase, and grammar rule you can remember from that topic. Include verbs with their conjugations, opinions (creo que, en mi opinión, me parece que), and connectives (sin embargo, además, por lo tanto). Aim for 5–8 minutes.
  5. 5
    Check and colour-code gaps — Open your notes and compare. Use a different colour to add anything you missed or got wrong. These gaps are your priority for next session.

When and How Often

Study
5 min Brain dump
8 min Check gaps
5 min

One cycle takes about 18 minutes. Do 2–3 cycles per session covering different topics or skills. Use retrieval practice every time you revise Spanish — it should be your default method.

First attempt — from memory only

la ciudad — city. el pueblo — village. hay — there is/are. las tiendas — shops. el cine — cinema. Me gusta vivir aquí porque es tranquilo…

After checking — gaps filled in green

la ciudad — city. el pueblo — village. las afueras — outskirts. el barrio — neighbourhood. hay — there is/are. las tiendas — shops. el cine — cinema. el polideportivo — sports centre. el ayuntamiento — town hall. la comisaria — police station. Me gusta vivir aquí porque es tranquilo. Lo mejor de mi ciudad es que hay mucho que hacer. Lo peor es que hay demasiado tráfico y contaminación.

What this reveals: The first attempt had basic nouns but missed specific places (polideportivo, ayuntamiento), neighbourhood vocabulary (afueras, barrio), and the key phrases for expressing positive/negative opinions (lo mejor/lo peor). These become the focus of the next retrieval session.

Cover the answers and test yourself:

  • Name 5 family members in Spanish with the correct article (el/la).
  • Conjugate tener (to have) in the present tense for all 6 persons.
  • Write 3 opinion phrases you could use in the writing exam.
  • Translate: “In my opinion, social media is useful but can be dangerous.”
  • Give 5 time phrases you could use to talk about your future plans (e.g. el año que viene).
  • Name 4 school subjects and say whether you like or dislike each one with a reason.
  • Write the preterite tense of ir (to go) for yo, él/ella, nosotros.
  • List 5 connectives beyond y (and) and pero (but).

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Re-reading vocab lists passively — Staring at a list of words feels productive but barely strengthens memory. Close the list and write the Spanish from memory.
  • ❌
    Only testing English → Spanish — You also need Spanish → English for the reading and listening exams. Practise both directions.
  • ❌
    Ignoring verb conjugations — Vocabulary on its own is not enough. If you can’t conjugate ir, ser, tener, hacer in present, preterite, and future, your writing and speaking will suffer.

Spaced Repetition for Vocabulary Retention

The science of when to revise each word

What It Is

Spaced repetition means reviewing vocabulary and grammar at increasing intervals — rather than cramming everything in one session. You revise a word the day after you first learn it, then three days later, then a week, then two weeks, and so on. Each time you successfully recall it, the gap before the next review gets longer.

For GCSE Spanish, this is transformative. You need to know approximately 1,700 words across three themes, plus verb conjugations in multiple tenses. Cramming the night before won’t work — spaced repetition will.

Why It Works

The “forgetting curve” (Ebbinghaus, 1885) shows that we forget roughly 70% of new information within 24 hours — unless we review it. Each review resets the curve and makes the memory last longer. Spaced repetition exploits this by timing your reviews at the exact point where you’re about to forget.

A meta-analysis by Cepeda et al. (2006) found that spaced practice was more effective than massed practice in 259 out of 271 cases. For language learning, where you’re building thousands of word-meaning associations, spacing is especially powerful.

How to Do It: Step-by-Step

  1. 1
    Choose your system — Use a digital app (Anki, Quizlet) or a physical card box with dividers labelled Day 1, Day 3, Day 7, Day 14, Day 30. Digital apps handle the scheduling automatically.
  2. 2
    Add 10–15 new words per day — Don’t add everything at once. Group by AQA theme and sub-topic (e.g. Theme 1: Mi familia). Include the Spanish, English, gender (el/la), and an example sentence.
  3. 3
    Review due cards daily — Each day, review words that are “due” according to the schedule. If you get a word right, it moves to a longer interval. If you get it wrong, it resets to the shortest interval.
  4. 4
    Include verb conjugations as separate cards — Don’t just learn infinitives. Create cards for: hablar (present) → hablo, hablas, habla, hablamos, habláis, hablan. Then separate cards for preterite, future, and conditional forms.
  5. 5
    Test both directions — You need English → Spanish (for writing and speaking) AND Spanish → English (for reading and listening). Create cards for both.

The Spacing Schedule

ReviewIntervalWhat Happens
1st review1 day after learningCatches words about to be forgotten — expect to struggle
2nd review3 days laterMemory starts to consolidate — correct words feel easier
3rd review7 days laterWords entering medium-term memory — most should feel familiar
4th review14 days laterLong-term storage forming — only forgotten words need extra work
5th review30 days laterIf you still remember it, it’s locked in for the exam

When and How Often

Review due words
10 min Add new words
5 min Example sentences
5 min

20 minutes daily is ideal. The key is consistency — 20 minutes every day beats 2 hours once a week. Start at least 3 months before the exam so words have time to reach long-term memory through multiple review cycles.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Adding too many words at once — Adding 50 words on Day 1 creates a review avalanche by Day 3. Stick to 10–15 new words per day maximum.
  • ❌
    Skipping days — Missing a day breaks the spacing schedule and lets words slip back down the forgetting curve. Even 10 minutes on a busy day is better than nothing.
  • ❌
    Learning words in isolation — A word without context is harder to remember and harder to use. Always include an example sentence on the back of each card.

Flashcard Strategies for Spanish

Master vocabulary, verb forms, and key phrases with active recall

What It Is

Active recall with flashcards means testing yourself by looking at one side of a card and trying to produce the answer before flipping it over. Unlike passive review (reading a vocab list), active recall forces your brain to search for and retrieve the information — which is exactly what you’ll need to do in the AQA Spanish exam.

For Spanish, flashcards aren’t just for vocabulary. You can use them for verb conjugations, key phrases, grammar rules, and even full sentences. The best flashcard systems combine active recall with spaced repetition for maximum retention.

Why It Works

Karpicke & Roediger (2008) found that students who used retrieval-based flashcard study recalled 80% of foreign language vocabulary after a week, compared to 36% for students who used repeated study alone. The act of generating the answer — not just recognising it — creates a much stronger memory trace.

For languages, flashcards are especially effective because they mirror the translation task: you see a prompt and must produce the target word. This is exactly what the writing and speaking exams demand.

How to Do It: Step-by-Step

  1. 1
    Create four types of card — Don’t limit yourself to simple word-for-word translations. Build a varied deck:
    • Vocab cards: English on front, Spanish (with gender) on back
    • Conjugation cards: Infinitive + tense on front, full conjugation table on back
    • Phrase cards: English phrase on front, Spanish phrase on back
    • Sentence cards: Gapped sentence on front, completed sentence on back
  2. 2
    Always include context — On the back of every vocab card, write a short example sentence. For el acoso (bullying), write: “El acoso escolar es un problema grave en muchos institutos.” Context makes words easier to remember and easier to use in writing.
  3. 3
    Say the answer out loud — Before flipping, say the Spanish word aloud. This builds pronunciation confidence for the speaking exam and engages an extra memory pathway (auditory).
  4. 4
    Sort into piles — After each session, sort cards into “know it” and “don’t know it.” Next session, start with the “don’t know” pile. Only retire a card after you’ve recalled it correctly three sessions in a row.
  5. 5
    Reverse the direction — Once you can go English → Spanish, flip the deck and practise Spanish → English. You need both directions for reading/listening (Spanish → English) and writing/speaking (English → Spanish).

When and How Often

Review existing cards
10 min Learn new cards
5 min Say aloud
5 min

20 minutes daily is optimal. Review your “don’t know” pile first, then work through due cards, then add 8–12 new cards. Little and often beats marathon sessions.

Gap-fill cards test grammar in context. The front shows a sentence with a blank; you must produce the correct form:

Front (gapped sentence)Back (answer)

These cards are especially useful for practising the trickier grammar structures that earn higher marks in the writing exam.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Only making English → Spanish cards — You need the reverse direction too. Reading and listening exams require you to understand Spanish, not just produce it.
  • ❌
    Single words with no context — A card that just says la biblioteca = library is harder to remember than one with a full sentence. Always add an example.
  • ❌
    Never saying answers aloud — The speaking exam requires you to pronounce words correctly. If you only ever read silently, you’ll hesitate on pronunciation under exam pressure.

How to Use Past Papers for AQA Spanish

Maximise your marks by understanding how the exam works

What It Is

Practice papers means working through real Spanish past papers under exam conditions, then self-marking against the official mark schemes. This is the single most effective way to prepare for the exam because it trains you to handle the specific question formats, timing pressures, and mark allocation that AQA uses.

Spanish (8692) has four papers: Listening (25%), Speaking (25%), Reading (25%), and Writing (25%). Each paper has its own format, timing, and mark scheme — and you need to practise all four.

Why It Works

Research consistently shows that practice testing is the most effective revision strategy (Dunlosky et al., 2013). For languages, past papers are especially valuable because they reveal the exact question styles AQA uses — such as “translate this passage into English” (reading), “write approximately 150 words about…” (writing), and the multi-step listening comprehension questions.

Examiners report that students lose marks not because they don’t know the Spanish, but because they don’t understand the question format. Practising past papers fixes this.

AQA Spanish Paper Overview

PaperDurationKey Question Types
Paper 1: Listening 35 min (F) / 45 min (H) 40 (F) / 50 (H) Multiple choice, gap-fill in English, answer in English/Spanish, match-up
Paper 2: Speaking 7–9 min (F) / 10–12 min (H) 60 Role play, photo card, general conversation
Paper 3: Reading 45 min (F) / 60 min (H) 60 Multiple choice, match-up, answer in English/Spanish, translation into English
Paper 4: Writing 1 hr (F) / 1 hr 15 min (H) 50 (F) / 60 (H) Structured writing, open writing (90/150 words), translation into Spanish

How to Do It: Step-by-Step

  1. 1
    Start with one paper at a time — Don’t try all four in one session. Begin with reading (the most accessible), then listening, then writing, then speaking. Do one paper per session in the first weeks.
  2. 2
    Use strict exam timing — Set a timer and stick to it. For Paper 3 Reading (Higher), that’s 60 minutes. If you run out of time, note where you stopped — time management is a skill that needs practice.
  3. 3
    Self-mark against the mark scheme — This is the most important step. mark schemes show exactly what earns marks. For the writing paper, check whether you’ve hit the content points, used a range of tenses, and included opinions with justifications.
  4. 4
    Track your errors by type — Keep a log of mistakes. Are you losing marks on verb tenses? Vocabulary gaps? Misreading question rubrics? Spelling? This tells you exactly what to revise next.
  5. 5
    Redo the same paper after 2 weeks — Revisiting a paper you’ve already attempted (and marked) shows whether you’ve actually fixed the problems. Your score should improve significantly.

When and How Often

Timed paper
45–75 min Self-mark
15 min Error log
10 min

In the final 6 weeks before the exam, aim for 2–3 timed papers per week, rotating between the four skills. In earlier months, do one per week alongside vocabulary and grammar revision.

Question (Higher, Q3): Write approximately 150 words in Spanish about a recent holiday. You must include: where you went and with whom, what you did, what you thought of the food, your plans for next year’s holiday.

El verano pasado fui a Barcelona con mi familia. Fuimos en avión. Visitamos la Sagrada Familia y nadamos en el mar. La comida era muy buena. Me gustó mucho la paella. El año que viene voy a ir a Francia.

El verano pasado fui a Barcelona con mi familia — mis padres y mi hermana menor. Viajamos en avión desde Manchester, lo cual fue emocionante porque era la primera vez que mi hermana volaba. Paper 1: Listening

  • Read all questions before the audio plays — you’ll know what to listen for.
  • On the first play, note key words. On the second play, confirm and add detail.
  • Watch for negatives (no, nunca, ni…ni) and distractors — AQA deliberately includes wrong answers in the audio.
  • If the question is in English, answer in English. If in Spanish, answer in Spanish.

Paper 2: Speaking

  • For the role play, practise all common scenarios (booking a hotel, buying tickets, describing problems).
  • For the photo card, prepare a structure: describe what you see, give an opinion, link to personal experience, use a different tense.
  • In the general conversation, aim for 3–4 sentences per answer. Include an opinion, a reason, and a different tense.

Paper 3: Reading

  • The translation into English section (at the end) is worth 10 marks — practise this specifically.
  • Use context clues for unfamiliar words. If you know contaminar (to pollute), you can guess contaminación.
  • Read the question carefully — “Why does Ana NOT want to go?” is very different from “Why does Ana want to go?”

Paper 4: Writing

  • Address every bullet point — missing one costs you content marks across the whole question.
  • For Higher, you MUST use three tenses (past, present, future/conditional) and include opinions with justifications.
  • The translation into Spanish (final question) is worth 10 marks. Practise translating sentences with mixed tenses.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Not checking the mark scheme — Doing a past paper without marking it is half the benefit wasted. The mark scheme shows you exactly what examiners reward.
  • ❌
    Only practising reading and writing — Listening and speaking are worth 50% of the total marks. Practise all four skills, not just the ones you can do at a desk.
  • ❌
    Ignoring the translation questions — Translation into English (reading) and into Spanish (writing) are worth 10 marks each. These are easy marks to gain with practice — or easy marks to lose without it.

Interleaving

Mix topics in one session — don’t block them.

What the Research Says

Most students revise by blocking — an hour on anatomy, an hour on training, an hour on psychology. It feels productive and the topic seems clear by the end. Interleaving is the opposite: you jump between topics inside a single session. It feels worse at the time, and you’ll make more mistakes. But when the real exam arrives, you will be dramatically better at knowing which technique to apply — and that is usually the hardest part of any exam question.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Rohrer & Taylor (2007)Students who interleaved topics scored 43% higher on delayed tests than blocked-practice students.Same time spent — huge difference in exam performance.
Birnbaum et al. (2013)Interleaved learners felt LESS confident during practice but performed BETTER in the test.If revision feels too easy, interleave.
Bjork & Bjork (2011)Desirable difficulties — including interleaving — create durable long-term learning at the cost of short-term performance.Short-term struggle is the price of long-term gain.
Taylor & Rohrer (2010)Benefit was largest when topics looked superficially similar — students learnt to DISTINGUISH them.Most useful where students confuse similar techniques.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Pick 3–5 related topics — topics that share a paper, a theme, or a question type. Similar enough that students confuse them.
  2. 2
    Make a mixed question set — 10–15 questions drawn randomly from all the topics. Don’t tell yourself which topic each question belongs to.
  3. 3
    Attempt each question cold — first step is identifying what’s being asked. That identification is the skill you’re training.
  4. 4
    Mark after every question — note which topic each one was. Pay attention to mis-identifications — those are the highest-value gaps.
  5. 5
    Rebuild a new mixed set tomorrow — same topics, different questions. Different order. Over time, misclassifications drop.
  6. 6
    Expect to feel worse than blocked practice — that’s the right feeling. Your exam self will thank you.
Example 1

Create a 15-question mixed set spanning Paper 1 topics: lever systems, antagonistic muscle pairs, types of muscle contraction (isotonic/isometric), components of fitness, and short-term effects of exercise. Because these areas all relate to movement and physiology, exam questions can sound deceptively similar. Working through them in random order forces you to identify whether a question is asking about classification, mechanism, or effect — a distinction that separates 4-mark answers from 6-mark ones.

Example 2

In the final weeks before the exam, interleave Paper 1 questions (e.g. “Explain the role of haemoglobin during aerobic exercise”) with Paper 2 questions (e.g. “Using Maslow’s hierarchy of needs, explain how a coach could motivate a young athlete”). Switching between physiology and sports psychology in one sitting closely mirrors the actual exam experience, where the paper moves between domains without warning.

Common Pitfalls

  • Random, not related. Interleaving PE with Geography is just subject-switching. Interleave WITHIN PE — related topics that students confuse.
  • Giving up when it feels hard. The discomfort is the signal that it’s working. Don’t revert to blocked practice because interleaving feels slow.
  • Labelling the topic at the top of each question. Defeats the point — the identification IS the training.
  • Using it too early in learning. You need baseline familiarity with each topic first. Interleaving is for consolidation, not first exposure.

When to Use This

Once you’ve covered a handful of related topics — usually partway through a term — start weaving them into mixed practice sessions. Very useful in the final 8–10 weeks before exams when you’re moving from learning to applying. Full past papers are the ultimate interleaving exercise, because they force you to identify question types cold.

Quick Reference
~30–45 minutes per session

Steps

  1. Pick 3–5 related topics
  2. Build a mixed set
  3. Attempt cold
  4. Mark & note topic
  5. Fix misclassifications
  6. Expect discomfort

Deep thinking

Elaborative Interrogation

Ask “why?” and “how?” until the facts become explanations.

What the Research Says

Facts in isolation are fragile. Facts connected by explanations survive. Elaborative interrogation is the habit of asking “why is that true?” and “how does that work?” about every fact you learn — and forcing yourself to answer. The answer doesn’t need to be perfect. The act of trying to answer is what builds the mental connections that turn memorised lists into understood explanations. This is exactly what examiners reward in the ‘explain’, ‘discuss’ and ‘evaluate’ questions.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Pressley et al. (1988)Asking “why?” during reading boosted recall by 40–70% compared to silent reading.Works even when the answer is imperfect.
Dunlosky et al. (2013)Rated “moderate utility” — robust across subjects and ages, especially when applied to new material that builds on existing knowledge.Best for consolidating material you half-know.
Smith & Holliday (2006)Students who self-explained while studying scored significantly higher on transfer questions requiring application.Builds the ability to USE the knowledge, not just recall it.
Chi et al. (1994)Self-explanation was a stronger predictor of understanding than prior knowledge.Even weaker students catch up by explaining to themselves.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Study a chunk of content — a lesson, a paragraph, a key fact. Anything where facts are being introduced.
  2. 2
    After each fact, ask “why?” — why is this true? Why does it matter for care? Why did the examiner include it?
  3. 3
    Then ask “how?” — how does this connect to the topic? How does it lead to what comes next? How would you explain it to someone else?
  4. 4
    Try to answer out loud or in writing — even if your answer is wrong, the attempt activates deeper processing. Write your answer in the margin.
  5. 5
    Check your answer against the source — does the lesson support your explanation? If not, update it. The correction matters more than the first guess.
  6. 6
    Build chains — once you’ve asked “why?” once, ask it again of your answer. Push until you hit a genuinely fundamental fact. This is where deep understanding forms.
Example 1 — Why Kohlberg’s moral stages matter for adolescent development

Fact: in the first stage of moral development, individuals obey rules to avoid punishment. Ask “why does this change in the second stage?” — because the individual begins to consider social agreements and relationships, not just personal consequences. Ask “how does that link to adolescence?” — Iona Stewart (16) moving into the second stage of moral reasoning is beginning to internalise social norms, which affects peer relationships and social development (S in PIES). Ask “why might some individuals not progress to the third stage?” — because limited education or social exposure can restrict moral reasoning development. That three-step chain is the reasoning structure a 4-mark applied question expects.

Example 2 — Why a high BMI does not automatically mean poor health

Fact: a BMI of ≥30 is classified as obese. Ask “why is BMI not the whole picture?” — because BMI does not distinguish between fat mass and muscle mass; a highly muscular individual may register as ‘obese’. Ask “how does the spec’s contributing-factors framework apply here?” — age, sex, lifestyle and environment all influence what a given BMI value means for that individual. Ask “why does this matter for interpreting Mr Caleb Owen’s (52) data?” — because his Type 2 diabetes is a comorbidity that affects how the health indicator data should be read alongside other indicators. You have just built the data-interpretation chain that 6-mark and 8-mark questions reward.

Common Pitfalls

  • Accepting “I don’t know”. Take a guess. Even a wrong guess activates the processing. Then check and correct.
  • One “why?” and moving on. The real gains come from the third or fourth “why?”, when you hit the fundamentals.
  • Only asking the obvious questions. Push toward the explanations your teacher never gave you — those are where genuine learning happens.
  • Skipping the check. Unchecked wrong answers reinforce misunderstanding. Always verify against the source.

When to Use This

Any time you are covering conceptual material — not just listing named items. Particularly powerful with cause-and-effect topics in Health & Social Care: why does low income affect physical and emotional PIES outcomes? How does insecure attachment in infancy affect social development in childhood? Why can two people with the same BMI have very different health states? Build it into every lesson revisit, not as a separate session. It adds around 50% to your reading time but makes everything else — retrieval, exam answers — significantly easier.

Quick Reference
Adds ~50% to reading time, transforms recall

The chain

  1. Read the fact
  2. Ask “why is this true?”
  3. Ask “how does it work?”
  4. Write your answer
  5. Check against the source
  6. Ask “why?” again of your answer

Retrieval Practice

Test yourself — don’t just re-read.

What the Research Says

Retrieval practice is the act of pulling information out of your memory, rather than pushing it in. It sounds simple but it is the most powerful revision technique we have — stronger than highlighting, stronger than re-reading, stronger than watching videos. The harder the retrieval feels, the more your long-term memory is strengthening.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Roediger & Karpicke (2006)Students who self-tested once remembered 50% more a week later than those who re-read four times.Self-testing > re-reading, even when it feels harder.
Karpicke & Blunt (2011)Retrieval practice beat concept-mapping and elaborative study on a delayed test by ~50%.Works better than other “active” strategies that feel productive.
Agarwal et al. (2017)Low-stakes retrieval quizzes raised GCSE-equivalent test scores by an average of one grade.Short regular quizzing moves your real exam score.
Smith et al. (2016)Students who practised retrieval scored higher even on questions testing information they didn’t specifically retrieve.Builds the skill of remembering itself, not just the facts.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Study a chunk of content — read through a StudyVault lesson, watch a video, or cover a topic in class. Don’t try to memorise. Just understand.
  2. 2
    Close everything — book shut, tab closed, notes flipped over. The whole point is that you cannot see the material.
  3. 3
    Write down everything you can remember — no looking back. This is called a “brain dump.” Write until you run out. It should feel uncomfortable.
  4. 4
    Check against the source — open the lesson. Mark what you missed in a different colour. Don’t just glance — properly compare.
  5. 5
    Target the gaps — re-study only the parts you missed. Not the whole lesson again. Just the holes.
  6. 6
    Retest tomorrow — hit the same topic again within 24 hours. The second attempt is where the learning locks in.
Example 1

After studying Islam, close your notes and brain-dump all Five Pillars from memory with one sentence explaining each (Shahadah, Salah, Zakah, Sawm, Hajj). Then test the Six Articles of Faith (Tawhid, Angels, Holy Books, Prophets, Day of Judgement, Al-Qadr). Check what you missed, then rewrite only the ones you got wrong. If you also confused the Sunni and Shi’a differences on leadership, that gap becomes your entire next session.

Example 2

After covering Paper 3 Philosophy, shut your notes and write down from memory Aquinas’s Five Ways — Unmoved Mover, Uncaused Cause, Contingency, Gradation, and Teleological Argument — with a one-sentence summary of each. Then attempt the Three Marks of Existence (impermanence, non-self, suffering) and the Four Noble Truths. The StudyVault Knowledge Check and Flashcard buttons in every lesson sidebar are retrieval practice in disguise — use them after every lesson.

Common Pitfalls

  • Peeking. If you look back during the brain dump, you’re not doing retrieval — you’re doing copying. Harder is better.
  • Only doing it once. One pass strengthens memory a little. Spaced repeats strengthen it permanently. Come back to the same topic 2–3 times over a week.
  • Doing it too soon after studying. If you retrieve while the material is still in short-term memory, it’s too easy to count. Leave at least 30 minutes between studying and testing.
  • Stopping when it feels difficult. Desirable difficulty is the whole point. If it feels easy, your memory isn’t being challenged and you’re not learning.

When to Use This

Build it in every week, from the start of Year 10 through to your exams. Aim for 15–20 minutes per subject, two or three times a week. The last two weeks before an exam is when retrieval practice becomes your main tool — swap passive reading for brain dumps and flashcards. On StudyVault, the Knowledge Check and Flashcard buttons in every lesson sidebar are retrieval practice in disguise — use them.

  2. Close everything
  3. Brain dump from memory
  4. Check gaps
  5. Re-study only the gaps
  6. Retest tomorrow

Retrieval Practice for French

Test yourself on vocab and grammar — don’t just re-read

What It Is

Retrieval practice means pulling French vocabulary, grammar rules, and phrases out of your memory without looking at your notes. Every time you successfully recall a word like l’environnement (the environment) or a verb form like j’ai (I have), the memory trace gets stronger. Re-reading your vocab list feels productive, but it creates a false sense of confidence — the words look familiar without actually being learned.

For GCSE French, retrieval practice is essential because the exam tests you across four skills — listening, speaking, reading, and writing — and all of them depend on vocabulary you can access quickly and accurately under pressure.

Why It Works

Research by Roediger & Karpicke (2006) showed that students who tested themselves remembered 80% of material after one week, compared to just 36% for those who re-read. For languages specifically, retrieval practice forces your brain to strengthen the link between the English meaning and the French word — exactly the connection you need in the exam.

The struggle to remember is the point. When you can’t quite recall the French for “unemployment” (le chômage), the effort of searching your memory — even if you fail — makes the word stick better when you check the answer.

How to Do It: Step-by-Step

  1. 1
    Pick a topic — Choose one theme from the spec, such as Theme 1: People and Lifestyle (family, relationships, technology) or Theme 3: Current and Future Study and Employment.
  2. 2
    Study for 5 minutes — Read through the vocabulary, key phrases, and grammar points for that topic. Don’t write anything yet.
  3. 3
    Close everything — Put your notes away completely. No peeking. This is where the learning actually happens.
  4. 4
    Brain dump in French — Write down every French word, phrase, and grammar rule you can remember from that topic. Include verbs with their conjugations, opinions (je pense que, à mon avis, il me semble que), and connectives (cependant, de plus, par conséquent). Aim for 5–8 minutes.
  5. 5
    Check and colour-code gaps — Open your notes and compare. Use a different colour to add anything you missed or got wrong. These gaps are your priority for next session.

When and How Often

Study
5 min Brain dump
8 min Check gaps
5 min

One cycle takes about 18 minutes. Do 2–3 cycles per session covering different topics or skills. Use retrieval practice every time you revise French — it should be your default method.

First attempt — from memory only

la ville — city. le village — village. il y a — there is/are. les magasins — shops. le cinéma — cinema. J’aime habiter ici parce que c’est tranquille…

After checking — gaps filled in green

la ville — city. le village — village. la banlieue — suburbs. le quartier — neighbourhood. il y a — there is/are. les magasins — shops. le cinéma — cinema. le centre sportif — sports centre. la mairie — town hall. le commissariat — police station. J’aime habiter ici parce que c’est tranquille. Ce que j’aime le plus dans ma ville, c’est qu’il y a beaucoup de choses à faire. Le pire, c’est qu’il y a trop de circulation et de pollution.

What this reveals: The first attempt had basic nouns but missed specific places (centre sportif, mairie), neighbourhood vocabulary (banlieue, quartier), and the key phrases for expressing positive/negative opinions (ce que j’aime le plus / le pire). These become the focus of the next retrieval session.

Cover the answers and test yourself:

  • Name 5 family members in French with the correct article (le/la).
  • Conjugate avoir (to have) in the present tense for all 6 persons.
  • Write 3 opinion phrases you could use in the writing exam.
  • Translate: “In my opinion, social media is useful but can be dangerous.”
  • Give 5 time phrases you could use to talk about your future plans (e.g. l’année prochaine).
  • Name 4 school subjects and say whether you like or dislike each one with a reason.
  • Write the passé composé of aller (to go) for je, il/elle, nous.
  • List 5 connectives beyond et (and) and mais (but).

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Re-reading vocab lists passively — Staring at a list of words feels productive but barely strengthens memory. Close the list and write the French from memory.
  • ❌
    Only testing English → French — You also need French → English for the reading and listening exams. Practise both directions.
  • ❌
    Ignoring verb conjugations — Vocabulary on its own is not enough. If you can’t conjugate aller, être, avoir, faire in present, passé composé, and future, your writing and speaking will suffer.

Spaced Repetition for Vocabulary Retention

The science of when to revise each word

What It Is

Spaced repetition means reviewing vocabulary and grammar at increasing intervals — rather than cramming everything in one session. You revise a word the day after you first learn it, then three days later, then a week, then two weeks, and so on. Each time you successfully recall it, the gap before the next review gets longer.

For GCSE French, this is transformative. You need to know approximately 1,700 words across three themes, plus verb conjugations in multiple tenses. Cramming the night before won’t work — spaced repetition will.

Why It Works

The “forgetting curve” (Ebbinghaus, 1885) shows that we forget roughly 70% of new information within 24 hours — unless we review it. Each review resets the curve and makes the memory last longer. Spaced repetition exploits this by timing your reviews at the exact point where you’re about to forget.

A meta-analysis by Cepeda et al. (2006) found that spaced practice was more effective than massed practice in 259 out of 271 cases. For language learning, where you’re building thousands of word-meaning associations, spacing is especially powerful.

How to Do It: Step-by-Step

  1. 1
    Choose your system — Use a digital app (Anki, Quizlet) or a physical card box with dividers labelled Day 1, Day 3, Day 7, Day 14, Day 30. Digital apps handle the scheduling automatically.
  2. 2
    Add 10–15 new words per day — Don’t add everything at once. Group by AQA theme and sub-topic (e.g. Theme 1: Ma famille). Include the French, English, gender (le/la), and an example sentence.
  3. 3
    Review due cards daily — Each day, review words that are “due” according to the schedule. If you get a word right, it moves to a longer interval. If you get it wrong, it resets to the shortest interval.
  4. 4
    Include verb conjugations as separate cards — Don’t just learn infinitives. Create cards for: parler (present) → je parle, tu parles, il/elle parle, nous parlons, vous parlez, ils/elles parlent. Then separate cards for passé composé, future, and conditional forms.
  5. 5
    Test both directions — You need English → French (for writing and speaking) AND French → English (for reading and listening). Create cards for both.

The Spacing Schedule

ReviewIntervalWhat Happens
1st review1 day after learningCatches words about to be forgotten — expect to struggle
2nd review3 days laterMemory starts to consolidate — correct words feel easier
3rd review7 days laterWords entering medium-term memory — most should feel familiar
4th review14 days laterLong-term storage forming — only forgotten words need extra work
5th review30 days laterIf you still remember it, it’s locked in for the exam

When and How Often

Review due words
10 min Add new words
5 min Example sentences
5 min

20 minutes daily is ideal. The key is consistency — 20 minutes every day beats 2 hours once a week. Start at least 3 months before the exam so words have time to reach long-term memory through multiple review cycles.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Adding too many words at once — Adding 50 words on Day 1 creates a review avalanche by Day 3. Stick to 10–15 new words per day maximum.
  • ❌
    Skipping days — Missing a day breaks the spacing schedule and lets words slip back down the forgetting curve. Even 10 minutes on a busy day is better than nothing.
  • ❌
    Learning words in isolation — A word without context is harder to remember and harder to use. Always include an example sentence on the back of each card.

Vocab & conjugations

Flashcard Strategies for French

Master vocabulary, verb forms, and key phrases with active recall

What It Is

Active recall with flashcards means testing yourself by looking at one side of a card and trying to produce the answer before flipping it over. Unlike passive review (reading a vocab list), active recall forces your brain to search for and retrieve the information — which is exactly what you’ll need to do in the AQA French exam.

For French, flashcards aren’t just for vocabulary. You can use them for verb conjugations, key phrases, grammar rules, and even full sentences. The best flashcard systems combine active recall with spaced repetition for maximum retention.

Why It Works

Karpicke & Roediger (2008) found that students who used retrieval-based flashcard study recalled 80% of foreign language vocabulary after a week, compared to 36% for students who used repeated study alone. The act of generating the answer — not just recognising it — creates a much stronger memory trace.

For languages, flashcards are especially effective because they mirror the translation task: you see a prompt and must produce the target word. This is exactly what the writing and speaking exams demand.

How to Do It: Step-by-Step

  1. 1
    Create four types of card — Don’t limit yourself to simple word-for-word translations. Build a varied deck:
    • Vocab cards: English on front, French (with gender) on back
    • Conjugation cards: Infinitive + tense on front, full conjugation table on back
    • Phrase cards: English phrase on front, French phrase on back
    • Sentence cards: Gapped sentence on front, completed sentence on back
  2. 2
    Always include context — On the back of every vocab card, write a short example sentence. For le harcèlement (bullying), write: “Le harcèlement scolaire est un problème grave dans beaucoup de collèges.” Context makes words easier to remember and easier to use in writing.
  3. 3
    Say the answer out loud — Before flipping, say the French word aloud. This builds pronunciation confidence for the speaking exam and engages an extra memory pathway (auditory). Pay attention to nasal vowels (an, en, on, in) and silent final consonants.
  4. 4
    Sort into piles — After each session, sort cards into “know it” and “don’t know it.” Next session, start with the “don’t know” pile. Only retire a card after you’ve recalled it correctly three sessions in a row.
  5. 5
    Reverse the direction — Once you can go English → French, flip the deck and practise French → English. You need both directions for reading/listening (French → English) and writing/speaking (English → French).

When and How Often

Review existing cards
10 min Learn new cards
5 min Say aloud
5 min

20 minutes daily is optimal. Review your “don’t know” pile first, then work through due cards, then add 8–12 new cards. Little and often beats marathon sessions.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌

  • ❌
    Never saying answers aloud — The speaking exam requires you to pronounce words correctly. If you only ever read silently, you’ll hesitate on pronunciation under exam pressure. French pronunciation rules are consistent but must be practised.

Vocab Building for French

Systematic strategies to grow and retain your French vocabulary

Why Vocabulary Is the Foundation

Every AQA French paper — listening, reading, speaking, and writing — depends on the same thing: how many French words you can recognise, recall, and use accurately. The specification covers approximately 1,200 words across themes like identity, local area, holidays, education, and global issues. You don’t need to memorise every word in the dictionary, but you need to build a large enough working vocabulary that you can understand most of what you hear and read, and express yourself precisely in speech and writing.

Vocabulary learning in French isn’t just about English–French pairs. Each word comes with a gender (le/la), a spelling (including accents), and often a pronunciation that doesn’t follow English rules. Effective vocab revision means learning all of these together from the start, not bolting them on later.

Strategy 1: Exploit Cognates and Near-Cognates

French and English share thousands of words with Latin and Norman French roots. Recognising cognate patterns gives you a massive head start, especially in the reading and listening papers where you need to decode unfamiliar words quickly.

English endingFrench endingExamples
-tion-tion (same spelling, French pronunciation)information, situation, education, pollution
-ty-téuniversity → université, society → société, equality → égalité
-ous-eux / -eusedangerous → dangereux, generous → généreux
-ly-mentnormally → normalement, quickly → rapidement
-ible / -able-ible / -ablepossible, comfortable, responsable

Warning — false friends: Some cognates don’t mean what you think. Actuellement means “currently” (not “actually”). Assister means “to attend” (not “to assist”). Blessé means “injured” (not “blessed”). Keep a separate list of false friends and test yourself on them regularly.

Strategy 2: Learn Gender With Every Noun

Every French noun is either masculine (le) or feminine (la). Getting gender wrong causes knock-on errors with adjective agreement, past participle agreement, and pronouns — all of which cost marks in writing and speaking. Learn the article with the noun from day one.

Gender Patterns That Work

PatternGenderExamples
Nouns ending in -ageMasculinele voyage, le village, le fromage
Nouns ending in -mentMasculinele gouvernement, le moment, le développement
Nouns ending in -eurMasculinele professeur, le directeur, l’ordinateur
Nouns ending in -tion / -sionFemininela situation, la décision, la pollution
Nouns ending in -téFemininela société, la beauté, l’égalité
Nouns ending in -ureFemininela voiture, la nature, la nourriture
Nouns ending in -ette / -ence / -anceFemininela fourchette, la différence, la connaissance

Tip: When you write a new word on a flashcard, always write the full article: la maison, not just maison. Say the article out loud every time you practise. After a few repetitions, the article will feel inseparable from the word.

Strategy 3: Master French Accents

Accents in French aren’t decoration — they change pronunciation and sometimes meaning. Missing or wrong accents lose marks in the writing paper. There are five accents to know:

AccentNameEffectExamples
éAccent aiguMakes “e” sound like “ay”école, café, étudier

êAccent circonflexeOpen “e” sound; often marks a lost “s”fête (feast), forêt (forest), île (isle)

Practical drill: Take 10 words you already know that contain accents. Write them from memory, then check every accent. Repeat daily until you get all 10 right three times in a row.

Strategy 4: Build Word Families

Instead of learning isolated words, group related words together. This multiplies your vocabulary efficiently and helps you guess unfamiliar words in the exam.

Strategy 5: Tackle Nasal Vowels

French nasal vowels are sounds that don’t exist in English, and they appear constantly. Learning them early prevents misunderstanding in listening and mispronunciation in speaking.

SpellingSoundCommon words
an / en“on” (as in “song” but through the nose)dans, enfant, vent, vacances, en, pendant
onDeeper “on” (rounder)bon, maison, avion, nous avons, bonjour

unSimilar to “in” (varies by region)un, lundi, brun

Practice method: Record yourself saying 10 words with nasal vowels, then compare with the TTS narration on the lesson pages. Focus on keeping the sound in your nose rather than letting it come through your mouth normally.

Daily Vocab Routine

  1. 1
    5 min — Review yesterday’s words — Cover the English side of your flashcards and try to recall the meaning, gender, and spelling of each French word. Remove any you get right three sessions in a row.
  2. 2
    5 min — Learn 8–10 new words — Always with the article. Say each word aloud. Write each word twice. Look for cognate patterns or gender clues in the ending.
  3. 3
    5 min — Use them in sentences — Write a short sentence using each new word. This moves words from passive recognition to active use. Example: Je vais au lycée en voiture (I go to school by car).
  4. 4
    5 min — Quick-fire test — Get someone to read the English definitions or cover your notes and write the French from memory. Mark yourself honestly and note any accent errors.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Learning words without gender — Writing maison instead of la maison means you’ll guess the gender in the exam. Always learn the article with the noun.
  • ❌
    Ignoring accents — Pere is not a word; père means father. Ou means “or”; où means “where.” Accents change meaning and examiners notice.
  • ❌
    Only learning French→English — For the writing and speaking papers you need to go from English to French. Always practise in both directions.
  • ❌
    Cramming huge lists the night before — Vocabulary sticks through spaced repetition, not marathon sessions. Ten words a day for 12 weeks beats 840 words in one night.

Accuracy & fluency

Grammar Drilling for French

Master the grammar patterns that unlock marks across all four papers

Why Grammar Matters for AQA French

AQA assesses grammar in every paper. In writing and speaking, your mark for “linguistic knowledge and accuracy” depends directly on how well you handle verb tenses, agreements, and sentence structures. In listening and reading, grammatical clues help you decode meaning — a negative (ne...pas) completely changes the meaning of a sentence, and recognising a past tense tells you the event has already happened.

Grammar drilling isn’t about learning rules in isolation — it’s about practising patterns until they become automatic. When you can form the passé composé without thinking, you free up mental energy to focus on what you actually want to say.

Avoir vs Être: The Foundation

The passé composé (perfect tense) is the most important past tense for GCSE. Most verbs use avoir as the auxiliary, but a crucial group use être. Getting this wrong is one of the most common errors in the exam.

Être Verbs — The DR MRS VANDERTRAMP Mnemonic

LetterVerbMeaningPast participle
DDevenirTo becomedevenu
RRevenirTo come backrevenu
MMonterTo go upmonté
RResterTo stayresté
SSortirTo go outsorti
VVenirTo comevenu
AAllerTo goallé
NNaîtreTo be bornné
DDescendreTo go downdescendu
EEntrerTo enterentré
RRentrerTo go homerentré
TTomberTo falltombé
RRetournerTo returnretourné
AArriverTo arrivearrivé
MMourirTo diemort
PPartirTo leaveparti

Plus all reflexive verbs: se lever (to get up), se coucher (to go to bed), s’amuser (to have fun).

Key rule: With être verbs, the past participle agrees with the subject. Elle est allée (she went) — add “e” for feminine. Ils sont arrivés (they arrived) — add “s” for masculine plural. Elles sont parties — add “es” for feminine plural.

Negation: Beyond Ne...Pas

Negation wraps around the verb. The mark schemes rewards students who use a variety of negative structures, not just ne...pas.

StructureMeaningExample
ne...pasnotJe ne mange pas de viande — I don’t eat meat
ne...jamaisneverIl ne fait jamais ses devoirs — He never does his homework
ne...riennothingJe ne comprends rien — I understand nothing
ne...plusno longerElle ne fume plus — She no longer smokes
ne...personnenobodyJe ne connais personne — I know nobody
ne...queonlyIl n’a que dix euros — He only has ten euros
ne...ni...nineither...norJe ne bois ni café ni thé — I drink neither coffee nor tea

In the passé composé: The negative wraps around the auxiliary, not the past participle. Je n’ai pas mangé (I didn’t eat). Il n’est jamais allé (He has never been).

Pronoun Order

French pronouns go before the verb, not after it like in English. When multiple pronouns appear, they follow a strict order that examiners test in the reading paper and reward in writing.

Position 1Position 2Position 3Position 4
me, te, se, nous, vousle, la, leslui, leury, en

Examples:

  • Il me le donne — He gives it to me
  • Je la lui prête — I lend it (fem.) to him/her
  • Il y va — He goes there
  • J’en ai trois — I have three of them

Tip for GCSE: You don’t need to master complex double-pronoun sentences. Focus on using y (replaces à + place: J’y vais = I go there) and en (replaces de + noun: J’en mange = I eat some) confidently. These impress examiners and are achievable at GCSE level.

Tense Toolkit: What You Need for Each Grade

AQA rewards students who use a range of tenses. Here’s what to aim for at each target grade:

TargetTenses neededKey structures
Grade 4–5Present + one otherPresent tense of common verbs; passé composé OR near future (je vais + infinitive)
Grade 6–7Present + past + futurePassé composé (avoir & être), simple future (je jouerai), imperfect for descriptions (il faisait beau)
Grade 8–9All of above + conditional + subjunctiveConditional (je voudrais, ce serait), pluperfect (j’avais mangé), subjunctive after il faut que and bien que

Subjunctive Basics

The subjunctive sounds advanced, but you only need a few key phrases to use it effectively at GCSE. It appears after expressions of necessity, doubt, and emotion.

Triggers to learn:

  • Il faut que + subjunctive — It is necessary that
  • Bien que + subjunctive — Although
  • Pour que + subjunctive — So that
  • Je veux que + subjunctive — I want (someone) to

High-value phrases to memorise:

  • Il faut que je fasse mes devoirs — I must do my homework (faire → fasse)
  • Bien que ce soit difficile — Although it is difficult (être → soit)
  • Pour que tout le monde puisse participer — So that everyone can participate (pouvoir → puisse)
  • Il faut que nous allions au collège — We have to go to school (aller → allions)

Exam tip: Even using one subjunctive correctly in your writing or speaking can push you into the top mark band. Learn 3–4 set phrases and slot them into your exam answers where they fit naturally.

Grammar Drilling Routine

  1. 1
    5 min — Verb conjugation sprint — Pick one verb (e.g., aller). Write it out in 4 tenses: present, passé composé, imperfect, future. All 6 persons (je, tu, il/elle, nous, vous, ils/elles). Time yourself.
  2. 2
    5 min — Sentence transformation — Take 5 present-tense sentences and rewrite each one in the passé composé, then the future. Example: Je mange une pomme → J’ai mangé une pomme → Je mangerai une pomme.
  3. 3
    5 min — Negation practice — Take 5 positive sentences and make each one negative using a different negative structure (ne...pas, ne...jamais, ne...rien, ne...plus, ne...personne).
  4. 4
    5 min — Check and correct — Compare your answers with your notes or the lesson content. For every error, write the correct version three times. Pay special attention to être verb agreement and accent placement.
Present → Passé composé → Future

1. Je joue au football → J’ai joué au football → Je jouerai au football
2. Elle va au cinéma → Elle est allée au cinéma (note: être + agreement) → Elle ira au cinéma
3. Nous mangeons à la cantine → Nous avons mangé à la cantine → Nous mangerons à la cantine
4. Ils se lèvent tôt → Ils se sont levés tôt (reflexive: être + agreement) → Ils se lèveront tôt
5. Tu fais du sport → Tu as fait du sport → Tu feras du sport

Check your work: Sentence 2 uses être (aller is a DR MRS VANDERTRAMP verb) and adds “e” because the subject is elle (feminine). Sentence 4 is reflexive, so it also uses être and adds “s” for masculine plural. These agreement rules are where most marks are lost.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Forgetting past participle agreement with être — Elle est allé is wrong; it must be elle est allée. Always check whether your verb uses être, then match the ending to the subject.
  • ❌
    Putting negation in the wrong place — In the passé composé, the negative wraps the auxiliary: Je n’ai pas mangé, NOT J’ai ne pas mangé.
  • ❌
    Only using the present tense — Even one correctly used past or future tense pushes you up the mark bands. Always include at least two tenses in any writing or speaking response.
  • ❌
    Learning rules without practising — Knowing that the passé composé uses avoir or être is useless if you can’t form it under time pressure. Drill, don’t just read.

Oral & aural skills

Listening & Speaking Practice

Train your ear and your voice for AQA French Papers 1 and 3

Why Listening and Speaking Need Separate Practice

The listening paper (Paper 1, 25% of your GCSE) and the speaking exam (Paper 3, 25%) together account for half your total grade. Yet many students focus almost entirely on reading and writing revision because those feel more like “normal” revision. Listening and speaking are skills that improve through regular, targeted practice — not last-minute cramming.

French pronunciation follows consistent rules, but those rules are very different from English. Silent letters, nasal vowels, liaison between words, and the rhythm of French sentences all need practice. The good news is that improving your pronunciation also improves your listening, because you learn to anticipate what French words should sound like.

French Pronunciation Rules

Understanding these core rules will help you decode listening passages and sound more natural in your speaking exam.

Silent Final Consonants

In French, consonants at the end of a word are usually silent. The useful mnemonic is CaReFuL — the letters C, R, F, and L are the main exceptions that are usually pronounced at the end of a word.

RuleExamples pronouncedExamples silent
Final -s, -t, -d, -x, -z, -p are silent—paris, petit, grand, voix, assez
Final -c, -r, -f, -l usually pronouncedavec, finir, sportif, animalExceptions: estomac, diner (some -er verbs)
Final -e is almost always silent—table, classe, moderne

Liaison

When a word ending in a normally silent consonant is followed by a word starting with a vowel, the final consonant “links” to the next word. This is liaison, and it catches out many students in the listening exam because words seem to merge together.

  • les amis → sounds like “lay-zah-mee”
  • nous avons → sounds like “noo-zah-von”
  • un petit enfant → sounds like “uh pe-ton-fon”
  • trois heures → sounds like “twah-zerr”

Listening tip: When you hear an unexpected consonant sound at the start of a word beginning with a vowel, it’s probably liaison from the previous word. Train yourself to separate words mentally.

Accent Rules and Pronunciation

SoundSpellingPronunciation guideExamples
ouou“oo” as in “food”vous, pour, toujours
uuPurse your lips and say “ee”tu, rue, voiture
eu / oeueu, œuRound your lips and say “uh”deux, heure, sœur
oioi“wah”moi, toi, boire, trois
ai / eiai, ei“eh” as in “bed”lait, maison, neige
eau / aueau, au“oh”beau, gâteau, aussi
gngn“ny” as in “onion”montagne, campagne, gagner

Listening Practice Methods

  1. 1
    Self-dictation (dictée) — Listen to the TTS narration on any French lesson page. Pause after each sentence and write down exactly what you heard. Then compare with the text on screen. This trains your ear to separate words and hear silent letters, liaison, and nasal vowels.
  2. 2
    Gist listening — Play a full lesson narration without pausing. Afterwards, write down the 3 main points you understood. Don’t worry about every word — the listening exam rewards understanding the overall message, not translating every word.
  3. 3
    Keyword spotting — Before listening, choose 5 keywords to listen for (e.g., time expressions, opinion phrases, negatives). Tally how many times you hear each one. This trains the selective listening skill you need in the exam.
  4. 4
    Speed adjustment — Start by listening at 0.75x speed to catch every word. Once you can understand at that speed, move to 1x. The AQA listening exam uses natural-speed recordings, so you need to build up to full speed.

Speaking Practice Methods

  1. 1
    Shadowing — Play the TTS narration and speak along with it simultaneously, matching the rhythm, intonation, and pronunciation as closely as possible. This builds natural-sounding French without translating in your head. Start with short phrases and build up to full paragraphs.
  2. 2
    Record and compare — Record yourself reading a paragraph of French, then play it back alongside the TTS version. Note where your pronunciation differs — especially nasal vowels, the French “r” sound, and the “u” vs “ou” distinction.
  3. 3
    Role play rehearsal — AQA Paper 3 includes a role play card. Practise by reading only the English prompts and responding in French out loud, timing yourself. Aim for natural, confident delivery rather than perfection.
  4. 4
    Photo card practice — The photo card task requires you to describe a photo and answer questions. Practise by taking any image from a lesson, describing it in French for 1 minute, then answering: Qu’est-ce qu’il y a sur la photo? Qu’est-ce que tu penses de...? Qu’est-ce que tu as fait récemment?

Nasal Vowels — Focused Practice

Nasal vowels are the single biggest pronunciation challenge for English speakers. They appear in the most common French words, so getting them right dramatically improves both your speaking and listening.

Practise distinguishing these pairs. Say each one aloud, exaggerating the nasal quality.

How to practise: Say each pair 5 times, focusing on making the sounds distinct. Then get someone to say one word from each pair at random — can you identify which one they said?

20 minutes daily: 6 minutes shadowing with lesson narration, 5 minutes self-dictation, 5 minutes speaking practice (role play or photo card), 4 minutes reviewing errors. Consistency beats long sessions — 20 minutes daily is more effective than 2 hours once a week.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Only practising reading and writing — Listening and speaking are 50% of your GCSE grade. You cannot revise them by reading notes. You must listen to French and speak French regularly.
  • ❌
    Pronouncing silent final consonants — English speakers instinctively pronounce every letter. Remember: final -s, -t, -d, -x, -z are silent in French. Petit sounds like “peh-tee”, not “peh-tit”.
  • ❌
    Confusing “u” and “ou” — Tu (you) and tout (all) use completely different vowel sounds. Rue (street) is not “roo.” Practise the French “u” by saying “ee” with rounded lips.
  • ❌
    Translating word-by-word in listening — If you try to translate every word, you’ll fall behind. Train yourself to understand the gist first, then pick out details. The exam gives you time to read the questions before listening.
