Retrieval Practice

Test yourself — don’t just re-read.

What the Research Says

Retrieval practice is the act of pulling information out of your memory, rather than pushing it in. It sounds simple but it is the most powerful revision technique we have — stronger than highlighting, stronger than re-reading, stronger than watching videos. The harder the retrieval feels, the more your long-term memory is strengthening.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Roediger & Karpicke (2006)Students who self-tested once remembered 50% more a week later than those who re-read four times.Self-testing > re-reading, even when it feels harder.
Karpicke & Blunt (2011)Retrieval practice beat concept-mapping and elaborative study on a delayed test by ~50%.Works better than other “active” strategies that feel productive.
Agarwal et al. (2017)Low-stakes retrieval quizzes raised GCSE-equivalent test scores by an average of one grade.Short regular quizzing moves your real exam score.
Smith et al. (2016)Students who practised retrieval scored higher even on questions testing information they didn’t specifically retrieve.Builds the skill of remembering itself, not just the facts.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Study a chunk of content — read through a StudyVault lesson, watch a video, or cover a topic in class. Don’t try to memorise. Just understand.
  2. 2
    Close everything — book shut, tab closed, notes flipped over. The whole point is that you cannot see the material.
  3. 3
    Write down everything you can remember — no looking back. This is called a “brain dump.” Write until you run out. It should feel uncomfortable.
  4. 4
    Check against the source — open the lesson. Mark what you missed in a different colour. Don’t just glance — properly compare.
  5. 5
    Target the gaps — re-study only the parts you missed. Not the whole lesson again. Just the holes.
  6. 6
    Retest tomorrow — hit the same topic again within 24 hours. The second attempt is where the learning locks in.
Example 1

After studying the Defined Vocabulary list alongside Accidence and Forms, close the book and brain-dump all five noun declensions from memory — the case endings for singular and plural (for example: first declension puella, puellae, puellam, puellae, puella; third declension rex, regis, regi, regem, rege; the irregular deus and vir). Then extend the challenge: for each declension, add one word from your vocabulary list that belongs to it, along with its gender and meaning. When you check back, pay particular attention to the case endings you confused or omitted — these are exactly the details that let you read a sentence’s grammar correctly, and gaps here are what cause mistranslations in the unseen passage.

Example 2

After covering Syntax and Translation, brain-dump the main types of subordinate clause you have studied and write down one signal word and one translation rule for each — purpose clauses (ut/ne + subjunctive, translated ‘in order to’ or ‘so that’), result clauses (ut/ut non + subjunctive, ‘so that…that’), indirect statement (accusative + infinitive after verbs of saying or thinking), and indirect command (ut/ne + subjunctive after verbs of ordering or asking). For each clause type note: the tense of the subjunctive or infinitive used, what it tells you about time relative to the main verb, and one example sentence drawn from a passage you have translated. Check back and mark what you missed. The ability to spot the signal word and apply the correct rule is exactly what separates an accurate translation from a guess.

Common Pitfalls

  • Peeking. If you look back during the brain dump, you’re not doing retrieval — you’re doing copying. Harder is better.
  • Only doing it once. One pass strengthens memory a little. Spaced repeats strengthen it permanently. Come back to the same topic 2–3 times over a week.
  • Doing it too soon after studying. If you retrieve while the material is still in short-term memory, it’s too easy to count. Leave at least 30 minutes between studying and testing.
  • Stopping when it feels difficult. Desirable difficulty is the whole point. If it feels easy, your memory isn’t being challenged and you’re not learning.

When to Use This

Build it in every week, from the start of the course through to your exams. Aim for 15–20 minutes per subject, two or three times a week. The last two weeks before an exam is when retrieval practice becomes your main tool — swap passive reading for brain dumps and flashcards. On StudyVault, the Knowledge Check and Flashcard buttons in every lesson sidebar are retrieval practice in disguise — use them.

Quick Reference
~20 minutes per topic

Steps

  1. Study one topic
  2. Close everything
  3. Brain dump from memory
  4. Check gaps
  5. Re-study only the gaps
  6. Retest tomorrow

Interleaving

Mix topics in one session — don’t block them.

What the Research Says

Most students revise by blocking — an hour on electoral systems, an hour on the courts, an hour on rights. It feels productive and the topic seems clear by the end. Interleaving is the opposite: you jump between topics inside a single session. It feels worse at the time, and you’ll make more mistakes. But when the real exam arrives, you will be dramatically better at knowing which topic is being tested — and that is usually the hardest part of any Citizenship question.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Rohrer & Taylor (2007)Students who interleaved topics scored 43% higher on delayed tests than blocked-practice students.Same time spent — huge difference in exam performance.
Birnbaum et al. (2013)Interleaved learners felt LESS confident during practice but performed BETTER in the test.If revision feels too easy, interleave.
Bjork & Bjork (2011)Desirable difficulties — including interleaving — create durable long-term learning at the cost of short-term performance.Short-term struggle is the price of long-term gain.
Taylor & Rohrer (2010)Benefit was largest when topics looked superficially similar — students learnt to DISTINGUISH them.Most useful where students confuse similar concepts.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Pick 3–5 related topics — topics that share a paper, a theme, or a question type. Similar enough that students confuse them.
  2. 2
    Make a mixed question set — 10–15 questions drawn randomly from all the topics. Don’t tell yourself which topic each question belongs to.
  3. 3
    Attempt each question cold — first step is identifying what’s being asked. That identification is the skill you’re training.
  4. 4
    Mark after every question — note which topic each one was. Pay attention to mis-identifications — those are the highest-value gaps.
  5. 5
    Rebuild a new mixed set tomorrow — same topics, different questions. Different order. Over time, misclassifications drop.
  6. 6
    Expect to feel worse than blocked practice — that’s the right feeling. Your exam self will thank you.
Example 1

Mix questions from three Paper 1 topics in one session: the role of the Prime Minister, the functions of Parliament, and the work of local government. Write a question from each on separate slips, shuffle them, and answer without knowing which topic it’s from. When you mistake a question about parliamentary scrutiny for one about local council accountability, that confusion is your highest-priority gap — the exam will test exactly that boundary.

Example 2

For Paper 2, interleave questions on the courts hierarchy (Magistrates’ Court → Crown Court → Court of Appeal → Supreme Court), on the role of the police, and on citizenship action methods. Shuffle short-answer questions from all three. By session three you will instinctively know whether a question is asking about legal process, law enforcement, or civic participation — the discrimination that earns marks in extended writing.

Common Pitfalls

  • Random, not related. Interleaving Citizenship with Maths is just subject-switching. Interleave WITHIN Citizenship — related topics that students confuse.
  • Giving up when it feels hard. The discomfort is the signal that it’s working. Don’t revert to blocked practice because interleaving feels slow.
  • Labelling the topic at the top of each question. Defeats the point — the identification IS the training.
  • Using it too early in learning. You need baseline familiarity with each topic first. Interleaving is for consolidation, not first exposure.

When to Use This

Once you’ve covered a handful of related topics — usually partway through a term — start weaving them into mixed practice sessions. Very useful in the final 8–10 weeks before exams when you’re moving from learning to applying. Full past papers are the ultimate interleaving exercise, because they force you to identify question types cold.

Quick Reference
~30–45 minutes per session

Steps

  1. Pick 3–5 related topics
  2. Build a mixed set
  3. Attempt cold
  4. Mark & note topic
  5. Fix misclassifications
  6. Expect discomfort

    Pick 3–5 related topics — topics that share a paper, a theme, or a question type. Similar enough that students confuse them.
  2. 2
    Make a mixed question set — 10–15 questions drawn randomly from all the topics. Don’t tell yourself which topic each question belongs to.
  3. 3
    Attempt each question cold — first step is identifying what’s being asked. That identification is the skill you’re training.
  4. 4
    Mark after every question — note which topic each one was. Pay attention to mis-identifications — those are the highest-value gaps.
  5. 5
    Rebuild a new mixed set tomorrow — same topics, different questions. Different order. Over time, misclassifications drop.
  6. 6
    Expect to feel worse than blocked practice — that’s the right feeling. Your exam self will thank you.
Example 1

Create a 15-question mixed set spanning Paper 1 topics: lever systems, antagonistic muscle pairs, types of muscle contraction (isotonic/isometric), components of fitness, and short-term effects of exercise. Because these areas all relate to movement and physiology, exam questions can sound deceptively similar. Working through them in random order forces you to identify whether a question is asking about classification, mechanism, or effect — a distinction that separates 4-mark answers from 6-mark ones.

Example 2

In the final weeks before the exam, interleave Paper 1 questions (e.g. “Explain the role of haemoglobin during aerobic exercise”) with Paper 2 questions (e.g. “Using Maslow’s hierarchy of needs, explain how a coach could motivate a young athlete”). Switching between physiology and sports psychology in one sitting closely mirrors the actual exam experience, where the paper moves between domains without warning.

Common Pitfalls

  • Random, not related. Interleaving PE with Geography is just subject-switching. Interleave WITHIN PE — related topics that students confuse.
  • Giving up when it feels hard. The discomfort is the signal that it’s working. Don’t revert to blocked practice because interleaving feels slow.
  • Labelling the topic at the top of each question. Defeats the point — the identification IS the training.
  • Using it too early in learning. You need baseline familiarity with each topic first. Interleaving is for consolidation, not first exposure.

When to Use This

Once you’ve covered a handful of related topics — usually partway through a term — start weaving them into mixed practice sessions. Very useful in the final 8–10 weeks before exams when you’re moving from learning to applying. Full past papers are the ultimate interleaving exercise, because they force you to identify question types cold.

Timed Practice

Simulate the real thing — including the time pressure.

What the Research Says

Knowing the content is only half of an exam. The other half is managing time, reading questions accurately under pressure, writing neatly when your hand hurts, and staying calm when a question tests a topic you feel shaky on. These are all skills — and like any skill, they need practice. Timed practice is how you build them.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Soderstrom & Bjork (2015)Transfer-appropriate processing: performance is best when the practice conditions closely match the test conditions.Practise in the conditions you’ll be tested in.
Agarwal et al. (2017)Students who did timed practice tests scored higher even on unseen questions.Builds generalisable exam skill, not just familiarity.
Yerkes & Dodson (1908)Performance is best at MODERATE arousal — some pressure helps, too much hurts.Simulated pressure builds tolerance for real pressure.
Hinze & Rapp (2014)Students who experienced test-like practice reported 30% less exam anxiety.Familiarity reduces fear. Fear reduces performance.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Start small — begin with one timed question or one section. Don’t jump straight to full papers. Build the muscle gradually.
  2. 2
    Match the Edexcel mark-to-time ratio — 4-mark “Explain Two” = 5 minutes; 5-mark “Explain with Sources of Wisdom” = 7 minutes; 12-mark “Discuss” = 18 minutes including SPaG. Give yourself the same allocation.
  3. 3
    Remove distractions — phone in another room, no music, no snacks, no notes. The real exam hall has none of these.
  4. 4
    Handwrite — the exam is handwritten. Typing is faster and feels more productive, but it doesn’t train the same skill. Your hand will hurt on the day and that’s normal.
  5. 5
    Mark with the mark scheme honestly — use StudyVault’s per-question mark schemes or a teacher-provided one. Be harsh on yourself — underscoring now prevents overconfidence later.
  6. 6
    Do a full paper under conditions a month before the exam — uninterrupted, correct time, no music. One per subject, one per week in the final stretch.
Example 1

Practise a timed 12-mark Discuss essay in exactly 18 minutes. Set a timer, read the statement once (1 minute), plan your argument structure (3 minutes: two religious arguments for, two against, one non-religious argument, conclusion), write (12 minutes), proofread for SPaG (2 minutes). The 12-mark question accounts for the largest single share of marks on each paper — students who skip timed practice consistently run out of time at exactly this question, losing the most-available marks on the paper.

Example 2

Build up to full-paper conditions progressively over six weeks: Week 1, one timed 4-mark “Explain Two” (5 min); Week 2, one timed 5-mark “Explain with Sources” (7 min); Week 3, a full section (mix of 4- and 5-mark questions); Weeks 4–6, complete past papers under exam-hall conditions. After each attempt, annotate the mark scheme: tick what you got, highlight exactly which trigger words the examiner was looking for. Patterns in the gaps (e.g. always dropping marks on SPaG in 12-mark responses, or forgetting to reference a sacred text) tell you where to focus the next retrieval session.

Common Pitfalls

  • Stopping when the timer runs out and ignoring the unfinished bit. Note what you’d have written — that’s the data about your pace.
  • Using notes during “timed” practice. It’s not timed practice — it’s open-book practice. Useful, but different.
  • Only doing it in the last fortnight. Too late — you’ve not left time to fix the weaknesses the practice reveals.
  • Not marking honestly. Marking your own work gently protects feelings now and destroys results later.

When to Use This

From 10 weeks out, do at least one timed practice per subject per week — usually a single question type at first, building to full papers. In the final month, do at least one full timed paper per subject. Always mark it against the actual scheme and note your pace across question types.

Quick Reference
Paper time + ~30 min marking

Question timings

  1. 4-mark “Explain Two” = 5 min
  2. 5-mark “Explain with Sources” = 7 min
  3. 12-mark “Discuss” = 18 min (incl. SPaG)
  4. Half a paper, timed
  5. Full paper, exam conditions
  6. Mock week, all papers

Interleaving

Mix topics in one session — don’t block them.

What the Research Says

Most students revise by blocking — an hour on the solar system, an hour on stars, an hour on cosmology. It feels productive and the topic seems clear by the end. Interleaving is the opposite: you jump between topics inside a single session. It feels worse at the time, and you’ll make more mistakes. But when the real exam arrives, you will be dramatically better at knowing which idea a question is testing — and that is usually the hardest part of an unfamiliar observational scenario.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Rohrer & Taylor (2007)Students who interleaved topics scored 43% higher on delayed tests than blocked-practice students.Same time spent — huge difference in exam performance.
Birnbaum et al. (2013)Interleaved learners felt LESS confident during practice but performed BETTER in the test.If revision feels too easy, interleave.
Bjork & Bjork (2011)Desirable difficulties — including interleaving — create durable long-term learning at the cost of short-term performance.Short-term struggle is the price of long-term gain.
Taylor & Rohrer (2010)Benefit was largest when topics looked superficially similar — students learnt to DISTINGUISH them.Most useful where students confuse related ideas.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Pick 3–5 related topics — topics that share a paper, a theme, or a question type. Similar enough that students confuse them.
  2. 2
    Make a mixed problem set — 10–15 questions drawn from all the topics. Don’t label which topic each question belongs to.
  3. 3
    Attempt each question cold — the first step is identifying what’s being asked. That identification is the skill you’re training.
  4. 4
    Mark after every question — note which topic area each one was. Pay attention to mis-identifications — those are the highest-value gaps.
  5. 5
    Rebuild a new mixed set tomorrow — same topics, different questions, different order. Over time, misclassifications drop.
  6. 6
    Expect to feel worse than blocked practice — that’s the right feeling. Your exam self will thank you.
Example 1 — Sidereal vs synodic vs orbital period topic mix

Mix questions covering sidereal period, synodic period, and Kepler’s third law in one 40-minute session. Write 12 questions on separate slips: four from each area, shuffled. Before each question, ask yourself: “Is this about the true orbital period, the observed repeat alignment, or the orbital radius relationship?” Students frequently confuse the sidereal period (star-referenced, the true period) with the synodic period (Sun-referenced, what Earth observers actually measure) — the identification exercise in revision prevents losing marks on what examiners confirm is the most-missed distinction. After each attempt, record whether you identified the concept correctly before calculating.

Example 2 — Naked-eye vs telescopic observation topic mix

The course splits cleanly across 12 naked-eye lessons (constellation patterns, seasonal visibility, planets to the unaided eye, eclipse geometry) and 14 telescopic lessons (refractors, reflectors, eyepiece calculations, CCD imaging, radio telescopes). Mix questions from both halves — for example: “Marina Vassilakis at Caerwyn Observatory uses a refractor with focal lengths \(f_o = 1200\) mm, \(f_e = 25\) mm. What magnification does she achieve?” alongside “Dr Halima Yousef observes that Orion is highest in the sky at midnight in January. Explain why, using the Earth’s orbital position.” The two question types demand different reasoning skills; interleaving forces you to switch between them rapidly, exactly as the exam paper does.

Common Pitfalls

  • Interleaving before you know the basics. You need to know each topic individually first. Use interleaving once you’ve studied both halves of the course — not as a first-pass strategy.
  • Giving up because it feels hard. Difficulty during interleaved practice is the signal it’s working. Persist.
  • Mixing unrelated topics. Interleaving works best when the topics are related enough to be confused. Mix topics within the same conceptual area — distance measures, stellar classification, or period types — not random combinations.
  • Not checking mis-identifications. The mistake is the data. If you mislabelled a question as being about ‘telescope design’ when it was about ‘eyepiece magnification’, that confusion is exactly what needs fixing.

When to Use This

Start interleaving once you have studied all major topic areas at least once. In the final six weeks before the exam, replace most blocked revision with interleaved mixed sets. Particularly powerful the week before the exam when you want to simulate the varied order in which questions appear on the actual papers.

Quick Reference
~40 minutes per interleaved session

Steps

  1. Pick 3–5 related topics
  2. Build mixed question set
  3. Identify the topic first
  4. Attempt the question
  5. Mark every question
  6. Rebuild tomorrow

Elaborative Interrogation

Ask “why?” and “how?” until the facts become explanations.

What the Research Says

Facts in isolation are fragile. Facts connected by explanations survive. Elaborative interrogation is the habit of asking “why is that true?” and “how does that work?” about every fact you learn — and forcing yourself to answer. The answer doesn’t need to be perfect. The act of trying to answer is what builds the mental connections that turn memorised facts into understood explanations.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Pressley et al. (1988)Asking “why?” during reading boosted recall by 40–70% compared to silent reading.Works even when the answer is imperfect.
Dunlosky et al. (2013)Rated “moderate utility” in the APS review — robust across subjects and ages, especially when applied to new material that builds on existing knowledge.Best for consolidating material you half-know.
Smith & Holliday (2006)Students who self-explained while studying scored significantly higher on transfer questions requiring application.Builds the ability to USE the knowledge, not just recall it.
Chi et al. (1994)Self-explanation was a stronger predictor of understanding than prior knowledge.Even weaker students catch up by explaining to themselves.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Study a chunk of content — a lesson, a paragraph, a key fact. Anything where facts are being introduced.
  2. 2
    After each fact, ask “why?” — why is this true? Why does it matter? Why did the Greeks respond this way?
  3. 3
    Then ask “how?” — how does this idea work? How does it connect to the next topic? How would you explain it to someone who has never studied the ancient world?
  4. 4
    Try to answer out loud — even if your answer is wrong, the attempt activates deeper processing. Write your answer in the margin.
  5. 5
    Check your answer against the source — does the text support your explanation? If not, update it. The correction matters more than the first guess.
  6. 6
    Build chains — once you’ve asked “why?” once, ask it again of your answer. Push until you hit a genuinely fundamental fact. This is where deep understanding forms.
Example 1

Fact: “The ablative case can express time, place, manner and means without needing a preposition.” Ask why: because Latin relies on its case endings rather than word order to signal grammatical relationships, so a single case can carry several different meanings depending on context. Ask why again: because the case ending itself was originally doing the grammatical work that a preposition would do in English — the preposition, where one appears, is only there to sharpen a meaning the ending alone would leave ambiguous. Ask how: this explains why “eo tempore” (at that time) needs no preposition, while “cum patre” (with father) does. Ask why that matters for an exam answer: recognising which use of the ablative you’re looking at before you translate stops you inserting the wrong preposition in English and losing sense on an unseen passage.

Example 2

Fact: “In the story of Hercules and Cacus, Cacus steals the hero’s cattle by dragging them backwards into his cave.” Ask why: because dragging the cattle backwards leaves hoofprints pointing away from the cave, disguising the direction they actually went — a deliberate act of trickery, not simple theft. Ask why again: because Cacus is characterised as a monster who relies on cunning and concealment rather than open strength, which marks him out as a villain in contrast to Hercules’ direct physical heroism. Ask how: this explains why Hercules eventually finds the cave by following the cattle’s cries rather than any clue Cacus has left — the trick is undone by effort, not by cleverness. Ask why that matters for the exam: the whole-narrative answer rewards students who can explain why a detail like the backwards hoofprints serves the contrast between hero and villain, not just describe what happens.

Common Pitfalls

  • Accepting “I don’t know”. Take a guess. Even a wrong guess activates the processing. Then check and correct.
  • One “why?” and moving on. The real gains come from the third or fourth “why?”, when you hit the fundamentals.
  • Only asking the obvious questions. Push toward the explanations your teacher never gave you — those are where genuine learning happens.
  • Skipping the check. Unchecked wrong answers reinforce misunderstanding. Always verify against the source.

When to Use This

Any time you’re covering conceptual material — not just listing facts. Particularly powerful with Latin’s recurring themes: why deponent verbs are passive in form but active in meaning, why Hannibal’s crossing of the Alps mattered strategically, why the ablative case marks time and place without needing a preposition, and why particular Roman festivals honoured particular gods at particular times of year. Build it into every lesson revisit. The exam rewards students who can explain the significance of a form or a detail, not just identify it.

Quick Reference
Adds ~50% to reading time, transforms recall

Questions to ask

  1. Why is this true?
  2. How does it work?
  3. Why does it matter?
  4. How does it connect?
  5. Why now and not before?
  6. How would I explain this to a friend?

Knowledge Organisers

One page per topic — the whole picture at a glance.

What the Research Says

A knowledge organiser is a single side of A4 that captures everything a student needs to know about a topic — key vocabulary, essential facts, core concepts, and connections between them. Used properly, it becomes the base layer of your revision: the thing you keep coming back to, the thing you redraw from memory, the thing you carry on the bus. Used badly, it becomes a wall of dense text that nobody reads.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Willingham (2017)Students need to store facts in long-term memory before they can think critically about them. Knowledge organisers are the storage scaffold.Not old-fashioned — cognitive prerequisite for analysis.
Counsell (2018)Used in UK schools to reduce cognitive load by pre-structuring the material students encounter.Reduces working memory demand during lessons.
Sweller (1988)Cognitive Load Theory: well-organised schemas free up working memory for higher-order tasks.A well-designed organiser makes hard questions easier.
Oakes & Griffin (2017)Students who made their OWN organisers outperformed those given finished ones.Making is learning. Receiving is not.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    One topic per organiser — a unit, a theme, a mythological cycle. Not the whole of Myth & Religion. Too broad and it becomes a dense textbook page.
  2. 2
    Divide the page into 4–6 sections — typically: Key Vocabulary, Key Sources (literary and material), Core Concepts, Sketch Visuals, Connections to Other Topics, Common Exam Questions. The structure forces you to categorise.
  3. 3
    Keep it to one side of A4 — the constraint is the point. If it doesn’t fit, the material isn’t yet compressed into the essentials.
  4. 4
    Use tiny structural visuals — a mini temple plan showing the naos and pronaos, a compact sketch of the Lion Gate, a small table of the three orders. Dual coding applies: words + visuals beat words alone.
  5. 5
    Redraw it from memory weekly — this is where the learning is. A finished organiser you never revisit is wasted. The redrawn one is retrieval practice in disguise.
  6. 6
    Annotate over time — when you learn something new that fits, add it. When a connection becomes clearer, draw the link. The organiser evolves.
Example 1

Create a knowledge organiser for the Nouns of the Five Declensions. Sections: Key Vocabulary (declension, case, stem, nominative, genitive, gender); a table of all five declensions with their nominative singular and genitive singular endings, typical gender, and one example noun (1st: mensa, mensae, f.; 2nd masc.: dominus, domini, m.; 2nd neut.: bellum, belli, n.; 3rd: rex, regis, m./f.; 3rd neut.: corpus, corporis, n.; 4th: manus, manus, f.; 5th: res, rei, f.); a mini sketch showing the six cases running down the side of each column; Key Rules (gender is not predictable from the nominative alone — it must be learned with each noun); Connections (links to Syntax and Translation — adjective agreement across declensions). Fit it on one side of A4, redraw from memory after three days. The genitive singular ending is the single most useful form on the page, because it reveals the declension and therefore every other ending.

Example 2

Create a knowledge organiser for Translating a Passage into English. Sections: Key Vocabulary (subordinate clause, connective, ablative absolute, historic present, indirect statement); Key Strategies (find the main verb first; identify the subject from the nominative, not from word order; mark off subordinate clauses with brackets before translating; watch for participles agreeing with a noun several words away); a tiny annotated sketch of a Latin sentence with arrows showing subject → object → verb rather than the English left-to-right order; Connections to Accidence and Forms (recognising perfect tense endings such as –it and –erunt on sight, so the tense of the whole clause is fixed early). Redraw the annotated sentence from memory a week later — misreading Latin word order as if it were English word order is the most frequent source of lost sense in a translation, and marking off clauses before writing anything down is the habit that prevents it.

Common Pitfalls

  • Copying the textbook. A dense page of 8pt text isn’t a knowledge organiser — it’s a photocopy. Compress ruthlessly.
  • One page per subject. Too much, too diffuse. One page per topic — one for the five declensions, one for verb tenses, one for an unseen translation technique, one for Hannibal’s march.
  • Making one and never revisiting. The value is in the redrawing — not the original creation.
  • Using a downloaded one instead of making your own. Research is clear: making beats receiving. Teacher-provided organisers are useful for structure only.

When to Use This

Start one at the beginning of each topic, as you’re learning it. Refine as your understanding grows. Redraw the whole set from memory in the final month before exams — one topic per day. Carry a folder of your organisers to every revision session. Use them as the spine of retrieval practice: cover the organiser, brain-dump, then check.

Quick Reference
~45 minutes to create, 15 to redraw

Sections

  1. Key Vocabulary
  2. Key Sources (literary + material)
  3. Sketch Visuals
  4. Core Concepts
  5. Connections to Other Topics
  6. Common Misconceptions

Example 1

Set an 8-minute timer and attempt this question cold: translate the following unseen sentence into natural English: ‘Mīlitēs, quī iam multōs diēs sine cibō ambulāverant, tandem castra hostium vīdērunt.’ Write by hand, no vocabulary list. Use the translation scaffold: identify the main verb and its tense (vīdērunt — perfect, ‘they saw’), find the subject via the nominative (mīlitēs, ‘the soldiers’), pick out the subordinate clause and its connective (quī…ambulāverant — a relative clause, ‘who had been walking’), note any tricky case usage (sine cibō — ablative after the preposition sine, ‘without food’), then build the full English sentence in natural word order. When the timer goes, stop. Mark it: did you get the verb tense right, name the case of at least one tricky word, resolve the relative clause correctly, and produce natural English rather than a word-for-word crib?

Example 2

Work through a 10-mark-style syntax exercise under timed conditions: translate this sentence containing indirect speech: ‘Caesar dīxit mīlitēs fortiter pugnāvisse et hostēs mox fugitūrōs esse.’ Allocate roughly 2 minutes to plan your translation scaffold before you write: identify the introductory verb of speaking (dīxit — signals an indirect statement will follow); identify the accusative subject of the first infinitive (mīlitēs) and the infinitive’s tense (pugnāvisse — perfect infinitive, translated as ‘had fought’); identify the second infinitive clause (hostēs…fugitūrōs esse — future infinitive, ‘would flee’); the alternative reading (check whether fortiter modifies pugnāvisse rather than the whole clause — it does, so ‘fought bravely’); your conclusion (full translation: ‘Caesar said that the soldiers had fought bravely and that the enemy would soon flee’). Write your answer in the remaining 8 minutes, then stop regardless of whether you have finished. Record which parts of the scaffold you reached — if you ran out before covering the second infinitive clause, practise spotting linked indirect statements in the next session.

  • Stopping when the timer runs out and ignoring the unfinished bit. Note what you’d have written — that’s the data about your pace.

Knowledge Organisers

What the Research Says

StudyFindingImpact
Willingham (2017)Students need to store facts in long-term memory before they can think critically about them. Knowledge organisers are the storage scaffold.Not old-fashioned — cognitive prerequisite for analysis.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    One topic per organiser — a unit, a theme, a system. Not the whole of Paper 1. Too broad and it becomes a dense textbook page.
  2. 2
    Divide the page into 4–6 sections — typically: Key Vocabulary, Key Facts / Formulae, Core Concepts, Worked Examples, Connections to Other Topics. The structure forces you to categorise.

    Keep it to one side of A4 — the constraint is the point. If it doesn’t fit, the material isn’t yet compressed into the essentials.

  6. 6

Example 1

Create a knowledge organiser for the cardiovascular system. Sections: Key Vocabulary (cardiac output, stroke volume, heart rate, Starling mechanism, venous return); Key Formulae (CO = SV × HR with resting and maximum values); Short-Term Effects of Exercise (increased HR, SV, CO); Long-Term Training Adaptations (cardiac hypertrophy, lower resting HR, increased stroke volume); Connections (links to respiratory system via gaseous exchange). Fit it on one side of A4, redraw from memory after 3 days.

Example 2

Create a knowledge organiser for sports psychology (Paper 2). Sections: Motivation Types (intrinsic vs extrinsic — definitions + examples); Goal-Setting (SMART goals — one-line definitions); Maslow’s Hierarchy (five levels with a small pyramid sketch and one sporting example per level); Arousal Theories (Inverted-U, Catastrophe Theory — diagrams with labels); Mental Rehearsal (definition + when used). Redraw the organiser from memory a week later — the pyramid and the U-curve are the most commonly missed in exams.

Elaborative Interrogation

Ask “why?” and “how?” until the facts become explanations.

What the Research Says

Facts in isolation are fragile. Facts connected by explanations survive. Elaborative interrogation is the habit of asking “why is that true?” and “how does that work?” about every fact you learn — and forcing yourself to answer. The answer doesn’t need to be perfect. The act of trying to answer is what builds the mental connections that turn memorised facts into understood explanations.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Pressley et al. (1988)Asking “why?” during reading boosted recall by 40–70% compared to silent reading.Works even when the answer is imperfect.
Dunlosky et al. (2013)Rated “moderate utility” in the APS review — robust across subjects and ages, especially when applied to new material that builds on existing knowledge.Best for consolidating material you half-know.
Smith & Holliday (2006)Students who self-explained while studying scored significantly higher on transfer questions requiring application.Builds the ability to USE the knowledge, not just recall it.
Chi et al. (1994)Self-explanation was a stronger predictor of understanding than prior knowledge.Even weaker students catch up by explaining to themselves.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Study a chunk of content — a lesson, a paragraph, a key fact. Anything where facts are being introduced.
  2. 2
    After each fact, ask “why?” — why is this true? Why does it matter? Why did the author include it?
  3. 3
    Then ask “how?” — how does this connect to the topic? How does it lead to what comes next? How would you explain it to someone else?
  4. 4
    Try to answer out loud — even if your answer is wrong, the attempt activates deeper processing. Write your answer in the margin.
  5. 5
    Check your answer against the source — does the text support your explanation? If not, update it. The correction matters more than the first guess.
  6. 6
    Build chains — once you’ve asked “why?” once, ask it again of your answer. Push until you hit a genuinely fundamental fact. This is where deep understanding forms.
Example 1

You learn the fact: “Parliamentary sovereignty means Parliament is the supreme law-making body.” Ask: why does this matter? Because no court can strike down a parliamentary Act. Then ask: how does this interact with the Human Rights Act 1998? Courts can declare legislation incompatible with the Act but cannot override it — Parliament must choose whether to amend. Push one more: why can’t courts override Parliament? Because the UK has no codified constitution entrenching the separation of powers. This chain — from a single fact to constitutional principle — is exactly what the 12-mark extended question rewards.

Example 2

You cover the rule of law and note: “Everyone is equal before the law.” Ask: why is this a cornerstone of democracy? Because it prevents arbitrary power by governments or officials. Then ask: how is the rule of law protected in the UK? Through an independent judiciary, access to legal representation, and the right to a fair trial. Ask why these protections exist: they prevent the concentration of power and hold the state accountable to its own laws. This elaborated chain gives you the building blocks for an “evaluate the importance of the rule of law” question.

Common Pitfalls

  • Accepting “I don’t know”. Take a guess. Even a wrong guess activates the processing. Then check and correct.
  • One “why?” and moving on. The real gains come from the third or fourth “why?”, when you hit the fundamentals.
  • Only asking the obvious questions. Push toward the explanations your teacher never gave you — those are where genuine learning happens.
  • Skipping the check. Unchecked wrong answers reinforce misunderstanding. Always verify against the source.

When to Use This

Any time you’re covering conceptual material — not just listing facts. Particularly powerful in Citizenship with cause-and-effect topics (why do rights exist? how does separation of powers work?) and with analytical questions that reward explanation over recall. Build it into every lesson revisit, not as a separate session.

Quick Reference
Adds ~50% to reading time, transforms recall

Questions to ask

  1. Why is this true?
  2. How does it work?
  3. Why does it matter?
  4. How does it connect?
  5. Why now and not before?
  6. How would I explain this to a friend?

Retrieval Practice

Test yourself — don’t just re-read.

What the Research Says

Retrieval practice is the act of pulling information out of your memory, rather than pushing it in. It sounds simple but it is the most powerful revision technique we have — stronger than highlighting, stronger than re-reading, stronger than watching videos. The harder the retrieval feels, the more your long-term memory is strengthening.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Roediger & Karpicke (2006)Students who self-tested once remembered 50% more a week later than those who re-read four times.Self-testing > re-reading, even when it feels harder.
Karpicke & Blunt (2011)Retrieval practice beat concept-mapping and elaborative study on a delayed test by ~50%.Works better than other “active” strategies that feel productive.
Agarwal et al. (2017)Low-stakes retrieval quizzes raised GCSE-equivalent test scores by an average of one grade.Short regular quizzing moves your real exam score.
Smith et al. (2016)Students who practised retrieval scored higher even on questions testing information they didn’t specifically retrieve.Builds the skill of remembering itself, not just the facts.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Study a chunk of content — read through a StudyVault lesson, watch a video, or cover a topic in class. Don’t try to memorise. Just understand.
  2. 2
    Close everything — book shut, tab closed, notes flipped over. The whole point is that you cannot see the material.
  3. 3
    Write down everything you can remember — no looking back. This is called a “brain dump.” Write until you run out. It should feel uncomfortable.
  4. 4
    Check against the source — open the lesson. Mark what you missed in a different colour. Don’t just glance — properly compare.
  5. 5
    Target the gaps — re-study only the parts you missed. Not the whole lesson again. Just the holes.
  6. 6
    Retest tomorrow — hit the same topic again within 24 hours. The second attempt is where the learning locks in.
Example 1

After studying lever systems, close the book and write down from memory: which class of lever the elbow joint forms during a bicep curl, what acts as the load, fulcrum, and effort, and the mechanical advantage the arrangement provides. Then solve a fresh example: a person performing a calf raise — identify the lever class and label the three components. Check your answer (third-class at the elbow; second-class at the ankle), then redo any step you got wrong the following day.

Example 2

After covering the cardiovascular response to exercise, close everything and brain-dump the cardiac output formula (CO = SV × HR), the typical resting values for a trained athlete, and at least three short-term effects on heart rate during exercise. When you check back, note whether you correctly explained the Starling mechanism — this is a common gap that the OCR mark scheme rewards specifically.

Common Pitfalls

  • Peeking. If you look back during the brain dump, you’re not doing retrieval — you’re doing copying. Harder is better.
  • Only doing it once. One pass strengthens memory a little. Spaced repeats strengthen it permanently. Come back to the same topic 2–3 times over a week.
  • Doing it too soon after studying. If you retrieve while the material is still in short-term memory, it’s too easy to count. Leave at least 30 minutes between studying and testing.
  • Stopping when it feels difficult. Desirable difficulty is the whole point. If it feels easy, your memory isn’t being challenged and you’re not learning.

When to Use This

Build it in every week, from the start of Year 10 through to your exams. Aim for 15–20 minutes per subject, two or three times a week. The last two weeks before an exam is when retrieval practice becomes your main tool — swap passive reading for brain dumps and flashcards. On StudyVault, the Knowledge Check and Flashcard buttons in every lesson sidebar are retrieval practice in disguise — use them.

Quick Reference
~20 minutes per topic

Steps

  1. Study one topic
  2. Close everything
  3. Brain dump from memory
  4. Check gaps
  5. Re-study only the gaps
  6. Retest tomorrow

Spaced Repetition

Forget, then retrieve — that’s where the learning happens.

What the Research Says

The brain remembers things better when you review them just as you’re about to forget them. Cram everything the night before and it’s gone within a week. Revisit the same material on day one, day three, day seven, day fourteen and it sticks for months. This is the single biggest difference between students who peak in mocks and students who peak in the real exam.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Ebbinghaus (1885)Without revisiting, 50% of what you learn is lost within an hour and 80% within a day.The forgetting curve is real — and steeper than most students realise.
Cepeda et al. (2006)Meta-analysis of 254 studies: spaced practice beat massed practice in 259 out of 271 comparisons.Spacing works across ages, subjects, and skills.
Kang (2016)Optimal gap ≈ 10–20% of the time until the test. For a May exam, that means revisiting material every 3–6 weeks from Year 10.You can plan exactly when to revisit a topic.
Sisti et al. (2007)Neurons form stronger connections during the “almost forgotten” moment of retrieval.Struggling to recall IS the learning, not a sign you’ve failed.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Learn a topic today — read the lesson, watch the video, write notes. Mark it in a diary or app with today’s date.
  2. 2
    Review in 24 hours — do a retrieval practice brain dump, or redo the knowledge check. 5–10 minutes.
  3. 3
    Review again in 3 days — if you got it right yesterday, push the gap. Repeat the retrieval.
  4. 4
    Review again in 7 days — by now the material is consolidating into long-term memory.
  5. 5
    Review again in 2–3 weeks — gap the next review to 14 days, then 30, then 60.
  6. 6
    If you fail a review — reset the schedule. Back to day 1. Don’t skip the reset — it’s the point of the system.
Example 1

Day 1: study the principles of training (FITT — Frequency, Intensity, Time, Type — and SPORT: Specificity, Progressive Overload, Reversibility, Tedium). Day 2: brain-dump all eight terms with one-sentence definitions from memory. Day 7: test yourself again, this time adding a practical example for each principle (e.g. progressive overload — a swimmer adding one extra length per session each week). Day 14: attempt a past-paper question applying the principles to a new sport cold. By this point, the material is locked into long-term memory.

Example 2

After first studying somatotypes (ectomorph, mesomorph, endomorph), schedule five reviews. By day 7, you should be able to recall not just the body-type descriptions but also which sports suit each, and why muscle-to-fat ratio matters for performance. By day 30, you should be applying somatotype knowledge to explain why a gymnast and a sumo wrestler would have different optimal body compositions — an OCR 4-mark application question.

Common Pitfalls

  • Reviewing too often. If it’s easy, the gap is too short. Make it harder by stretching the interval.
  • Reviewing too late. If you’ve completely forgotten, you’re essentially re-learning from scratch — you lose the benefit of spacing.
  • No written schedule. Spaced repetition works only if you actually do the reviews. Use a calendar, the StudyVault flashcard system, or a simple Leitner box.
  • Skipping resets when you fail. If you couldn’t recall the material, you haven’t learnt it — regardless of how far through the schedule you were.

When to Use This

This is the organising principle of your whole revision year — not a technique you pull out near the exam. From the first lesson of Year 10, log every topic you cover and schedule reviews at 1 day, 3 days, 7 days, 14 days, and 30 days. The StudyVault flashcard system does this automatically via the Leitner method — questions move between five boxes with intervals of 1, 2, 4, 7, and 14 days. When a card comes up, do it. When it doesn’t, don’t.

Quick Reference
5 touches per topic, across a month

Intervals

  1. Learn today
  2. Retest tomorrow
  3. Retest day 3
  4. Retest day 7
  5. Retest day 14
  6. Retest day 30

Timed Practice

Simulate the real thing — including the time pressure.

What the Research Says

Knowing the content is only half of an exam. The other half is managing time, reading questions accurately under pressure, writing neatly when your hand hurts, and staying calm when you don’t know one of the questions. These are all skills — and like any skill, they need practice. Timed practice is how you build them.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Soderstrom & Bjork (2015)Transfer-appropriate processing: performance is best when the practice conditions closely match the test conditions.Practise in the conditions you’ll be tested in.
Agarwal et al. (2017)Students who did timed practice tests scored higher even on unseen questions.Builds generalisable exam skill, not just familiarity.
Yerkes & Dodson (1908)Performance is best at MODERATE arousal — some pressure helps, too much hurts.Simulated pressure builds tolerance for real pressure.
Hinze & Rapp (2014)Students who experienced test-like practice reported 30% less exam anxiety.Familiarity reduces fear. Fear reduces performance.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Start small — begin with one timed question or one section. Don’t jump straight to full papers. Build the muscle gradually.
  2. 2
    Match the exam mark-to-time ratio — if the real paper gives 1 mark per minute, give yourself the same. If you go over, stop and mark what you have.
  3. 3
    Remove distractions — phone in another room, no music, no snacks, no notes. The real exam hall has none of these.
  4. 4
    Handwrite — the exam is handwritten. Typing is faster and feels more productive, but it doesn’t train the same skill. Your hand will hurt on the day and that’s normal.
  5. 5
    Mark with the mark scheme honestly — use StudyVault’s per-question mark schemes or a teacher-provided one. Be harsh on yourself — underscoring now prevents overconfidence later.
  6. 6
    Do a full paper under conditions a month before the exam — uninterrupted, correct time, no music. One per subject, one per week in the final stretch.
Example 1

Practise a timed 8-mark “Do you think the UK should change its voting system?” question in 10 minutes. Structure your answer: define FPTP, identify one advantage (strong single-party government), identify one alternative (AMS), evaluate one advantage of the alternative (greater proportionality), then reach a reasoned conclusion. Mark your response against the AQA descriptor for Level 3 (clear, consistent argument with evidence) — check whether your conclusion is supported by the points you made, not just stated.

Example 2

Tackle the 12-mark extended writing question under timed conditions: allow 15 minutes for “Evaluate the effectiveness of citizenship action in bringing about change.” Before starting, spend 2 minutes planning: name two real examples of citizenship action (e.g. a local campaign, a petition to Parliament), one strength and one limitation of each. Write, then mark against the AQA level descriptors — does your answer show knowledge of how change happens, or does it only describe the action? The distinction is what separates Level 2 from Level 3.

Common Pitfalls

  • Stopping when the timer runs out and ignoring the unfinished bit. Note what you’d have written — that’s the data about your pace.
  • Using notes during “timed” practice. It’s not timed practice — it’s open-book practice. Useful, but different.
  • Only doing it in the last fortnight. Too late — you’ve not left time to fix the weaknesses the practice reveals.
  • Not marking honestly. Marking your own work gently protects feelings now and destroys results later.

When to Use This

From 10 weeks out, do at least one timed practice per subject per week — usually a single section at first, building to full papers. In the final month, do at least one full timed paper per subject. Always mark it against the actual scheme and note your pace.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Soderstrom & Bjork (2015)Transfer-appropriate processing: performance is best when the practice conditions closely match the test conditions.Practise in the conditions you’ll be tested in.
Agarwal et al. (2017)Students who did timed practice tests scored higher even on unseen questions.Builds generalisable exam skill, not just familiarity.
Yerkes & Dodson (1908)Performance is best at MODERATE arousal — some pressure helps, too much hurts.Simulated pressure builds tolerance for real pressure.
Hinze & Rapp (2014)Students who experienced test-like practice reported 30% less exam anxiety.Familiarity reduces fear. Fear reduces performance.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Start small — begin with one timed question or one section. Don’t jump straight to full papers. Build the muscle gradually.
  2. 2
    Match the exam mark-to-time ratio — OCR PE allocates approximately 1 minute per mark. A 9-mark extended response should take no more than 9 minutes. Time yourself accordingly.
  3. 3
    Remove distractions — phone in another room, no music, no notes. The real exam hall has none of these.
  4. 4
    Handwrite — the exam is handwritten. Typing is faster and feels more productive, but it doesn’t train the same skill. Your hand will hurt on the day and that’s normal.
  5. 5
    Mark with the mark scheme honestly — use StudyVault’s per-question mark schemes or a teacher-provided one. Be harsh on yourself — underscoring now prevents overconfidence later.
  6. 6
    Do a full paper under conditions a month before the exam — uninterrupted, correct time, no music. One per subject, one per week in the final stretch.
Example 1

Set a 9-minute timer and attempt this past-paper question cold: “Evaluate the use of interval training for a 400m runner. Refer to the principles of training in your answer.” Write by hand, no notes. When the timer goes, stop. Mark it against the OCR mark scheme: check that your answer names specific principles (progressive overload, specificity, reversibility), applies them to the athlete, and includes a reasoned evaluation — not just a list. The gap between what you wrote and what the scheme awards is exactly what to practise next.

Example 2

Work through a full Paper 2 section on sports psychology under timed conditions: allocate 1 minute per mark, answer all questions including the 9-mark extended response, and stop when the time is up regardless of whether you have finished. Mark your work and record which question types overran — typically the extended response and the 4-mark “explain using an example” questions. Practise those types specifically in the following session.

Common Pitfalls

  • Stopping when the timer runs out and ignoring the unfinished bit. Note what you’d have written — that’s the data about your pace.
  • Using notes during “timed” practice. It’s not timed practice — it’s open-book practice. Useful, but different.
  • Only doing it in the last fortnight. Too late — you’ve not left time to fix the weaknesses the practice reveals.
  • Not marking honestly. Marking your own work gently protects feelings now and destroys results later.

When to Use This

From 10 weeks out, do at least one timed practice per subject per week — usually a single section at first, building to full papers. In the final month, do at least one full timed paper per subject. Always mark it against the actual scheme and note your pace.

Quick Reference
Paper time + ~30 min marking

  2. One section, timed
  3. Half a paper, timed
  4. Full paper, timed
  5. Full paper, exam conditions
  6. Mock week, all papers

Spaced Repetition

Forget, then retrieve — that’s where the learning happens.

What the Research Says

The brain remembers things better when you review them just as you’re about to forget them. Cram everything the night before and it’s gone within a week. Revisit the same material on day one, day three, day seven, day fourteen and it sticks for months. This is the single biggest difference between students who peak in mocks and students who peak in the real exam.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Ebbinghaus (1885)Without revisiting, 50% of what you learn is lost within an hour and 80% within a day.The forgetting curve is real — and steeper than most students realise.
Cepeda et al. (2006)Meta-analysis of 254 studies: spaced practice beat massed practice in 259 out of 271 comparisons.Spacing works across ages, subjects, and skills.
Kang (2016)Optimal gap ≈ 10–20% of the time until the test. For a May exam, that means revisiting material every 3–6 weeks from Year 10.You can plan exactly when to revisit a topic.
Sisti et al. (2007)Neurons form stronger connections during the “almost forgotten” moment of retrieval.Struggling to recall IS the learning, not a sign you’ve failed.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Learn a topic today — read the lesson, watch the video, write notes. Mark it in a diary or app with today’s date.
  2. 2
    Review in 24 hours — do a retrieval practice brain dump, or redo the knowledge check. 5–10 minutes.
  3. 3
    Review again in 3 days — if you got it right yesterday, push the gap. Repeat the retrieval.
  4. 4
    Review again in 7 days — by now the material is consolidating into long-term memory.
  5. 5
    Review again in 2–3 weeks — gap the next review to 14 days, then 30, then 60.
  6. 6
    If you fail a review — reset the schedule. Back to day 1. Don’t skip the reset — it’s the point of the system.
Example 1

Plan a four-week cycle that rotates through the four main areas weekly: anatomy and movement in week one, physical training principles in week two, sports psychology in week three, and health and well-being in week four. Each week you revisit the previous week’s area briefly before moving on, so no topic gets more than seven days without a recall attempt.

Example 2

When you first learn the cardiac output formula (CO = HR × SV), write a worked example with real numbers and put it in your flashcard deck. Review it tomorrow, in three days, in a week. By the time Component 1 arrives, calculating stroke volume from given cardiac output and heart rate values will feel automatic rather than stressful.

Common Pitfalls

  • Reviewing too often. If it’s easy, the gap is too short. Make it harder by stretching the interval.
  • Reviewing too late. If you’ve completely forgotten, you’re essentially re-learning from scratch — you lose the benefit of spacing.
  • No written schedule. Spaced repetition works only if you actually do the reviews. Use a calendar, the StudyVault flashcard system, or a simple Leitner box.
  • Skipping resets when you fail. If you couldn’t recall the material, you haven’t learnt it — regardless of how far through the schedule you were.

When to Use This

This is the organising principle of your whole revision year — not a technique you pull out near the exam. From the first lesson of Year 10, log every topic you cover and schedule reviews at 1 day, 3 days, 7 days, 14 days, and 30 days. The StudyVault flashcard system does this automatically via the Leitner method — questions move between five boxes with intervals of 1, 2, 4, 7, and 14 days. When a card comes up, do it. When it doesn’t, don’t.

Intervals

  1. Learn today
  2. Retest tomorrow
  3. Retest day 3
  4. Retest day 7
  5. Retest day 14
  6. Retest day 30

Elaborative Interrogation

Ask “why?” and “how?” until the facts become explanations.

What the Research Says

Facts in isolation are fragile. Facts connected by explanations survive. Elaborative interrogation is the habit of asking “why is that true?” and “how does that work?” about every fact you learn — and forcing yourself to answer. The answer doesn’t need to be perfect. The act of trying to answer is what builds the mental connections that turn memorised lists into understood physics. This is exactly what examiners reward in ‘explain’ and ‘evaluate’ questions.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Pressley et al. (1988)Asking “why?” during reading boosted recall by 40–70% compared to silent reading.Works even when the answer is imperfect.
Dunlosky et al. (2013)Rated “moderate utility” — robust across subjects and ages, especially when applied to new material that builds on existing knowledge.Best for consolidating material you half-know.
Smith & Holliday (2006)Students who self-explained while studying scored significantly higher on transfer questions requiring application.Builds the ability to USE the knowledge, not just recall it.
Chi et al. (1994)Self-explanation was a stronger predictor of understanding than prior knowledge.Even weaker students catch up by explaining to themselves.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Study a chunk of content — a lesson, a paragraph, a key fact. Anything where facts are being introduced.
  2. 2
    After each fact, ask “why?” — why is this true? Why does it work this way? Why does the examiner care about it?
  3. 3
    Then ask “how?” — how does this connect to the topic? How does it lead to what comes next? How would you explain it to someone else?
  4. 4
    Try to answer out loud or in writing — even if your answer is wrong, the attempt activates deeper processing. Write your answer in the margin.
  5. 5
    Check your answer against the source — does the lesson support your explanation? If not, update it. The correction matters more than the first guess.
  6. 6
    Build chains — once you’ve asked “why?” once, ask it again of your answer. Push until you hit a genuinely fundamental fact. This is where deep understanding forms.
Example 1 — Why redshift constitutes evidence for an expanding universe

Fact: the spectral lines of distant galaxies are shifted toward longer (redder) wavelengths. Ask “why does that happen?” — because the galaxies are moving away from us; the Doppler effect stretches the wavelength of emitted light, and \(\Delta\lambda / \lambda = v/c\). Ask “how does the degree of shift relate to distance?” — Hubble found that recession speed is proportional to distance: \(v = H_0 d\), with \(H_0 \approx 70\) km s\(^{-1}\) Mpc\(^{-1}\). Ask “why does this mean the universe is expanding rather than just that galaxies are moving through space?” — because the relationship holds in every direction with no central point, which means space itself is stretching. That three-step chain is exactly the reasoning a 4-mark ‘explain’ question on Big Bang evidence expects.

Example 2 — Why a high-mass star ends its life differently from a low-mass star

Fact: stars above approximately 8 solar masses end as supernovae rather than planetary nebulae. Ask “why does mass determine the endpoint?” — because higher mass means higher core temperature and pressure, which allows fusion to continue beyond helium to carbon, neon, oxygen, silicon, and eventually iron. Ask “why does iron end fusion?” — because iron has the highest binding energy per nucleon; fusing iron absorbs energy rather than releasing it, so the energy source driving the star switches off. Ask “why does the core then collapse?” — because without radiation pressure, gravity overwhelms the electron degeneracy pressure if the core exceeds the Chandrasekhar limit of 1.4 M☉, producing a neutron star or black hole. That chain converts a memorised fact into an explained mechanism.

Common Pitfalls

  • Accepting “I don’t know”. Take a guess. Even a wrong guess activates the processing. Then check and correct.
  • One “why?” and moving on. The real gains come from the third or fourth “why?”, when you hit the fundamentals.
  • Only asking the obvious questions. Push toward the explanations your teacher never gave you — those are where genuine learning happens.
  • Skipping the check. Unchecked wrong answers reinforce misunderstanding. Always verify against the source.

When to Use This

Any time you are covering conceptual material — not just recalling named items. Particularly powerful for the three Big Bang evidence strands (redshift, CMB at 2.7 K, quasar distribution), the mass-dependent stellar evolution tracks, and the eclipse geometry questions. Build it into every lesson revisit, not as a separate session. It adds around 50% to your reading time but makes everything else — retrieval, exam answers — significantly easier.

Quick Reference
Adds ~50% to reading time, transforms recall

The chain

  1. Read the fact
  2. Ask “why is this true?”
  3. Ask “how does it work?”
  4. Write your answer
  5. Check against the source
  6. Ask “why?” again of your answer

Retrieval Practice

Test yourself — don’t just re-read.

What the Research Says

Retrieval practice is the act of pulling information out of your memory, rather than pushing it in. It sounds simple but it is the most powerful revision technique we have — stronger than highlighting, stronger than re-reading, stronger than watching videos. The harder the retrieval feels, the more your long-term memory is strengthening.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Roediger & Karpicke (2006)Students who self-tested once remembered 50% more a week later than those who re-read four times.Self-testing > re-reading, even when it feels harder.
Karpicke & Blunt (2011)Retrieval practice beat concept-mapping and elaborative study on a delayed test by ~50%.Works better than other “active” strategies that feel productive.
Agarwal et al. (2017)Low-stakes retrieval quizzes raised GCSE-equivalent test scores by an average of one grade.Short regular quizzing moves your real exam score.
Smith et al. (2016)Students who practised retrieval scored higher even on questions testing information they didn’t specifically retrieve.Builds the skill of remembering itself, not just the facts.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Study a chunk of content — read through a StudyVault lesson, watch a video, or cover a topic in class. Don’t try to memorise. Just understand.
  2. 2
    Close everything — book shut, tab closed, notes flipped over. The whole point is that you cannot see the material.
  3. 3
    Write down everything you can remember — no looking back. This is called a “brain dump.” Write until you run out. It should feel uncomfortable.
  4. 4
    Check against the source — open the lesson. Mark what you missed in a different colour. Don’t just glance — properly compare.
  5. 5
    Target the gaps — re-study only the parts you missed. Not the whole lesson again. Just the holes.
  6. 6
    Retest tomorrow — hit the same topic again within 24 hours. The second attempt is where the learning locks in.
Example 1

After studying Brecht’s epic theatre, close the book and write the four key alienation techniques from memory: Verfremdungseffekt, gestus, direct address, and song/placard interruption. Then describe — in two sentences each — how a director would use each technique in a production of Blood Brothers (for example, using gestus to physicalise Mickey’s working-class slump versus Eddie’s upright posture in the park scene). Mark your answers, then redo any technique you missed the following day.

Example 2

After covering stage configurations, close everything and brain-dump all four types from memory — proscenium arch, thrust, in-the-round, traverse — with one sentence on the audience relationship each creates. Then add one advantage and one limitation per type for a designer choosing between them. Check your answers against the lesson, note which configuration you confused, and test yourself on it again tomorrow.

Common Pitfalls

  • Peeking. If you look back during the brain dump, you’re not doing retrieval — you’re doing copying. Harder is better.
  • Only doing it once. One pass strengthens memory a little. Spaced repeats strengthen it permanently. Come back to the same topic 2–3 times over a week.
  • Doing it too soon after studying. If you retrieve while the material is still in short-term memory, it’s too easy to count. Leave at least 30 minutes between studying and testing.
  • Stopping when it feels difficult. Desirable difficulty is the whole point. If it feels easy, your memory isn’t being challenged and you’re not learning.

When to Use This

Build it in every week, from the start of Year 10 through to your exams. Aim for 15–20 minutes per subject, two or three times a week. The last two weeks before an exam is when retrieval practice becomes your main tool — swap passive reading for brain dumps and flashcards. On StudyVault, the Knowledge Check and Flashcard buttons in every lesson sidebar are retrieval practice in disguise — use them.

Quick Reference
~20 minutes per topic

Steps

  1. Study one topic
  2. Close everything
  3. Brain dump from memory
  4. Check gaps
  5. Re-study only the gaps
  6. Retest tomorrow

Interleaving

Mix topics in one session — don’t block them.

What the Research Says

Most students revise by blocking — an hour on the set play, an hour on practitioners, an hour on design. It feels productive and the topic seems clear by the end. Interleaving is the opposite: you jump between topics inside a single session. It feels worse at the time, and you’ll make more mistakes. But when the real exam arrives, you will be dramatically better at knowing which technique to apply — and that is usually the hardest part of any exam question.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Rohrer & Taylor (2007)Students who interleaved topics scored 43% higher on delayed tests than blocked-practice students.Same time spent — huge difference in exam performance.
Birnbaum et al. (2013)Interleaved learners felt LESS confident during practice but performed BETTER in the test.If revision feels too easy, interleave.
Bjork & Bjork (2011)Desirable difficulties — including interleaving — create durable long-term learning at the cost of short-term performance.Short-term struggle is the price of long-term gain.
Taylor & Rohrer (2010)Benefit was largest when topics looked superficially similar — students learnt to DISTINGUISH them.Most useful where students confuse similar techniques.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Pick 3–5 related topics — topics that share a paper, a theme, or a question type. Similar enough that students confuse them.
  2. 2
    Make a mixed question set — 10–15 questions drawn from all the topics. Don’t tell yourself which topic each question belongs to.
  3. 3
    Attempt each question cold — first step is identifying what’s being asked. That identification is the skill you’re training.
  4. 4
    Mark after every question — note which topic each one was. Pay attention to mis-identifications — those are the highest-value gaps.
  5. 5
    Rebuild a new mixed set tomorrow — same topics, different questions. Different order. Over time, misclassifications drop.
  6. 6
    Expect to feel worse than blocked practice — that’s the right feeling. Your exam self will thank you.
Example 1

Mix Section A and Section B question types in a single 40-minute session: answer a 4-mark question on the role of the sound designer, then switch to a Section B question asking how you as a director would stage the opening scene of your set play, then return to a Section A question on the differences between a lighting designer and a lighting operator. Switching trains you to shift rapidly between the technical-knowledge register and the analytical-design register — exactly as the real exam requires.

Example 2

When revising practitioners, mix Stanislavski, Brecht, and Artaud questions in a single set rather than studying each one in isolation. A question might ask you to identify which practitioner used “the system” to develop realistic performance, then the next might ask how Brecht’s concept of gestus differs from Stanislavski’s psychological realism. Forcing yourself to switch between practitioners builds the discrimination skill the exam tests directly in Section A comparison questions.

Common Pitfalls

  • Random, not related. Interleaving Drama with History is just subject-switching. Interleave WITHIN Drama — related topics that students confuse.
  • Giving up when it feels hard. The discomfort is the signal that it’s working. Don’t revert to blocked practice because interleaving feels slow.
  • Labelling the topic at the top of each question. Defeats the point — the identification IS the training.
  • Using it too early in learning. You need baseline familiarity with each topic first. Interleaving is for consolidation, not first exposure.

When to Use This

Once you’ve covered a handful of related topics — usually partway through a term — start weaving them into mixed practice sessions. Very useful in the final 8–10 weeks before exams when you’re moving from learning to applying. Full past papers are the ultimate interleaving exercise, because they force you to shift between question types cold.

Quick Reference
~30–45 minutes per session

Steps

  1. Pick 3–5 related topics
  2. Build a mixed set
  3. Attempt cold
  4. Mark & note topic
  5. Fix misclassifications
  6. Expect discomfort

Knowledge Organisers

One page per topic — the whole picture at a glance.

What the Research Says

A knowledge organiser is a single side of A4 that captures everything a student needs to know about a topic — key vocabulary, essential facts, core concepts, and connections between them. Used properly, it becomes the base layer of your revision: the thing you keep coming back to, the thing you redraw from memory, the thing you carry on the bus. Used badly, it becomes a wall of dense text that nobody reads.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Willingham (2017)Students need to store facts in long-term memory before they can think critically about them. Knowledge organisers are the storage scaffold.Not old-fashioned — cognitive prerequisite for analysis.
Counsell (2018)Used in UK schools to reduce cognitive load by pre-structuring the material students encounter.Reduces working memory demand during lessons.
Sweller (1988)Cognitive Load Theory: well-organised schemas free up working memory for higher-order tasks.A well-designed organiser makes hard questions easier.
Oakes & Griffin (2017)Students who made their OWN organisers outperformed those given finished ones.Making is learning. Receiving is not.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    One topic per organiser — a practitioner, a set play, a design specialism, or an exam section. Not the whole subject on one page.
  2. 2
    Divide the page into 4–6 sections — typically: Key Vocabulary, Core Techniques / Methods, Key Quotes or Stage Directions, Design Choices, Connections to Practitioners, Example from Set Play. The structure forces you to categorise.
  3. 3
    Keep it to one side of A4 — the constraint is the point. If it doesn’t fit, the material isn’t yet compressed into the essentials.
  4. 4
    Use tiny structural visuals — a mini stage plan, a 2×2 practitioner grid, a small timeline of theatre movements. Dual coding applies: words + visuals beat words alone.
  5. 5
    Redraw it from memory weekly — this is where the learning is. A finished organiser you never revisit is wasted. The redrawn one is retrieval practice in disguise.
  6. 6
    Annotate over time — when you learn something new that fits, add it. When a connection becomes clearer, draw the link. The organiser evolves.
Example 1

Create a one-page organiser for Brecht. Sections: Key Vocabulary (Verfremdungseffekt, gestus, direct address, Epic Theatre), Core Techniques (five alienation devices with one-line definitions), Example from Set Play (two specific moments in your set play where a director could use gestus or direct address), and a mini comparison column: Brecht vs Stanislavski in four rows. Redraw the whole page from memory the following week and check which section you left blank first.

Example 2

Make a one-page organiser for your set play’s design requirements. Sections: Key Staging Vocabulary (proxemics, levels, sight lines, blocking), Set Design choices (three key set pieces and their symbolic functions), Lighting (three key states and their emotional effect), Sound (three key cues and their purpose), and a mini stage plan in the corner showing the configuration you would use and why. Carry this to every revision session as your reference point for Section B writing.

Common Pitfalls

  • Copying the textbook. A dense page of 8pt text isn’t a knowledge organiser — it’s a photocopy. Compress ruthlessly.
  • One page per subject. Too much, too diffuse. One page per topic — practitioner, design specialism, or set-play unit.
  • Making one and never revisiting. The value is in the redrawing — not the original creation.
  • Using a downloaded one instead of making your own. Research is clear: making beats receiving. Teacher-provided organisers are useful for structure only.

When to Use This

Start one at the beginning of each topic, as you’re learning it. Refine as your understanding grows. Redraw the whole set from memory in the final month before exams — one topic per day. Carry a folder of your organisers to every revision session. Use them as the spine of retrieval practice: cover the organiser, brain-dump, then check.

~45 minutes to create, 15 to redraw

Sections

  2. Core Techniques / Methods
  3. Key Quotes / Stage Directions
  4. Design Choices
  5. Example from Set Play
