Timed Practice

Simulate the real thing — including the time pressure.

What the Research Says

Knowing the content is only half of an exam. The other half is managing time, reading questions accurately under pressure, writing neatly when your hand hurts, and staying calm when you don’t know one of the questions. These are all skills — and like any skill, they need practice. Timed practice is how you build them.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Soderstrom & Bjork (2015)Transfer-appropriate processing: performance is best when the practice conditions closely match the test conditions.Practise in the conditions you’ll be tested in.
Agarwal et al. (2017)Students who did timed practice tests scored higher even on unseen questions.Builds generalisable exam skill, not just familiarity.
Yerkes & Dodson (1908)Performance is best at MODERATE arousal — some pressure helps, too much hurts.Simulated pressure builds tolerance for real pressure.
Hinze & Rapp (2014)Students who experienced test-like practice reported 30% less exam anxiety.Familiarity reduces fear. Fear reduces performance.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Start small — begin with one timed question or one section. Don’t jump straight to full papers. Build the muscle gradually.
  2. 2
    Match the exam mark-to-time ratio — AQA Drama is a 1 hour 45 minute paper worth 80 marks, so roughly 1 mark per minute. If you go over, stop and mark what you have.
  3. 3
    Remove distractions — phone in another room, no music, no snacks, no notes. The real exam hall has none of these.
  4. 4
    Handwrite — the exam is handwritten. Typing is faster and feels more productive, but it doesn’t train the same skill. Your hand will hurt on the day and that’s normal.
  5. 5
    Mark with the mark scheme honestly — use StudyVault’s per-question mark schemes or a teacher-provided one. Be harsh on yourself — underscoring now prevents overconfidence later.
  6. 6
    Do a full paper under conditions a month before the exam — uninterrupted, correct time, no music. One per subject, one per week in the final stretch.
Example 1

Practise a Section B set-play question under timed conditions: set a 45-minute timer and write a full response to “As a director, how would you use staging and proxemics to communicate the power relationship between two characters in one scene of your set play?” When time is up, mark your answer against the AQA band descriptors: did you sustain the director’s perspective throughout, reference specific moments from the play, and justify every choice with reference to effect on the audience? Note which band descriptor you fell short of and target it in your next attempt.

Example 2

Practise a Section C live theatre review under timed conditions. Set 35 minutes and write an evaluative response to a performance you have seen, focusing on one design element — for example, lighting. Your response should name specific moments, use technical vocabulary accurately (wash, gobo, follow spot, colour temperature), and evaluate the effect on the audience using evidence from the performance. Marking your own work against the AQA mark scheme trains you to see what “perceptive and detailed” looks like at the top band — before the real exam tests you on it.

Common Pitfalls

  • Stopping when the timer runs out and ignoring the unfinished bit. Note what you’d have written — that’s the data about your pace.
  • Using notes during “timed” practice. It’s not timed practice — it’s open-book practice. Useful, but different.
  • Only doing it in the last fortnight. Too late — you’ve not left time to fix the weaknesses the practice reveals.
  • Not marking honestly. Marking your own work gently protects feelings now and destroys results later.

When to Use This

From 10 weeks out, do at least one timed practice per subject per week — usually a single section at first, building to full papers. In the final month, do at least one full timed paper. AQA Drama Section B extended answers (up to 32 marks) take practice to pace correctly — start timed Section B writing long before the exam so the fluency is already there on the day.

Quick Reference
Paper time (1h 45m) + ~30 min marking

Build-up schedule

  1. One Section A question, timed
  2. One Section B passage, timed
  3. Full Section B response, timed
  4. Section C review, timed
  5. Full paper, timed
  6. Mock week, exam conditions

Interleaving

Mix topics in one session — don’t block them.

What the Research Says

Most students revise by blocking — an hour on anatomy, an hour on training principles, an hour on sports psychology. It feels productive and the topic seems clear by the end. Interleaving is the opposite: you jump between topics inside a single session. It feels worse at the time, and you’ll make more mistakes. But when the real exam arrives, you will be dramatically better at knowing which technique to apply — and that is usually the hardest part of any exam question.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Rohrer & Taylor (2007)Students who interleaved topics scored 43% higher on delayed tests than blocked-practice students.Same time spent — huge difference in exam performance.
Birnbaum et al. (2013)Interleaved learners felt LESS confident during practice but performed BETTER in the test.If revision feels too easy, interleave.
Bjork & Bjork (2011)Desirable difficulties — including interleaving — create durable long-term learning at the cost of short-term performance.Short-term struggle is the price of long-term gain.
Taylor & Rohrer (2010)Benefit was largest when topics looked superficially similar — students learnt to DISTINGUISH them.Most useful where students confuse similar concepts.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Pick 3–5 related topics — topics that share a paper, a theme, or a question type. Similar enough that students confuse them.
  2. 2
    Make a mixed problem set — 10–15 questions drawn randomly from all the topics. Don’t tell yourself which topic each question belongs to.
  3. 3
    Attempt each question cold — first step is identifying what’s being asked. That identification is the skill you’re training.
  4. 4
    Mark after every question — note which topic each one was. Pay attention to mis-identifications — those are the highest-value gaps.
  5. 5
    Rebuild a new mixed set tomorrow — same topics, different questions. Different order. Over time, misclassifications drop.
  6. 6
    Expect to feel worse than blocked practice — that’s the right feeling. Your exam self will thank you.
Example 1

Within a single revision session, alternate between Component 1 and Component 2 content: answer a question on lever systems, then one on arousal theory, then one on training methods (FITT principle), then one on barriers to participation. This forces your brain to switch contexts in the same way the exam paper does — topics are never neatly grouped on the actual paper.

Example 2

Mix up questions on the three muscle fibre types, the three axes of movement, and the five components of fitness in one set. All three are list-based classification topics that students muddle under pressure. Interleaving them until you can answer any one cold — without being “in the zone” for that topic — is exactly what exam conditions require.

Common Pitfalls

  • Random, not related. Interleaving PE with English is just subject-switching. Interleave WITHIN PE — related topics that students confuse.
  • Giving up when it feels hard. The discomfort is the signal that it’s working. Don’t revert to blocked practice because interleaving feels slow.
  • Labelling the topic at the top of each question. Defeats the point — the identification IS the training.
  • Using it too early in learning. You need baseline familiarity with each topic first. Interleaving is for consolidation, not first exposure.

When to Use This

Once you’ve covered a handful of related topics — usually partway through a term — start weaving them into mixed practice sessions. Very useful in the final 8–10 weeks before exams when you’re moving from learning to applying. Full past papers are the ultimate interleaving exercise, because they force you to identify question types cold.

Quick Reference
~30–45 minutes per session

Steps

  1. Pick 3–5 related topics
  2. Build a mixed set
  3. Attempt cold
  4. Mark & note topic
  5. Fix misclassifications
  6. Expect discomfort

Knowledge Organisers

One page per topic — everything you need to know, nothing you don’t.

What the Research Says

A knowledge organiser is a single page that captures all the essential facts, definitions, named lists and examples for one topic. The page itself is not the product — redrawing it from memory is. When you can reconstruct a complete knowledge organiser without looking, you have achieved the kind of well-organised memory that makes exam questions feel familiar rather than surprising.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Kirschner, Sweller & Clark (2006)Structured, explicit knowledge organisation significantly outperforms unguided discovery for complex material.Organised knowledge is recalled faster and more accurately.
Sweller (1988) — Cognitive Load TheoryBreaking complex content into manageable chunks prevents working memory from becoming overloaded.One-page structure prevents the “where do I start?” freeze.
Rosenshine (2012)Reviewing key information in small doses and checking for understanding produces the highest retention rates.Brief, structured review beats long unstructured sessions.
Willingham (2009)Prior knowledge is the single biggest predictor of how much new knowledge sticks. Well-organised schemas grow themselves.Building strong knowledge organisers early accelerates all later learning.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Choose one topic — one lesson or one spec topic area. Not a whole unit at once — the page must fit on one side of A4.
  2. 2
    Plan the sections — key terms and definitions, equations with symbol glossaries and units, named classifications (spectral types, stellar populations, telescope types), a worked numerical example, a mini diagram or sketch. These sections cover the structure of every Astronomy topic.
  3. 3
    Build the page using the lesson as source — write in your own words. If you cannot paraphrase it, you do not understand it yet.
  4. 4
    Turn the page face-down and reconstruct it — blank paper, no notes. Fill in as much as you can. This converts the note-making activity into retrieval practice.
  5. 5
    Compare and mark in red — every item you missed gets circled. Those circles are tomorrow’s revision targets.
  6. 6
    Repeat at spaced intervals — reconstruct the same organiser on day 3, day 7, day 14. Each attempt should take less time and produce fewer red circles.
Example 1 — Equations and distance measures organiser

Build a one-page organiser covering the six key equations. Sections: (1) Parallax — \(d\,(\text{pc}) = 1 / p\,(\text{arcsec})\); baseline = 1 AU; only reliable within ~1000 pc. (2) Distance modulus — \(m - M = 5\log(d) - 5\); \(m\) = apparent magnitude, \(M\) = absolute magnitude, \(d\) in parsecs. (3) Hubble’s law — \(v = H_0 d\); \(H_0 \approx 70\) km s\(^{-1}\) Mpc\(^{-1}\). (4) Telescope magnification — \(M = f_o / f_e\); \(f_o\) = objective focal length, \(f_e\) = eyepiece focal length. (5) Kepler’s third law — \(T^2 \propto r^3\) (same for all planets orbiting the same star). (6) Redshift — \(\Delta\lambda / \lambda = v / c\). Include a worked example for each. Reconstruct on day 3 — the symbol-to-quantity mapping is the first thing students drop, and incorrect units lose marks even when the method is right.

Example 2 — Big Bang evidence strands organiser

Build a one-page organiser for the three Big Bang evidence strands. Sections: (1) Galactic redshift — Hubble (1929) found all galaxies recede; recession speed proportional to distance (\(v = H_0 d\)); implies universe expanding from a common origin. (2) Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) — uniform 2.7 K radiation across the entire sky; predicted as the cooled relic of the hot early universe; discovered by Penzias & Wilson (1965). (3) Quasar distribution — quasars are only observed at high redshift (i.e. great distances, early universe); none nearby — evidence the universe was different in the past, inconsistent with a steady-state model. Add one counter-argument per strand (e.g. CMB: could have another source?) and a rebuttal. Reconstruct in one week. Students who can reproduce all three strands with their rebuttals are ready for any extended-response cosmology question.

Common Pitfalls

  • Making it too long. If it doesn’t fit on one A4 side, split it into two topics. Length signals you haven’t condensed the content yet.
  • Copying instead of paraphrasing. If you paste sentences from the lesson word-for-word, you are not processing — you are transcribing. Rephrase everything.
  • Never reconstructing from memory. A knowledge organiser you don’t rebuild from scratch is just a note. The reconstruction is the revision.
  • Building all pages at once. Spreading organiser-building across the year — one page per lesson — works far better than building all 26 pages the week before the exam.

When to Use This

Build each organiser within a day of studying the lesson — while the material is fresh enough to paraphrase. Then use spaced reconstruction to keep the knowledge active. For Astronomy, the highest-value organisers to build are: the six core equations with symbol glossaries and units; the HR diagram with all four stellar populations; the stellar evolution flowchart for low-mass and high-mass paths; the three Big Bang evidence strands with rebuttals; and the sidereal vs synodic period comparison with worked numerical examples. These are the topics that appear most consistently in mark scheme breakdowns.

Quick Reference
~30 min build + 10 min per reconstruction

Five sections

  1. Key terms & definitions
  2. Equations with symbol glossary
  3. Named classifications
  4. Worked numerical example
  5. Mini diagram or sketch

Elaborative Interrogation

Ask “why?” and “how?” until the facts become explanations.

What the Research Says

Facts in isolation are fragile. Facts connected by explanations survive. Elaborative interrogation is the habit of asking “why is that true?” and “how does that work?” about every fact you learn — and forcing yourself to answer. The answer doesn’t need to be perfect. The act of trying to answer is what builds the mental connections that turn memorised facts into understood explanations.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Pressley et al. (1988)Asking “why?” during reading boosted recall by 40–70% compared to silent reading.Works even when the answer is imperfect.
Dunlosky et al. (2013)Rated “moderate utility” in the APS review — robust across subjects and ages, especially when applied to new material that builds on existing knowledge.Best for consolidating material you half-know.
Smith & Holliday (2006)Science students who self-explained while studying scored significantly higher on transfer questions requiring application.Builds the ability to USE the knowledge, not just recall it.
Chi et al. (1994)Self-explanation was a stronger predictor of understanding than prior knowledge.Even weaker students catch up by explaining to themselves.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Study a chunk of content — a lesson, a paragraph, a key fact. Anything where facts are being introduced.
  2. 2
    After each fact, ask “why?” — why is this true? Why does it matter? Why does this happen in the body?
  3. 3
    Then ask “how?” — how does this connect to performance? How does it lead to what comes next physiologically? How would you explain it to someone who has never studied PE?
  4. 4
    Try to answer out loud — even if your answer is wrong, the attempt activates deeper processing. Write your answer in the margin.
  5. 5
    Check your answer against the source — does the lesson support your explanation? If not, update it. The correction matters more than the first guess.
  6. 6
    Build chains — once you’ve asked “why?” once, ask it again of your answer. Push until you hit a genuinely fundamental physiological principle. This is where deep understanding forms.
Example 1

Fact: when the biceps brachii contracts, the triceps brachii relaxes. Ask WHY: because antagonistic pairs work by reciprocal inhibition — the nervous system suppresses the opposing muscle to allow smooth movement. Ask HOW: the motor neurones to the agonist activate while an inhibitory signal prevents the antagonist from contracting simultaneously. That chain of “why” turns a one-line fact into an explanation you can apply to any joint action question.

Example 2

Fact: Type I (slow-twitch) muscle fibres are used in endurance events; Type IIx (fast-twitch) in explosive power events. Ask WHY: Type I fibres have more mitochondria and myoglobin, so they generate energy aerobically and resist fatigue. Ask WHY Type IIx fibres fatigue faster: they rely on anaerobic glycolysis, which produces lactic acid as a by-product. That chain explains not just what the fibres do but why — exactly what a 6-mark exam question demands.

Common Pitfalls

  • Accepting “I don’t know”. Take a guess. Even a wrong guess activates the processing. Then check and correct.
  • One “why?” and moving on. The real gains come from the third or fourth “why?”, when you hit the fundamentals.
  • Only asking the obvious questions. Push toward the explanations your teacher never gave you — those are where genuine learning happens.
  • Skipping the check. Unchecked wrong answers reinforce misunderstanding. Always verify against the source.

When to Use This

Any time you’re covering conceptual material — not just listing facts. Particularly powerful with cause-and-effect physiology (why cardiac output increases during exercise, why the body shunts blood to working muscles) and with applied scenarios where the exam gives you a sport and asks you to explain a physiological response. Build it into every lesson revisit, not as a separate session.

Quick Reference
Adds ~50% to reading time, transforms recall

Questions to ask

  1. Why is this true?
  2. How does it work?
  3. Why does it matter?
  4. How does it connect?
  5. Why does this happen in the body?
  6. How would I explain this to a friend?

Interleaving

Mix topics in one session — don’t block them.

What the Research Says

Most students revise by blocking — an hour on the Elizabethan Age, an hour on Germany, an hour on Crime & Punishment. It feels productive and the topic seems clear by the end. Interleaving is the opposite: you jump between topics inside a single session. It feels worse at the time, and you’ll make more mistakes. But when the real exam arrives, you will be dramatically better at knowing which second-order concept a question is targeting — cause, consequence, significance, change — and that identification is often the hardest part of a History response.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Rohrer & Taylor (2007)Students who interleaved topics scored 43% higher on delayed tests than blocked-practice students.Same time spent — huge difference in exam performance.
Birnbaum et al. (2013)Interleaved learners felt LESS confident during practice but performed BETTER in the test.If revision feels too easy, interleave.
Bjork & Bjork (2011)Desirable difficulties — including interleaving — create durable long-term learning at the cost of short-term performance.Short-term struggle is the price of long-term gain.
Taylor & Rohrer (2010)Benefit was largest when topics looked superficially similar — students learnt to DISTINGUISH them.Most useful where students confuse related ideas — exactly the problem with second-order concepts.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Pick 3–5 related topics or question types — topics that share a paper, a second-order concept, or a question format. Similar enough that students confuse them.
  2. 2
    Make a mixed problem set — 10–15 questions drawn from all the topics. Don’t label which topic each question belongs to.
  3. 3
    Attempt each question cold — the first step is identifying what’s being asked. Is this a cause question, a significance question, or a change-and-continuity question? That identification is the skill you’re training.
  4. 4
    Mark after every question — note which concept or topic area each question targeted. Pay attention to mis-identifications — those are the highest-value gaps.
  5. 5
    Rebuild a new mixed set tomorrow — same topics, different questions, different order. Over time, misclassifications drop.
  6. 6
    Expect to feel worse than blocked practice — that’s the right feeling. Your exam self will thank you.
Example 1 — Mixing depth-study and thematic-study question types

Mix questions from your British depth study, your period study and your thematic study in one 40-minute session. Write 12 questions on separate slips: four from each area, shuffled. Before each question, ask yourself: “Is this a cause/consequence question, a significance question, a source utility question, or a change/continuity question?” Students regularly confuse a 6-mark ‘explain a cause’ question (which wants developed causation) with an 8-mark ‘explain the significance of’ question (which wants a judgement about lasting impact). The interleaving drill trains that distinction directly, preventing the common error of writing a narrative response to a significance question.

Example 2 — Mixing content from across the three thematic eras

For a thematic study such as Crime & Punishment or Warfare, mix questions from the medieval (c.500–1500), early modern (c.1500–1750) and modern (c.1750–present) eras in one session without labelling which era each question comes from. This trains you to recognise which era the evidence belongs to and whether it represents change or continuity — the exact discrimination the thematic essay demands. Students who revise each era in isolation often produce essays that list events chronologically instead of weighing change against continuity across all three periods. Interleaving prevents this by making era-to-era comparison the natural reflex.

Common Pitfalls

  • Interleaving before you know the basics. You need to know each topic individually first. Use interleaving once you’ve studied all your options — not as a first-pass strategy.
  • Giving up because it feels hard. Difficulty during interleaved practice is the signal it’s working. Persist.
  • Mixing completely unrelated subjects. Interleaving works best when the topics are related enough to be confused. Mix History question types together — not History with Geography.
  • Not checking mis-identifications. The mistake is the data. If you approached a ‘why do interpretations differ?’ question as if it were a ‘describe a feature’ question, that confusion is exactly what needs fixing before the exam.

When to Use This

Start interleaving once you have studied all your options at least once. In the final six weeks before the exam, replace most blocked revision with interleaved mixed sets. Particularly powerful the week before the exam when you want to simulate the unpredictable order in which questions appear — the exam will not group all the causation questions together, and neither should your revision.

Quick Reference
~40 minutes per interleaved session

Steps

  1. Pick 3–5 related topics
  2. Build mixed question set
  3. Identify the concept first
  4. Attempt the question
  5. Mark every question
  6. Rebuild tomorrow

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Choose one option or topic — one depth study, one period, or one era of a thematic study. Not a whole paper at once — the page must fit on one side of A4.
  2. 2
    Plan the sections — key dates and events (exact years), named individuals and their roles, key terms and definitions, second-order concept judgements (e.g. most significant cause, greatest point of change), and for thematic studies a change-across-eras tracker. These sections cover the structure of every History option.
  3. 3
    Build the page using the lesson as source — write in your own words. If you cannot paraphrase it, you do not understand it yet.
  4. 4
    Turn the page face-down and reconstruct it — blank paper, no notes. Fill in as much as you can. This converts the note-making activity into retrieval practice.
  5. 5
    Compare and mark in red — every item you missed gets circled. Those circles are tomorrow’s revision targets.
  6. 6
    Repeat at spaced intervals — reconstruct the same organiser on day 3, day 7, day 14. Each attempt should take less time and produce fewer red circles.
Example 1 — Depth study knowledge organiser (Elizabethan Age or Germany 1919–1939)

Build a one-page organiser for your British or non-British depth study. Sections: (1) Chronology — 8–10 key events in date order, each with the exact year. For Germany: Weimar Republic founded (1919), Munich Putsch (1923), Wall Street Crash impact (1929), Hitler Chancellor (1933), Enabling Act (1933), Night of the Long Knives (1934), Anschluss (1938), Kristallnacht (1938). (2) Named figures and roles — for Germany: Hindenburg (President who appointed Hitler), Rohm (SA leader, Night of the Long Knives), Goebbels (propaganda). (3) Key terms — Lebensraum, Reichstag fire, Gestapo, NEP, perestroika (for USSR options). (4) Second-order judgement — “Most significant cause of Hitler’s rise: economic crisis — because without mass unemployment Nazi promises of jobs and order would have had no audience.” Reconstruct on day 3 — the dates and specialist vocabulary are consistently the first sections students fail.

Example 2 — Thematic study knowledge organiser with three-era change tracker

Build a one-page organiser for your thematic study (Crime & Punishment, Health & Medicine, Warfare, or Entertainment & Leisure). Sections: (1) Three-era change tracker — one row per era (Medieval, Early Modern, Modern), columns for: key crime/health issue/warfare method/leisure form, key response/treatment/weapon/venue, key turning point and date. (2) Named Acts, battles and individuals per era. (3) Historic environment link — for Crime & Punishment: Policing in Liverpool — what the site shows about policing development, and how it connects to the modern era column. (4) Change vs continuity judgements — “Greatest point of change in Health & Medicine: Germ Theory 1861 (Pasteur) — because it replaced miasma theory and made targeted treatment scientifically possible for the first time.” The historic environment link is the section most often missing in student organis ers, and it always carries marks.

Common Pitfalls

  • Making it too long. If it doesn’t fit on one A4 side, split it into two topics. Length signals you haven’t condensed the content yet.
  • Copying instead of paraphrasing. If you paste sentences from the lesson word-for-word, you are not processing — you are transcribing. Rephrase everything.
  • Never reconstructing from memory. A knowledge organiser you don’t rebuild from scratch is just a note. The reconstruction is the revision.
  • Building all pages at once. Spreading organiser-building across the year — one page per lesson — works far better than building ten pages the week before the exam.

When to Use This

Build each organiser within a day of studying the lesson — while the material is fresh enough to paraphrase. Then use spaced reconstruction to keep the knowledge active. For History, the highest-value organisers to build are: one per depth study option (key dates, named figures, specialist vocabulary, top second-order judgement); one per period study unit (chronological anchor points, turning points, change vs continuity judgements); and one per thematic study era (key evidence per era, the change/continuity verdict, the historic environment site link). The thematic study organisers are particularly important because the 12-mark and 16-mark essays demand confident movement across all three eras simultaneously.

Quick Reference
~30 min build + 10 min per reconstruction

Five sections

  1. Key dates & events (exact years)
  2. Named figures & roles
  3. Key terms & definitions
  4. Second-order judgements
  5. Thematic era change tracker

Active recall

Retrieval Practice

Test yourself — don’t just re-read.

What the Research Says

Retrieval practice is the act of pulling information out of your memory, rather than pushing it in. It sounds simple but it is the most powerful revision technique we have — stronger than highlighting, stronger than re-reading, stronger than watching videos. The harder the retrieval feels, the more your long-term memory is strengthening.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Roediger & Karpicke (2006)Students who self-tested once remembered 50% more a week later than those who re-read four times.Self-testing > re-reading, even when it feels harder.
Karpicke & Blunt (2011)Retrieval practice beat concept-mapping and elaborative study on a delayed test by ~50%.Works better than other “active” strategies that feel productive.
Agarwal et al. (2017)Low-stakes retrieval quizzes raised GCSE-equivalent test scores by an average of one grade.Short regular quizzing moves your real exam score.
Smith et al. (2016)Students who practised retrieval scored higher even on questions testing information they didn’t specifically retrieve.Builds the skill of remembering itself, not just the facts.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Study a chunk of content — read through a StudyVault lesson, watch a video, or cover a topic in class. Don’t try to memorise. Just understand.
  2. 2
    Close everything — book shut, tab closed, notes flipped over. The whole point is that you cannot see the material.
  3. 3
    Write down everything you can remember — no looking back. This is called a “brain dump.” Write until you run out. It should feel uncomfortable.
  4. 4
    Check against the source — open the lesson. Mark what you missed in a different colour. Don’t just glance — properly compare.
  5. 5
    Target the gaps — re-study only the parts you missed. Not the whole lesson again. Just the holes.
  6. 6
    Retest tomorrow — hit the same topic again within 24 hours. The second attempt is where the learning locks in.
Example 1

After studying the title sequence of Singin’ in the Rain, close the book and write down from memory: three specific cinematographic choices Donen and Kelly make during the rain number (camera height, shot distance, camera movement), three mise-en-scène elements (Kelly’s costume, the studio-set rain effect, the glistening wet pavement), and the audience effect of the famous puddle-jumping shot. Then sketch the iconic medium shot from memory and label the key visual elements. Mark against your notes and redo any element you missed the following day.

Example 2

After covering Todorov’s narrative equilibrium theory, close everything and brain-dump the five stages from memory — equilibrium, disruption, recognition, repair, new equilibrium — with one specific example from Skyfall for each stage (for instance: the disruption when the hard drive containing agents’ identities is stolen). Check your examples against the lesson and note which stage you struggled to anchor to a film event; test yourself on it again the next day.

Common Pitfalls

  • Peeking. If you look back during the brain dump, you’re not doing retrieval — you’re doing copying. Harder is better.
  • Only doing it once. One pass strengthens memory a little. Spaced repeats strengthen it permanently. Come back to the same topic 2–3 times over a week.
  • Doing it too soon after studying. If you retrieve while the material is still in short-term memory, it’s too easy to count. Leave at least 30 minutes between studying and testing.
  • Stopping when it feels difficult. Desirable difficulty is the whole point. If it feels easy, your memory isn’t being challenged and you’re not learning.

When to Use This

Build it in every week, from the start of Year 10 through to your exams. Aim for 15–20 minutes per subject, two or three times a week. The last two weeks before an exam is when retrieval practice becomes your main tool — swap passive watching for brain dumps and flashcards. On StudyVault, the Knowledge Check and Flashcard buttons in every lesson sidebar are retrieval practice in disguise — use them.

Quick Reference
~20 minutes per topic

Steps

  1. Study one topic
  2. Close everything
  3. Brain dump from memory
  4. Check gaps
  5. Re-study only the gaps
  6. Retest tomorrow

Active recall

Retrieval Practice

Test yourself, don't just re-read

What the Research Says

Retrieval practice means pulling information out of your memory rather than putting it back in. Every time you successfully recall a fact, the memory trace gets stronger. Re-reading your notes feels productive, but it creates a false sense of confidence — the information looks familiar without actually being learned.

Evidence Base

Study Finding Impact
Roediger & Karpicke (2006) Students who practised retrieval remembered 80% after one week; those who re-read remembered 36% More than double the retention
Dunlosky et al. (2013) Major review of 10 revision strategies rated practice testing as HIGH utility One of only two top-rated techniques
Karpicke & Blunt (2011) Retrieval practice outperformed concept mapping for learning science texts Works even for complex material
EEF Cognitive Science Report (2021) Recommended retrieval practice as one of six key principles for effective learning Endorsed for UK classroom use

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Read one topic — Spend 5 minutes reading through a single lesson or section. Don't highlight or make notes yet — just read to understand.
  2. 2
    Close your notes — Put everything away. No peeking. This is the crucial moment where learning actually happens.
  3. 3
    Brain dump on a blank page — Write down everything you can remember about the topic. Use bullet points, sketches, equations — whatever comes to mind. Aim for 5–8 minutes.
  4. 4
    Check and highlight gaps — Open your notes and compare. Use a different colour pen to fill in anything you missed or got wrong. These gaps are your priority for next time.
  5. 5
    Repeat on the gaps — Next session, focus your retrieval attempt on the parts you couldn't remember. Keep cycling until the gaps are filled.

When and How Often

Read
5 min Brain dump
8 min Check gaps
5 min

One full cycle takes about 18 minutes. Do 2–3 cycles per revision session, covering different topics. Use retrieval practice every time you revise — it should be your default method, not an occasional extra.

First attempt — from memory only

The atomic model changed over time. First there was a solid sphere model — I think that was Dalton. Then Thomson discovered the electron and made a plum-pudding model. Rutherford did an experiment that showed there was a nucleus in the middle. Then Bohr added orbits. Chadwick discovered neutrons at some point. The modern model has a nucleus with protons and neutrons, and electrons in shells or energy levels.

After checking — gaps filled in green

The atomic model changed over time. Dalton (early 1800s) proposed a solid sphere — all matter made of indivisible atoms. Thomson (1897) discovered the electron using cathode rays, producing the plum-pudding model (positive "dough" with negative electrons embedded). Rutherford (1909–1911) fired alpha particles at gold foil — most passed straight through, but some bounced back at large angles, proving there is a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus. Bohr (1913) refined this by proposing that electrons orbit the nucleus in fixed energy levels (shells) and can move between them by absorbing or emitting specific amounts of energy. Chadwick (1932) discovered the neutron by bombarding beryllium with alpha particles, explaining why the nucleus was heavier than protons alone could account for. The modern model treats electrons as a cloud of probability rather than fixed orbits.

What this reveals: The first attempt had the sequence right but missed every date and the mechanism of each discovery. Dates (1897, 1909–11, 1913, 1932) and the gold-foil experiment details become the focus of the next retrieval cycle.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Re-reading instead of recalling — Reading your notes five times feels like revision but barely strengthens memory. Close the book and test yourself.
  • ❌
    Peeking at notes too soon — The struggle to remember is the point. If you look at your notes the moment you get stuck, you skip the part that builds memory.
  • ❌
    Only testing what you already know — It feels good to recall easy facts, but the real gains come from practising the topics you find hardest.
  • ❌
    Not returning to the same topic — One brain dump is a start, not the finish. You need to revisit each topic multiple times at increasing intervals (see Spaced Repetition).

Scheduling

Spaced Repetition

Spread it out over days and weeks

What the Research Says

Your brain forgets things on a predictable curve. Hermann Ebbinghaus discovered this in 1885: without review, you lose about 70% of new information within 24 hours. But each time you revisit material at the right moment — just as you're about to forget — the memory becomes stronger and lasts longer. This is the spacing effect, and it's one of the most reliable findings in all of psychology.

Evidence Base

Study Finding Impact
Ebbinghaus (1885) Discovered the forgetting curve — memory decays exponentially without review Foundation of all spacing research
Cepeda et al. (2006) Meta-analysis of 254 studies confirmed spacing produces stronger long-term retention than massing Effect holds across ages and subjects
Dunlosky et al. (2013) Distributed (spaced) practice rated HIGH utility across all learning contexts One of only two top-rated techniques
Bjork & Bjork (1992) "Desirable difficulties" — spacing feels harder but produces deeper learning Explains why cramming feels effective but isn't

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    List all your topics — Write out every lesson across Biology, Chemistry, and Physics. You have around 22 lessons — this is your master list.
  2. 2
    Build a 6-week timetable — Start at least 6 weeks before your exam. Schedule 2–3 topics per day, 30–45 minutes per session.
  3. 3
    Schedule at increasing intervals — After studying a topic, schedule it again at Day 1, Day 3, Day 7, Day 14, then Day 30. Each review gets shorter because you remember more.
  4. 4
    Traffic-light after each test — After each retrieval attempt, rate the topic: Green (confident), Amber (some gaps), Red (major gaps). Reds get shorter intervals; greens can be spaced further apart.
  5. 5
    Adjust your spacing — Move green topics to longer gaps (14–30 days). Keep red topics on short cycles (1–3 days) until they turn amber or green.

When and How Often

Day 1
Study Day 2
Review Day 4
Review Day 8
Review Day 22
Review

Plan once, then follow the schedule daily. Each review session uses retrieval practice (brain dumps or self-quizzing) — not re-reading. Start 6–8 weeks before your exam to give every topic at least 4 review cycles.

Week 1 — Initial study + Day 1 review

Monday: Study rates of reaction for 20 minutes. Brain dump key facts: rate increases with temperature (more particles have activation energy), concentration (more collisions per second), surface area (more particles exposed), and catalyst (provides alternative pathway with lower activation energy). PAG C3 used marble chips and HCl — measured CO₂ volume over time using a gas syringe.

Tuesday: 10-minute retrieval — write down everything from yesterday. Rate: Amber (forgot the catalyst mechanism and the PAG method details).

Week 1 — Day 3 review

Thursday: 10-minute retrieval. Better recall of factors. Still fuzzy on why increasing temperature also increases the rate at which particles react (not just collision frequency). Rate: Amber.

Week 2 — Day 7 review

Monday: 8-minute retrieval. Now confident on all four factors and the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution link. Can describe the marble chips/HCl PAG and identify independent, dependent, and control variables. Rate: Green. Move to 14-day gap.

Week 4 — Day 21 review

Monday: 5-minute retrieval. Still solid. Quick check confirms all key content intact. Rate: Green. Final review scheduled for exam week.

Total time spent on this one topic: about 53 minutes spread over 6 weeks — far more effective than cramming it all in one sitting the night before.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Cramming the night before — Massed practice creates short-term familiarity that fades within days. Spacing the same time across weeks produces lasting memory.
  • ❌
    Revising the same topic every day — Daily repetition of the same material gives diminishing returns. Space it out and use the gaps to study other topics.
  • ❌
    Ignoring weaker topics — It's tempting to keep reviewing what you already know. Use the traffic-light system to force yourself back to red topics.
  • ❌
    Starting too late — Spacing only works if you start early enough to fit in multiple review cycles. Six weeks is the minimum; eight is better.

Deep thinking

Elaborative Interrogation

Ask "why?" and "how?" to deepen understanding

What the Research Says

Most students revise by memorising facts: equations, definitions, names. But science exams reward explanation — you need to say WHY things happen and HOW they connect. Elaborative interrogation forces you to ask these questions while revising, which builds the deeper understanding that turns a basic answer into a top-band response.

Evidence Base

Study Finding Impact
Pressley et al. (1987) Students who asked "why?" while reading recalled 72% of material, vs. 37% for those who just read Nearly double the recall
Dunlosky et al. (2013) Rated elaborative interrogation as MODERATE utility — highly effective when students already have some background knowledge Ideal for revision (not first learning)
Chi et al. (1994) Self-explanation — explaining material to yourself — produced better learning than simply studying examples Explaining builds understanding

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Read a section of your notes — Pick one lesson or part of a lesson. Read through it once to remind yourself of the content.
  2. 2
    Stop at each key fact — Every time you hit an important equation, observation, or claim, pause. Don't just move on.
  3. 3
    Ask "Why?" or "How?" — Why does this happen? How does this link to a concept you already know? Why was this experiment designed this way? How does changing one variable affect the others?
  4. 4
    Answer from memory first — Try to explain the answer in your own words before checking your notes. Write it down in one or two sentences.
  5. 5
    Build a causal chain — Link your "why" answers together: A happens because of B, which leads to C, which causes D. This is exactly the kind of analysis science examiners reward.
  6. 6
    Self-test — Close your notes and try to reconstruct the causal chain from memory. Check for gaps.

When and How Often

Read
3 min Why/How
6 min Chain
4 min Test
2 min

Each topic takes about 15 minutes with this method. Use it after you've already studied a topic at least once — you need some background knowledge for the "why" questions to work. Best combined with retrieval practice: do a brain dump first, then use elaborative interrogation on the parts you recalled.

Fact → Why question → Answer

Fact: A spring obeys Hooke's Law — the extension is directly proportional to the force applied, up to the limit of proportionality.

Why? Why does the relationship break down beyond the limit of proportionality?

Answer: Within the limit of proportionality, the bonds between atoms in the spring stretch but the internal structure stays intact. Beyond this point, the spring is permanently deformed — the atoms are displaced far enough that they cannot return to their original positions, so the extension is no longer proportional to the force. This is called the elastic limit.

Building the causal chain

How does PAG P4 (Hooke's Law investigation) test this? → Masses are added to a spring in steps; extension is measured with a ruler after each mass. A force–extension graph is plotted. The straight-line section shows proportionality; the curve shows where the limit has been exceeded.

Why is the area under a force–extension graph important? → It equals the elastic potential energy stored in the spring: E = ½ke², where k is the spring constant. A stiffer spring (larger k) stores more energy for the same extension.

How does this link to energy conservation? → When the spring is released, elastic potential energy converts to kinetic energy, then to other forms — demonstrating the conservation of energy principle.

Complete causal chain

Force applied → spring extends proportionally (Hooke's Law) → limit of proportionality reached → permanent deformation → elastic potential energy stored (E = ½ke²) → energy released as kinetic energy when spring returns → energy conserved throughout

Why this works: Instead of just memorising F = ke, you now understand the underlying physics — exactly what "explain" and "describe and explain" questions demand.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Only asking "what" questions — "What is Hooke's Law?" tests recall but doesn't build understanding. Always push to "why" and "how".
  • ❌
    Accepting vague answers — "Because the force increases" is not an explanation. Push yourself to give specific mechanistic reasons.
  • ❌
    Skipping the self-test — Building the causal chain is only half the work. You need to close your notes and reconstruct it from memory to lock it in.
  • ❌
    Not connecting across lessons — The best causal chains link concepts from different topics. Hooke's Law connects to energy stores, which connects to conservation of energy across all of Physics.

Mixed practice

Interleaving

Mix topics to strengthen recall

What the Research Says

Most students study one topic at a time until they feel confident, then move on. This is called "blocking". Interleaving is the opposite: you deliberately mix different topics within the same session. It feels harder and less productive, but research consistently shows it produces better long-term retention and the ability to tell different types of questions apart in the exam.

Evidence Base

Study Finding Impact
Rohrer & Taylor (2007) Students who interleaved practice scored 43% higher on a delayed test than those who blocked 43% improvement in scores
Kornell & Bjork (2008) Students felt they learned more from blocking, but actually performed better after interleaving — a metacognitive illusion Feeling harder ≠ less effective
Dunlosky et al. (2013) Rated interleaved practice as MODERATE utility — particularly effective for learning to discriminate between problem types Helps identify question types in exams

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Choose 3 topics from different sciences — Pick one from Biology, one from Chemistry, one from Physics. The more different they are, the stronger the interleaving effect.
  2. 2
    12 minutes per topic with retrieval practice — For each topic, do a quick brain dump (5 min), check gaps (3 min), then answer one practice question from memory (4 min). Then switch.
  3. 3
    Switch between topics — After 12 minutes, move to the next topic even if you don't feel "done". The switch is the point — it forces your brain to reload different information.
  4. 4
    End with a mixed quiz — In the final 9 minutes, answer one question from each of the three topics. This tests your ability to retrieve the right knowledge for the right question — exactly what your exam demands.

When and How Often

Topic 1
12 min Topic 2
12 min Topic 3
12 min Mixed quiz
9 min

A full interleaved session takes about 45 minutes. Use this 2–3 times per week in the final 4 weeks before the exam. It works best once you've already studied each topic at least once — interleaving is for strengthening and connecting, not for first-time learning.

Block 1: Biology — Cell Division (12 min)

Brain dump (5 min): Mitosis — 4 phases (PMAT), produces 2 genetically identical daughter cells, diploid. Used for growth and repair. Meiosis — 2 divisions, produces 4 haploid gametes, genetic variation through crossing over and independent assortment. DNA replication occurs before division. Working Scientifically link: WS1.2 — cells viewed under a microscope (PAG B1).

Gap check (3 min): Missed — specific names of mitosis stages (prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase) and the difference between homologous chromosomes and chromatids.

Quick question (4 min): "Explain why meiosis produces genetic variation." Wrote two sentences from memory.

Block 2: Chemistry — Electrolysis (12 min)

Brain dump (5 min): Electrolysis uses electricity to decompose an ionic compound. Requires molten or dissolved ionic compound. Cathode (−) → cations reduced. Anode (+) → anions oxidised. Electrolysis of brine: chlorine at anode, hydrogen at cathode, sodium hydroxide left in solution. PAG C5 involves electrolysis.

Gap check (3 min): Missed — half equations for each electrode; why graphite or platinum electrodes are used (inert, don't react).

Quick question (4 min): "Write a half equation for the production of chlorine at the anode."

Block 3: Physics — Waves (12 min)

Brain dump (5 min): Transverse waves — vibration perpendicular to direction of travel (light, water). Longitudinal — vibration parallel (sound). Wave speed = frequency × wavelength. Ripple tank (PAG P7) measures wave speed. Waves refract when they change speed at a boundary. Diffraction — waves spread around obstacles.

Gap check (3 min): Missed — how a ripple tank is set up (vibrating bar, strobe to freeze image), and that the angle of refraction depends on the change in speed.

Quick question (4 min): "Describe how you would measure the speed of waves using a ripple tank."

Mixed quiz (9 min) — 3 minutes each

Q1 (Biology): State two differences between mitosis and meiosis. Answered well.

Q2 (Chemistry): Why must an ionic compound be molten or dissolved for electrolysis to work? Got it — ions must be free to move.

Q3 (Physics): Calculate wave speed if frequency = 50 Hz and wavelength = 2 m. v = 100 m/s — correct.

Why this works: Switching between Biology, Chemistry, and Physics forces your brain to reload fresh knowledge each time, rather than coasting on short-term familiarity. The mixed quiz at the end mimics your exam, where you move between different papers.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Studying one subject all session — Blocking feels productive because you get "into the zone", but the comfort is a sign your brain isn't working hard enough to build lasting memory.
  • ❌
    Switching every 2 minutes — Too-fast switching doesn't give you time to engage meaningfully with each topic. Aim for 10–15 minutes per block.
  • ❌
    Only interleaving within one science — Mixing three Biology lessons is better than blocking, but mixing across Biology, Chemistry, and Physics gives the strongest effect because the topics are most different.
  • ❌
    Giving up because it feels harder — Interleaving should feel harder than blocking. That difficulty is the signal that deeper learning is happening. Trust the research.

Summarising

Knowledge Organisers

Condense each topic onto one page

What the Research Says

A knowledge organiser is a single A4 page that contains all the essential information for one topic: key definitions, equations, processes, and required practicals. The real value isn't the finished page — it's the process of creating it from memory. When you decide what to include, how to organise it, and fill it in without looking at your notes, you're combining summarising, retrieval practice, and organisation into one activity.

Evidence Base

Study Finding Impact
Fiorella & Mayer (2016) Generative learning — students learn better when they create their own summaries rather than receiving pre-made ones Making it yourself matters
Dunlosky et al. (2013) Summarisation alone rated LOW utility, but combined with self-testing it becomes much more effective Must test from it, not just create it
EEF Cognitive Science Report (2021) Recommended structured knowledge organisers as tools for building substantive knowledge Endorsed for GCSE science

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Read one lesson — Go through the full lesson page once to refresh your memory. Pay attention to key fact boxes, equations, and glossary terms.
  2. 2
    Set up your A4 page with sections — Divide the page into a grid with these headings: Key Definitions, Key Equations, Key Processes / Mechanisms, Required Practical (PAG), Common Exam Questions.
  3. 3
    Fill it in from memory first — Close your notes and write what you can remember in each section. This is retrieval practice built into the process.
  4. 4
    Check and complete in a different colour — Open your notes and fill in anything you missed using a different colour pen. The colour difference shows you exactly what you didn't know.
  5. 5
    Self-test from it — In your next revision session, cover the knowledge organiser and try to recreate it from memory. Alternatively, use it to quiz yourself: cover one column and try to recall what's there.

When and How Often

Read
5 min Set up
3 min Fill in
15 min Check
5 min Test
7 min

Creating one knowledge organiser takes about 35 minutes. Aim to create one per revision session. Over 6 weeks you can build a complete set — one per lesson — covering all three sciences. Then use them as retrieval practice tools.

Key Definitions

Ohmic conductor — a component where current is directly proportional to voltage (constant resistance) at constant temperature
Resistance — opposition to the flow of current, measured in ohms (Ω)
LDR — light-dependent resistor; resistance decreases as light intensity increases
Thermistor — resistance decreases as temperature increases

Key Equations

V = IR (voltage = current × resistance)
P = IV (power = current × voltage)
P = I²R (power = current² × resistance)
E = Pt (energy = power × time)

Key Processes / Mechanisms

• Series circuit: same current throughout, voltages add up, total R = R₁ + R₂
• Parallel circuit: voltage same across branches, currents add up, total R is less than smallest branch
• Non-ohmic conductors (filament bulb, diode): resistance changes with temperature or direction

Required Practical (PAG P3)

Investigate how resistance varies with length of wire. Variables: independent = length (cm), dependent = resistance (Ω), control = wire material and cross-sectional area, temperature. Method: connect wire in series with ammeter; voltmeter in parallel. Calculate R = V/I. Plot graph — should be linear through origin.

Common Exam Questions

• Calculate resistance from V and I readings
• Explain why a filament bulb is not ohmic
• Describe how an LDR is used in a circuit (e.g. automatic street light)
• Compare series and parallel circuits

What the colours reveal: The second-colour additions clustered in Key Equations and the PAG method — showing these need more practice in future retrieval sessions.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Copying from notes instead of recalling — If you fill it in while looking at your notes, you're just rewriting, not learning. The retrieval step is where the memory is built.
  • ❌
    Making it too detailed — One A4 page is the limit. If you can't fit it on one page, you're including too much. The constraint forces you to identify what really matters.
  • ❌
    Creating but never testing from it — A knowledge organiser in a folder is just a piece of paper. You must use it for self-testing in future sessions to get the full benefit.
  • ❌
    Using someone else's instead of making your own — Pre-made knowledge organisers skip the generative learning process. The act of deciding what to include and organising it is where most of the learning happens.

Exam readiness

Timed Practice

Write like it's the real thing

What the Research Says

Knowing the content is not enough — you also need to practise applying it under exam conditions. Timed practice combines retrieval (recalling knowledge), application (using the right exam structure), and time management. Examiner reports repeatedly highlight the same weaknesses: running out of time, not answering the question asked, and failing to show working in calculations. The only way to fix these is practice.

Evidence Base

Study Finding Impact
Dunlosky et al. (2013) Practice testing rated HIGH utility — one of the two most effective revision strategies across all research Top-rated technique
Roediger & Karpicke (2006) Transfer-appropriate processing — practising in the same format as the test produces the best results Practice under exam conditions
Examiner reports Recurring weaknesses: students don't show working in calculations, run out of time on long-answer questions, and describe instead of explain Timed practice directly addresses these

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Choose a practice question — Use the practice questions on each lesson page. Make sure you know which question type it is (recall, calculation, "explain", "evaluate") so you can use the right approach.
  2. 2
    Set your timer — Use the correct time allocation: roughly 1 minute per mark. A 2-mark question = 2 min; a 6-mark "explain" = 6 min; a 6-mark calculation = 6 min. Start the timer before you write anything.
  3. 3
    Write without notes — Closed-book only. This is retrieval practice in exam format. If you can't remember something in a written question, leave a gap and move on. For calculations, show all working — even partial working earns marks.
  4. 4
    Stop when the timer ends — Even if you haven't finished. Learning to work within the time limit is part of the skill. Note where you ran out.
  5. 5
    Self-mark against the mark scheme — Use the model answers on the lesson page or your exam's mark scheme. Be honest about which marks you would and wouldn't earn.
  6. 6
    Note 2–3 specific improvements — Don't just write "do better". Identify exactly what would gain more marks: missing a key term? Forgot to include units? Didn't link cause to effect?

When and How Often

Pick Q
1 min Write under timed conditions
2–8 min Self-mark
5 min Notes
3 min

Practise 2–3 timed answers per week in the final 4 weeks before the exam. Vary the question types — don't just practise your favourites. Use roughly 1 minute per mark and stick to it strictly.

Question (timer set to 6 minutes)

"A transformer has 500 turns on the primary coil and 2000 turns on the secondary coil. The input voltage is 25 V. Calculate the output voltage and state whether this is a step-up or step-down transformer. Then explain why transformers are used in the National Grid." [6 marks]

Calculation part (3 min)

Using Vp/Vs = Np/Ns:
25/Vs = 500/2000
Vs = 25 × (2000/500) = 25 × 4 = 100 V
This is a step-up transformer (output voltage greater than input voltage, more turns on secondary).

Explain part (3 min)

Transformers are used in the National Grid because transmitting electricity at very high voltage reduces the current. Since power loss in cables = I²R, reducing current dramatically reduces energy wasted as heat in the transmission cables. Step-up transformers at power stations increase the voltage (and reduce current) for long-distance transmission. Step-down transformers near homes reduce the voltage to safe levels for domestic use.

Self-marking

Calculation: 2/2 — correct method, correct answer with unit.
Step-up identification: 1/1 — correct with reason.
Explain: 2/3 — explained I²R correctly and the step-up/step-down logic, but didn't explicitly state that P = IV means same power can be transmitted at lower current with higher voltage.
Improvements: (1) State P = IV to justify why high voltage = low current for same power. (2) Include that cables have resistance — this was implied but not explicit.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Writing without a timer — Untimed practice doesn't prepare you for exam conditions. If you always have "as long as you need", you'll run out of time on the real thing.
  • ❌
    Not showing working in calculations — Even if you get the wrong answer, you can earn method marks. A blank or "= 100 V" with no working scores nothing if the answer is wrong.
  • ❌
    Not self-marking — Writing an answer and moving on wastes half the learning opportunity. Self-marking against the mark scheme is where you identify what to improve.
  • ❌
    Only practising favourite question types — Students tend to avoid the questions they find hardest, which are exactly the ones that need the most practice. Make sure you practise all question types including 6-mark extended writing.
  • ❌
    Forgetting units — In science, an answer without a unit is often wrong. Build the habit of always checking: does this number need a unit? (V, A, Ω, W, J, m/s, etc.)

Maths skills

Practising Calculations

Drill equations until they're automatic

What the Research Says

Calculation questions are among the most predictable in your science exam — the equations are given (or can be learned), the method is fixed, and full marks are achievable through practice. Yet students regularly lose marks by forgetting to rearrange equations, omitting units, or making arithmetic errors. Deliberate practice of the full calculation process — not just memorising the formula — closes these gaps.

Evidence Base

Study Finding Impact
Ericsson et al. (1993) Deliberate practice — focused repetition with feedback — produces expertise faster than unstructured practice Quality of practice matters, not just quantity
Sweller (1988) — Cognitive Load Theory Worked examples reduce cognitive load; once the method is automatised, problem-solving speed increases First study worked examples, then practise independently
Roediger & Karpicke (2006) Retrieval practice beats re-reading even for procedural skills — practising calculations is more effective than re-reading how to do them Do problems, don't just read solutions

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Write out the equation from memory — Before you see the numbers, write the equation. If you can't recall it, note this as a gap. Then write the rearranged versions too (e.g. V = IR → I = V/R → R = V/I).
  2. 2
    Identify what you're solving for — Read the question, highlight the known values and the unknown. This prevents substituting into the wrong form.
  3. 3
    Check units before substituting — Convert any values that aren't in standard units (e.g. km → m, kΩ → Ω, minutes → seconds). Write the conversion step explicitly.
  4. 4
    Substitute and calculate — Show every line of working. Write the equation, substitution, rearrangement, and final answer on separate lines. Do not skip steps.
  5. 5
    State the answer with the correct unit — A number without a unit is incomplete. Check whether the answer seems physically reasonable (e.g. a resistance of 5,000,000 Ω for a household circuit is a red flag).
  6. 6
    Mark your own answer and note the error type — Wrong formula? Wrong rearrangement? Unit conversion error? Arithmetic slip? Each error type has a specific fix.

When and How Often

Write eq.
2 min Solve
4 min Mark
2 min Note
1 min

One calculation cycle takes about 9 minutes. Do 3–4 calculations per session, covering different equations and different sciences. Practise all variants: solve for each variable in the equation, not just the most common one. Aim for at least 2 calculation sessions per week in the 4 weeks before your exam.

Step 1: Write the equation from memory

Wave speed = frequency × wavelength
v = f × λ
Rearranged: f = v/λ and λ = v/f

Step 2: Question

"In a ripple tank experiment, a student uses a strobe to observe waves. The frequency of the waves is 4.0 Hz and the wavelength is measured as 2.5 cm. Calculate the wave speed."

Known: f = 4.0 Hz, λ = 2.5 cm = 0.025 m
Unknown: v

Step 3: Unit check

λ is given in cm — must convert to metres: 2.5 cm ÷ 100 = 0.025 m. Frequency is already in Hz (s⁻¹). ✔

Step 4: Substitution and calculation

v = f × λ
v = 4.0 × 0.025
v = 0.10 m/s

Step 5: Answer with unit

Wave speed = 0.10 m/s

Step 6: Self-mark and error check

Correct. Common errors here: (1) forgetting to convert cm to m — gives answer of 10 m/s (100× too large); (2) multiplying frequency by wavelength the wrong way round if confused about which variable is which. Writing the equation first prevents both.

Common Mistakes

  • ❌
    Not converting units before substituting — Substituting cm for m or kJ for J is the most common calculation error in science exams. Always check units first, every time.
  • ❌
    Skipping working — If you write only the answer and it's wrong, you score zero. If you show the equation and correct substitution, you can still earn method marks even with an arithmetic error.
  • ❌
    Only practising the most common variable — Your exam will ask you to solve for any variable. If you only ever practise "find v" in v = fλ, you'll struggle when asked to "find λ". Practise all three forms of every equation.
  • ❌
    Forgetting the unit in the final answer — A bare number is often marked wrong. Build the habit: finish every calculation by writing the number, then the unit.
  • ❌
    Practising only easy questions — If every calculation you attempt takes 30 seconds, you're not building resilience for the harder multi-step problems. Deliberately include questions where you need to rearrange and convert.

Structured notes

Knowledge Organisers

One page per topic — the whole picture at a glance.

What the Research Says

A knowledge organiser is a single side of A4 that captures everything a student needs to know about a topic — key vocabulary, essential facts, core concepts, and connections between them. Used properly, it becomes the base layer of your revision: the thing you keep coming back to, the thing you redraw from memory, the thing you carry on the bus. Used badly, it becomes a wall of dense text that nobody reads.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Willingham (2017)Students need to store facts in long-term memory before they can think critically about them. Knowledge organisers are the storage scaffold.Not old-fashioned — cognitive prerequisite for analysis.
Counsell (2018)Used in UK schools to reduce cognitive load by pre-structuring the material students encounter.Reduces working memory demand during lessons.
Sweller (1988)Cognitive Load Theory: well-organised schemas free up working memory for higher-order tasks.A well-designed organiser makes hard questions easier.
Oakes & Griffin (2017)Students who made their OWN organisers outperformed those given finished ones.Making is learning. Receiving is not.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    One topic per organiser — one body system, one training principle, one mental strategy. Not a whole component. Too broad and it becomes a dense textbook page.
  2. 2
    Divide the page into 4–6 sections — typically: Key Vocabulary, Key Facts / Formulae, Core Concepts, Anatomical Examples, Connections to Performance. The structure forces you to categorise.
  3. 3
    Keep it to one side of A4 — the constraint is the point. If it doesn’t fit, the material isn’t yet compressed into the essentials.
  4. 4
    Use tiny structural visuals — a mini-skeleton outline, a lever diagram, a formula box. Dual coding applies: words + visuals beat words alone.
  5. 5
    Redraw it from memory weekly — this is where the learning is. A finished organiser you never revisit is wasted. The redrawn one is retrieval practice in disguise.
  6. 6
    Annotate over time — when you learn something new that fits, add it. When a connection becomes clearer, draw the link. The organiser evolves.
Example 1

Create one A4 organiser for each body system: skeletal (5 bone shapes + examples, 4 joint types + sites, key bones labelled), muscular (3 fibre types with speed/fatigue/sport, agonist/antagonist pairs, key muscles labelled), cardiovascular (CO = HR × SV with values, cardiac changes during exercise, blood redistribution), respiratory (lung volumes, gaseous exchange, breathing rate changes). Four organisers, one per system — the backbone of Component 1 revision.

Example 2

Build a “psychology terms” organiser for Component 2 that captures all the mental strategies (goal-setting, imagery, self-talk, arousal control) with a one-line definition and a sporting scenario for each. Add a second mini-section listing the barriers to participation (cost, access, social influences, disability) with one counter-strategy each. Redraw it without looking the night before the exam.

Common Pitfalls

  • Copying the textbook. A dense page of 8pt text isn’t a knowledge organiser — it’s a photocopy. Compress ruthlessly.
  • One page per component. Too much, too diffuse. One page per body system or topic area.
  • Making one and never revisiting. The value is in the redrawing — not the original creation.
  • Using a downloaded one instead of making your own. Research is clear: making beats receiving. Teacher-provided organisers are useful for structure only.

When to Use This

Start one at the beginning of each topic, as you’re learning it. Refine as your understanding grows. Redraw the whole set from memory in the final month before exams — one topic per day. Carry a folder of your organisers to every revision session. Use them as the spine of retrieval practice: cover the organiser, brain-dump, then check.

Active recall

Retrieval Practice

Test yourself — don’t just re-read.

What the Research Says

Retrieval practice is the act of pulling information out of your memory, rather than pushing it in. It sounds simple but it is the most powerful revision technique we have — stronger than highlighting, stronger than re-reading, stronger than watching videos. The harder the retrieval feels, the more your long-term memory is strengthening.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Roediger & Karpicke (2006)Students who self-tested once remembered 50% more a week later than those who re-read four times.Self-testing > re-reading, even when it feels harder.
Karpicke & Blunt (2011)Retrieval practice beat concept-mapping and elaborative study on a delayed test by ~50%.Works better than other “active” strategies that feel productive.
Agarwal et al. (2017)Low-stakes retrieval quizzes raised test scores by an average of one grade.Short regular quizzing moves your real exam score.
Smith et al. (2016)Students who practised retrieval scored higher even on questions testing information they didn’t specifically retrieve.Builds the skill of remembering itself, not just the facts.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Study a chunk of content — read through a lesson, watch a video, or cover a topic in class. Don’t try to memorise. Just understand.
  2. 2
    Close everything — book shut, tab closed, notes flipped over. The whole point is that you cannot see the material.
  3. 3
    Write down everything you can remember — no looking back. This is called a “brain dump.” Write until you run out. It should feel uncomfortable.
  4. 4
    Check against the source — open the lesson. Mark what you missed in a different colour. Don’t just glance — properly compare.
  5. 5
    Target the gaps — re-study only the parts you missed. Not the whole lesson again. Just the holes.
  6. 6
    Retest tomorrow — hit the same topic again within 24 hours. The second attempt is where the learning locks in.
Example 1 — Exact dates, treaties and Acts of Parliament

After studying the Hundred Years War or the Elizabethan period, close the lesson and write every named event from memory with its precise date: the Statute of Labourers (1351), the Treaty of Brétigny (1360), the Peasants’ Revolt (1381), the Armada (1588), the Poor Law (1601). Next to each, add the named individual most closely associated with it. Examiners award marks only for accurate factual recall, so a date one year out or a misspelled name can cost you. Precision matters far more than volume — ten facts you know cold beat thirty you half-know. Check back and highlight anything you misplaced by more than five years or misidentified the person behind.

Example 2 — Key terms and specialist vocabulary

Brain-dump specialist vocabulary completely from memory for one option. For Germany 1919–1939: Anschluss, Enabling Act, Kristallnacht, Lebensraum, the Reichstag fire and Night of the Long Knives with their dates and a one-sentence definition for each. For the thematic studies, terms like chevauchée (Hundred Years War tactics), recusancy (Elizabethan religious non-conformity) and perestroika (Soviet reform under Gorbachev) carry marks in both recall questions and the SPaG band of extended responses. Spell them correctly in your dump. Wait three days and retest cold.

Common Pitfalls

  • Peeking. If you look back during the brain dump, you’re not doing retrieval — you’re doing copying. Harder is better.
  • Only doing it once. One pass strengthens memory a little. Spaced repeats strengthen it permanently. Come back to the same topic 2–3 times over a week.
  • Doing it too soon after studying. If you retrieve while the material is still in short-term memory, it’s too easy to count. Leave at least 30 minutes between studying and testing.
  • Stopping when it feels difficult. Desirable difficulty is the whole point. If it feels easy, your memory isn’t being challenged and you’re not learning.

When to Use This

Build it in every week, from the start of your course through to your exams. Aim for 15–20 minutes per session, two or three times a week. The last two weeks before an exam is when retrieval practice becomes your main tool — swap passive reading for brain dumps and flashcards. On StudyVault, the Knowledge Check and Flashcard buttons in every lesson sidebar are retrieval practice in disguise — use them.

Quick Reference
~20 minutes per topic

Steps

  1. Study one topic
  2. Close everything
  3. Brain dump from memory
  4. Check gaps
  5. Re-study only the gaps
  6. Retest tomorrow
